reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System" /v PromptOnSecureDesktop /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System" /v FilterAdministratorToken /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System" /v EnableInstallerDetection /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System" /v EnableSecureUIAPaths /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System" /v EnableVirtualization /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System" /v EnableUIADesktopToggle /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

    SMB signing for the client and server:

    reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanWorkstation\Parameters" /v RequireSecuritySignature /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanWorkstation\Parameters" /v EnableSecuritySignature /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanWorkstation\Parameters" /v EnablePlainTextPassword /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters" /v RequireSecuritySignature /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters" /v EnableSecuritySignature /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

    SMB signing and old file servers

    Digitally sign communications (always) can break connections to very old SMB devices. On a CyberPatriot image this is fine unless the README describes connecting to a legacy share.

    #Settings that only secpol or secedit can change

    These live in [System Access] and have no registry value. Add them to a template and apply it with the secedit method:

    [System Access]
LSAAnonymousNameLookup = 0
ForceLogoffWhenHourExpire = 1
EnableGuestAccount = 0
EnableAdminAccount = 0

    Leave out EnableAdminAccount = 0 if whoami shows you are signed in as the built-in Administrator, or if no other admin account has a password you know.

    Verify

    Close and reopen secpol.msc and read the values back, or run reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa" and reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System".

    #User rights assignment

    secpol.msc > Local Policies > User Rights Assignment. Double-click a right, then Add User or Group or Remove. "No one" means remove every entry.

    User right Set to Notes
    Access Credential Manager as a trusted caller No one
    Access this computer from the network Administrators, Users (or Administrators, Remote Desktop Users) Remove Everyone and Guest. Keep Users or Authenticated Users if the README requires file sharing.
    Act as part of the operating system No one
    Allow log on locally Administrators, Users Never remove Administrators. Remove Guest.
    Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services Administrators, Remote Desktop Users (no one if RDP is not required)
    Back up files and directories Administrators Remove Backup Operators unless the README needs it, and any single user.
    Change the system time Administrators, LOCAL SERVICE
    Create a token object No one
    Create global objects Administrators, LOCAL SERVICE, NETWORK SERVICE, SERVICE
    Create permanent shared objects No one
    Create symbolic links Administrators
    Debug programs Administrators Anyone with this can read any process's memory, including passwords.
    Deny access to this computer from the network Guests
    Deny log on as a batch job Guests
    Deny log on as a service Guests
    Deny log on locally Guests Never add Users or Administrators.
    Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services Guests
    Enable computer and user accounts to be trusted for delegation No one
    Force shutdown from a remote system Administrators
    Impersonate a client after authentication Administrators, LOCAL SERVICE, NETWORK SERVICE, SERVICE
    Load and unload device drivers Administrators
    Lock pages in memory No one
    Manage auditing and security log Administrators
    Modify an object label No one
    Modify firmware environment values Administrators
    Perform volume maintenance tasks Administrators
    Profile single process Administrators
    Replace a process level token LOCAL SERVICE, NETWORK SERVICE
    Restore files and directories Administrators
    Shut down the system Administrators, Users
    Take ownership of files or other objects Administrators

    Do not lock yourself out

    Never remove Administrators from Allow log on locally, and never add Administrators, Users or Everyone to any Deny right. If you do and sign out, you cannot get back in.

    #Find planted user rights

    Planted vulnerabilities usually add one user or Everyone to a powerful right: Debug programs, Act as part of the operating system, Take ownership, Load and unload device drivers, Back up or Restore. Export the rights in elevated PowerShell and read the Se... lines:

    secedit /export /cfg "$env:TEMP\ur.inf" /areas USER_RIGHTS | Out-Null
Get-Content "$env:TEMP\ur.inf" | Select-String '^Se'

    Read the SIDs with this table. A plain username or a long *S-1-5-21-... SID is a single user and is usually the planted entry.

    SID in the export Means
    *S-1-5-32-544 Administrators
    *S-1-5-32-545 Users
    *S-1-5-32-546 Guests
    *S-1-5-32-551 Backup Operators
    *S-1-5-32-555 Remote Desktop Users
    *S-1-1-0 Everyone
    *S-1-5-11 Authenticated Users
    *S-1-5-19 LOCAL SERVICE
    *S-1-5-20 NETWORK SERVICE
    *S-1-5-6 SERVICE

    Remove the entry in secpol.msc > User Rights Assignment, or with the template below.

    #Set user rights with secedit

    Use this on Home edition or to fix many rights at once. Only the rights listed in the template change, and an empty value means No one. Back up first:

    secedit /export /cfg "$env:USERPROFILE\Documents\rights-backup.inf" /areas USER_RIGHTS | Out-Null

    Write the template:

    $inf = "$env:TEMP\rights.inf"
@'
[Unicode]
Unicode=yes
[Privilege Rights]
SeDebugPrivilege = *S-1-5-32-544
SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege = *S-1-5-32-544
SeLoadDriverPrivilege = *S-1-5-32-544
SeBackupPrivilege = *S-1-5-32-544
SeRestorePrivilege = *S-1-5-32-544
SeDenyInteractiveLogonRight = *S-1-5-32-546
SeDenyRemoteInteractiveLogonRight = *S-1-5-32-546
SeDenyNetworkLogonRight = *S-1-5-32-546
SeDenyBatchLogonRight = *S-1-5-32-546
SeDenyServiceLogonRight = *S-1-5-32-546
SeTcbPrivilege =
SeCreateTokenPrivilege =
SeTrustedCredManAccessPrivilege =
SeEnableDelegationPrivilege =
SeLockMemoryPrivilege =
[Version]
signature="$CHICAGO$"
Revision=1
'@ | Set-Content -Path $inf -Encoding Unicode

    Apply it:

    secedit /configure /db "$env:TEMP\rights.sdb" /cfg "$env:TEMP\rights.inf" /areas USER_RIGHTS

    Verify

    Close and reopen secpol.msc > User Rights Assignment and check the rights above. To restore the backup, run secedit /configure /db "$env:TEMP\restore.sdb" /cfg "$env:USERPROFILE\Documents\rights-backup.inf" /areas USER_RIGHTS.

    Other user right constant names
    Constant User right
    SeNetworkLogonRight Access this computer from the network
    SeInteractiveLogonRight Allow log on locally
    SeRemoteInteractiveLogonRight Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services
    SeShutdownPrivilege Shut down the system
    SeRemoteShutdownPrivilege Force shutdown from a remote system
    SeSecurityPrivilege Manage auditing and security log
    SeSystemEnvironmentPrivilege Modify firmware environment values
    SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege Create symbolic links
    SeCreatePermanentPrivilege Create permanent shared objects
    SeRelabelPrivilege Modify an object label
    SeImpersonatePrivilege Impersonate a client after authentication
    SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege Replace a process level token
    PreviousAudit policyNextWindows Defender Firewall
    W11

    Windows Defender Firewall

    jump:w11-firewall

    Never block outbound traffic

    Leave DefaultOutboundAction = Allow. Blocking outbound stops the scoring client from reporting and breaks Windows Update.

    Fast path

    1. Open PowerShell as administrator.

    2. Turn on all three profiles:

      Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Domain,Private,Public -Enabled True -DefaultInboundAction Block -DefaultOutboundAction Allow -NotifyOnListen True

    3. Turn on logging:

      Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Domain,Private,Public -LogAllowed True -LogBlocked True -LogMaxSizeKilobytes 16384 -LogFileName "$env:SystemRoot\System32\LogFiles\Firewall\pfirewall.log"

    4. List inbound allow rules with no group and remove the planted ones (how).

    5. Confirm all three profiles show True, Block, Allow:

      Get-NetFirewallProfile | Select-Object Name, Enabled, DefaultInboundAction, DefaultOutboundAction

    #Turn on all three profiles

    Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Domain,Private,Public -Enabled True -DefaultInboundAction Block -DefaultOutboundAction Allow -NotifyOnListen True

    netsh advfirewall set allprofiles state on
netsh advfirewall set allprofiles firewallpolicy blockinbound,allowoutbound

    Settings > Privacy & security > Windows Security > Firewall & network protection > turn on Domain network, Private network and Public network.

    Or Win+R > firewall.cpl > Turn Windows Defender Firewall on or off > Turn on for both private and public settings, and check "Notify me when Windows Defender Firewall blocks a new app".

    Verify

    Get-NetFirewallProfile | Select-Object Name, Enabled, DefaultInboundAction, DefaultOutboundAction shows Enabled True, Inbound Block and Outbound Allow on all three. In cmd, netsh advfirewall show allprofiles shows State ON and Firewall Policy BlockInbound,AllowOutbound.

    #Turn on firewall logging

    Logging is off by default. Turn on logging for dropped and allowed connections:

    Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Domain,Private,Public -LogAllowed True -LogBlocked True -LogMaxSizeKilobytes 16384 -LogFileName "$env:SystemRoot\System32\LogFiles\Firewall\pfirewall.log"

    netsh advfirewall set allprofiles logging droppedconnections enable
netsh advfirewall set allprofiles logging allowedconnections enable
netsh advfirewall set allprofiles logging maxfilesize 16384
netsh advfirewall set allprofiles logging filename %SystemRoot%\System32\LogFiles\Firewall\pfirewall.log

    Win+R > wf.msc > right-click Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security on Local Computer > Properties > on each of the Domain, Private and Public Profile tabs: Logging > Customize > Log dropped packets = Yes, Log successful connections = Yes > OK.

    Check with Get-NetFirewallProfile | Select-Object Name, LogAllowed, LogBlocked, LogFileName. The log file appears once traffic is logged.

    #Check the firewall services

    Get-Service mpssvc, BFE | Select-Object Name, Status, StartType

    Both must be Running and Automatic. If either is Disabled, fix it in elevated cmd. Start BFE first because the firewall depends on it:

    sc config BFE start= auto
sc config mpssvc start= auto
net start BFE
net start mpssvc

    In PowerShell, type sc.exe; plain sc there is an alias for Set-Content.

    #Firewall turns itself back off

    A policy is forcing the setting. Look at the effective result and at the policy key:

    Get-NetFirewallProfile -PolicyStore ActiveStore | Select-Object Name, Enabled, DefaultInboundAction

    reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\WindowsFirewall" /s

    Under DomainProfile, StandardProfile (private) and PublicProfile, EnableFirewall must be 1 or absent. Delete a planted 0, for example:

    reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\WindowsFirewall\PublicProfile" /v EnableFirewall /f

    Also check gpedit.msc > Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security, then run gpupdate /force.

    #Find suspicious inbound allow rules

    Built-in rules almost always have a group (DisplayGroup); planted rules usually do not. List enabled inbound allow rules with no group, with their ports and programs:

    Get-NetFirewallRule -Direction Inbound -Action Allow -Enabled True |
  Where-Object { -not $_.DisplayGroup } |
  ForEach-Object {
    $pf = $_ | Get-NetFirewallPortFilter
    $af = $_ | Get-NetFirewallApplicationFilter
    [pscustomobject]@{
      Name     = $_.DisplayName
      Profile  = $_.Profile
      Protocol = $pf.Protocol
      Port     = ($pf.LocalPort -join ',')
      Program  = $af.Program
    }
  } | Format-Table -AutoSize -Wrap

    Also list enabled inbound allow rules on risky ports (FTP, SSH, Telnet, TFTP, RPC, NetBIOS, SNMP, SMB, SQL, RDP, VNC, WinRM and common backdoor ports). This takes a few seconds:

    $risky = @('20','21','22','23','69','135','137','138','139','161','445','1433','3306','3389','4444','5900','5985','5986','6667','31337')
Get-NetFirewallPortFilter | Where-Object { @($_.LocalPort | Where-Object { $_ -in $risky }).Count -gt 0 } |
  Get-NetFirewallRule | Where-Object { $_.Enabled -eq 'True' -and $_.Direction -eq 'Inbound' -and $_.Action -eq 'Allow' } |
  Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayGroup, Profile

    In the GUI: wf.msc > Inbound Rules, sort by Group (blank groups first) and by Action. Suspicious signs are names like "nc", "backdoor" or "Allow All", program paths in C:\Users, C:\Temp or AppData, and Local port Any with Action Allow.

    Keep rules for README-required services

    If the README requires a web server, FTP, RDP or file sharing, its allow rule must stay. Remove only rules for things that are not required.

    #Disable or remove a rule

    Disable-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "<rule-name>"

    Remove-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "<rule-name>"

    netsh advfirewall firewall set rule name="<rule-name>" new enable=no

    netsh advfirewall firewall delete rule name="<rule-name>"

    wf.msc > Inbound Rules > right-click the rule > Disable Rule or Delete.

    Disable a whole built-in group, for example Remote Desktop when it is not required:

    Disable-NetFirewallRule -DisplayGroup "Remote Desktop"

    #Block a port or a program

    New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Block Telnet In" -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 23 -Action Block -Profile Any

    netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="Block Telnet In" dir=in action=block protocol=TCP localport=23

    Block a program by its full path:

    New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Block <app-name>" -Direction Inbound -Program "<path>" -Action Block

    A Block rule overrides an Allow rule for the same traffic.

    #Reset the firewall to defaults

    Last resort. A reset removes every custom rule, including rules that README-required services need. Export a backup first:

    netsh advfirewall export "%USERPROFILE%\Documents\fw-backup.wfw"

    netsh advfirewall reset

    Afterwards re-add the required rules and run the turn on all three profiles and logging commands again.

    PreviousSecurity options and user rightsNextMicrosoft Defender Antivirus
    W11

    Microsoft Defender Antivirus

    jump:w11-defender

    Fast path

    1. Open PowerShell as administrator.

    2. Look for planted policy values that turn Defender off and delete them (how):

      reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender" /s

    3. Remove planted exclusions (how).

    4. Turn on protection (full list):

      Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $false -MAPSReporting Advanced -PUAProtection Enabled -EnableNetworkProtection Enabled

    5. Answer forensics questions about suspicious files, then update and scan:

      Update-MpSignature
Start-MpScan -ScanType QuickScan

    6. Turn on Tamper Protection last in Windows Security (how).

    Work in that order. Policy values override Set-MpPreference, and Tamper Protection blocks changes you may still need to make.

    #Remove policies that disable Defender

    Planted vulnerabilities often set these. Look first:

    reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender" /s

    Delete the bad values in elevated cmd. Each line stands alone, and "unable to find the specified registry key or value" means that value was not set:

    reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender" /v DisableAntiSpyware /f
reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender" /v DisableAntiVirus /f
reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender" /v DisableRoutinelyTakingAction /f
reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Real-Time Protection" /v DisableRealtimeMonitoring /f
reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Real-Time Protection" /v DisableBehaviorMonitoring /f
reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Real-Time Protection" /v DisableOnAccessProtection /f
reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Real-Time Protection" /v DisableIOAVProtection /f
reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Real-Time Protection" /v DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable /f
reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Spynet" /v SpynetReporting /f
reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Spynet" /v SubmitSamplesConsent /f

    The same settings in gpedit.msc > Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Microsoft Defender Antivirus:

    Policy Set to
    Turn off Microsoft Defender Antivirus Not Configured (or Disabled)
    Real-time Protection > Turn off real-time protection Not Configured (or Disabled)
    Real-time Protection > Turn on behavior monitoring Not Configured (or Enabled)
    Real-time Protection > Scan all downloaded files and attachments Not Configured (or Enabled)
    MAPS > Join Microsoft MAPS Not Configured (or Enabled, Advanced MAPS)
    Configure detection for potentially unwanted applications Enabled, Block

    Then run gpupdate /force and check Get-MpComputerStatus again.

    DisableAntiSpyware on current Windows 11

    Current Defender platform versions ignore DisableAntiSpyware on client Windows, so Defender may already be running with the value present. Delete it anyway; scoring can check for the value itself.

    #Remove Defender exclusions

    Show them. This needs an elevated window; otherwise each field shows "N/A: Must be an administrator to view exclusions".

    Get-MpPreference | Select-Object ExclusionPath, ExclusionExtension, ExclusionProcess, ExclusionIpAddress

    Remove every exclusion of each type:

    $p = Get-MpPreference
if ($p.ExclusionPath)      { Remove-MpPreference -ExclusionPath $p.ExclusionPath }
if ($p.ExclusionExtension) { Remove-MpPreference -ExclusionExtension $p.ExclusionExtension }
if ($p.ExclusionProcess)   { Remove-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess $p.ExclusionProcess }
if ($p.ExclusionIpAddress) { Remove-MpPreference -ExclusionIpAddress $p.ExclusionIpAddress }

    Remove one exclusion:

    Remove-MpPreference -ExclusionPath "<path>"

    Planted exclusions look like whole drives (C:\), user folders, .exe or .ps1 extensions, or unknown tools. Do not add an exclusion for the CyberPatriot folder.

    Exclusion comes back or will not delete

    Group Policy set it. Delete the value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths (or \Extensions, \Processes), or set each policy under gpedit.msc > Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Microsoft Defender Antivirus > Exclusions to Not Configured.

    #Turn on protection with PowerShell

    Run in elevated PowerShell. Each line can run alone.

    Real-time scanning engines:

    Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $false
Set-MpPreference -DisableBehaviorMonitoring $false
Set-MpPreference -DisableIOAVProtection $false
Set-MpPreference -DisableScriptScanning $false
Set-MpPreference -DisableBlockAtFirstSeen $false

    Scanning of archives, removable drives and email:

    Set-MpPreference -DisableArchiveScanning $false
Set-MpPreference -DisableRemovableDriveScanning $false
Set-MpPreference -DisableEmailScanning $false

    Cloud protection, sample submission, PUA blocking and network protection:

    Set-MpPreference -MAPSReporting Advanced
Set-MpPreference -SubmitSamplesConsent SendSafeSamples
Set-MpPreference -CloudBlockLevel High
Set-MpPreference -PUAProtection Enabled
Set-MpPreference -EnableNetworkProtection Enabled

    Controlled folder access is optional. Turn it on only if the README does not forbid it, and check that required apps still work:

    Set-MpPreference -EnableControlledFolderAccess Enabled

    Verify

    Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AMRunningMode, AMServiceEnabled, AntivirusEnabled, RealTimeProtectionEnabled, BehaviorMonitorEnabled, IoavProtectionEnabled, OnAccessProtectionEnabled, IsTamperProtected, AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated shows AMRunningMode Normal, every other field True and a recent signature date.

    Get-MpPreference | Select-Object DisableRealtimeMonitoring, MAPSReporting, PUAProtection, EnableNetworkProtection shows False, 2, 1, 1.

    Value does not change

    If Set-MpPreference runs without error but the value stays the same, a policy value overrides it (remove it) or Tamper Protection is blocking the change.

    #Turn on protection in Windows Security

    Settings > Privacy & security > Windows Security > Open Windows Security, or Win+R > windowsdefender:.

    Location in Windows Security Setting Value
    Virus & threat protection > Manage settings Real-time protection On
    Virus & threat protection > Manage settings Cloud-delivered protection On
    Virus & threat protection > Manage settings Automatic sample submission On
    Virus & threat protection > Manage settings Tamper Protection On, last
    Virus & threat protection > Manage settings Controlled folder access > Manage On only if the README allows; it can block real apps
    Virus & threat protection > Manage settings Exclusions > Add or remove exclusions Remove every exclusion the README does not require
    App & browser control > Reputation-based protection settings Check apps and files On
    App & browser control > Reputation-based protection settings SmartScreen for Microsoft Edge On
    App & browser control > Reputation-based protection settings Phishing protection On
    App & browser control > Reputation-based protection settings Potentially unwanted app blocking On, with Block apps and Block downloads checked
    App & browser control > Reputation-based protection settings SmartScreen for Microsoft Store apps On
    App & browser control > Exploit protection settings System settings (CFG, DEP, ASLR, SEHOP) Use default (On)
    Device security > Core isolation details Memory integrity On (needs a restart; may be unavailable in a VM)
    Firewall & network protection Domain, Private and Public network On

    Tamper Protection can only be turned on here in the GUI. Once it is on, Set-MpPreference cannot turn real-time, behavior or cloud protection off, and it also stops you from changing them, so do it after everything else.

    #SmartScreen is greyed out

    A policy controls it. Check:

    reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\System" /v EnableSmartScreen

    Turn it on in Warn and prevent bypass mode:

    reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\System" /v EnableSmartScreen /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\System" /v ShellSmartScreenLevel /t REG_SZ /d Block /f

    The matching policy is gpedit.msc > Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > File Explorer > Configure Windows Defender SmartScreen = Enabled, Warn and prevent bypass.

    #Update signatures and scan

    Answer forensics questions before scanning

    A scan can quarantine a file a forensics question asks about. Answer questions about suspicious files first.

    Update signatures, then run a quick scan:

    Update-MpSignature
Start-MpScan -ScanType QuickScan

    A full scan takes a long time, so run it in a separate window:

    Start-MpScan -ScanType FullScan

    Scan one folder:

    Start-MpScan -ScanType CustomScan -ScanPath "C:\Users"

    -ScanType 1 is a quick scan and 2 is a full scan.

    "%ProgramFiles%\Windows Defender\MpCmdRun.exe" -SignatureUpdate
"%ProgramFiles%\Windows Defender\MpCmdRun.exe" -Scan -ScanType 1

    Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Protection updates > Check for updates. Then Scan options > Quick scan or Full scan > Scan now. Results are under Protection history.

    See what was found:

    Get-MpThreatDetection | Select-Object ThreatID, ProcessName, Resources, InitialDetectionTime
Get-MpThreat

    Remove all active threats:

    Remove-MpThreat

    #When another antivirus is installed

    Check which antivirus Windows Security sees:

    Get-CimInstance -Namespace root/SecurityCenter2 -ClassName AntivirusProduct | Select-Object displayName, pathToSignedReportingExe

    On Windows 11 without Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Defender Antivirus turns itself off automatically when a third-party antivirus registers with Windows Security. It does not run in passive mode on these machines. WinDefend shows Stopped and Defender stops getting updates.

    If the README does not authorize the other product, uninstall it (w11-software); Defender turns back on afterwards. A fake or planted "antivirus" is a common trick for keeping Defender off.

    #Defender services

    Get-Service WinDefend, WdNisSvc, SecurityHealthService, wscsvc | Select-Object Name, Status, StartType

    WinDefend (Microsoft Defender Antivirus Service) should be Running. Its startup type is greyed out in services.msc because the service is protected, so fix it by removing the policies above or the other antivirus.

    PreviousWindows Defender FirewallNextWindows Update and app updates
    W11

    Windows Update and app updates

    jump:w11-updates

    Agree before you reboot

    Updates often need a restart, which interrupts everyone. Agree as a team first and re-check the score afterwards. Updates are slow, so start them early and let them run in the background.

    Fast path

    1. Open Windows Update and start a check:

      start ms-settings:windowsupdate

    2. If it shows "Updates paused", click Resume updates. Then Check for updates > Download & install all.

    3. Check that the update services are not Disabled (how).
    4. Delete planted policy values that block updates (how).
    5. Set Configure Automatic Updates to Enabled, option 4 (how).

    6. List app updates with winget upgrade, check the list against the README, then update them all:

      winget upgrade --all --accept-source-agreements --accept-package-agreements

    #Check for and install Windows updates

    Start > Settings > Windows Update > Check for updates > Download & install all. If the page shows "Updates paused", click Resume updates first.

    Open the Windows Update page and trigger a scan:

    start ms-settings:windowsupdate
UsoClient StartInteractiveScan

    UsoClient is undocumented and prints nothing; watch progress on the Settings page.

    #Advanced options worth setting

    Settings > Windows Update > Advanced options:

    • Receive updates for other Microsoft products: On
    • Get me up to date: On (optional)
    • Notify me when a restart is required to finish updating: On

    #Update services must not be disabled

    Get-Service wuauserv, BITS, UsoSvc, WaaSMedicSvc, DoSvc, CryptSvc -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Name, Status, StartType
    Service Name Default start type
    Windows Update wuauserv Manual (Trigger Start). Automatic is also fine.
    Background Intelligent Transfer Service BITS Manual
    Update Orchestrator Service UsoSvc Automatic (Delayed Start)
    Windows Update Medic Service WaaSMedicSvc Manual, protected (you cannot change it)
    Delivery Optimization DoSvc Automatic (Delayed Start)
    Cryptographic Services CryptSvc Automatic

    Fix any that show Disabled, in elevated cmd:

    sc config wuauserv start= auto
sc config bits start= demand
sc config UsoSvc start= delayed-auto
net start wuauserv
net start bits

    Set-Service -Name wuauserv -StartupType Automatic
Start-Service -Name wuauserv

    Windows PowerShell 5.1 cannot set Automatic (Delayed Start); use sc.exe config UsoSvc start= delayed-auto for that.

    sc config syntax

    sc config needs a space after start= and none before it: start= auto. Values are auto, delayed-auto, demand (Manual) and disabled.

    #Remove policies that block updates

    reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate" /s
    Key Value Bad Fix
    ...\WindowsUpdate\AU NoAutoUpdate 1 0, or delete
    ...\WindowsUpdate\AU AUOptions 1 or 2 4
    ...\WindowsUpdate\AU UseWUServer 1 with a fake WUServer delete
    ...\WindowsUpdate WUServer, WUStatusServer Unknown URL delete
    ...\WindowsUpdate DisableWindowsUpdateAccess 1 delete
    ...\WindowsUpdate SetDisableUXWUAccess 1 delete
    ...\WindowsUpdate DoNotConnectToWindowsUpdateInternetLocations 1 delete

    Set the automatic update values:

    reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate\AU" /v NoAutoUpdate /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate\AU" /v AUOptions /t REG_DWORD /d 4 /f

    Delete the WSUS redirect and the blocking values. "Unable to find" errors mean that value was not set:

    reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate\AU" /v UseWUServer /f
reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate" /v WUServer /f
reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate" /v WUStatusServer /f
reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate" /v DisableWindowsUpdateAccess /f
reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate" /v SetDisableUXWUAccess /f
reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate" /v DoNotConnectToWindowsUpdateInternetLocations /f

    #Set the Configure Automatic Updates policy

    1. Win+R > gpedit.msc.
    2. Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows Update > Manage end user experience.
    3. Double-click Configure Automatic Updates > Enabled.
    4. Configure automatic updating: 4 - Auto download and schedule the install. Scheduled install day: 0 - Every day. OK.
    5. In the same folder, set Remove access to use all Windows Update features to Not Configured.
    6. Run gpupdate /force.

    On Windows 10 and early Windows 11 builds the policy sits directly under Windows Update. Home edition has no gpedit.msc; use the reg add commands.

    Verify

    reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate\AU" shows NoAutoUpdate REG_DWORD 0x0 and AUOptions REG_DWORD 0x4, and Settings > Windows Update checks for updates without an error.

    #Update third-party apps with winget

    List apps that have updates:

    winget upgrade

    Update everything on the list:

    winget upgrade --all --accept-source-agreements --accept-package-agreements

    Update one app by its ID:

    winget upgrade --id <package-id> -e --accept-source-agreements --accept-package-agreements

    Common IDs: Mozilla.Firefox, Mozilla.Thunderbird, Google.Chrome, Notepad++.Notepad++, 7zip.7zip, VideoLAN.VLC, Microsoft.VisualStudioCode, TheDocumentFoundation.LibreOffice, Adobe.Acrobat.Reader.64-bit, PuTTY.PuTTY, WinSCP.WinSCP. Find any other ID with winget search <app-name>.

    winget missing or failing

    If winget is "not recognized", update App Installer from the Microsoft Store or use each app's own updater below. Read the winget upgrade list before running --all; the README may (rarely) ask you to keep an app at a version.

    #Update apps with their own updater

    App How
    Firefox Menu (three lines) > Help > About Firefox. It downloads and asks to restart.
    Chrome chrome://settings/help
    Edge edge://settings/help
    Thunderbird Menu > Help > About Thunderbird
    Notepad++ ? menu > Update Notepad++
    7-Zip No updater. Download the current x64 installer from 7-zip.org and install over the old version.
    VLC Help > Check for Updates
    Microsoft Store apps Microsoft Store > Library (left bar) > Get updates
    Microsoft Office File > Account > Update Options > Update Now

    Check installed versions with winget list, or read them from the registry:

    Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*, HKLM:\Software\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* | Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion | Sort-Object DisplayName
    PreviousMicrosoft Defender AntivirusNextServices
    W11

    Services

    jump:w11-services

    README first

    If the README says the machine is a web, FTP, file or print server, or that users connect over RDP or SSH, the matching service is required. Stopping it costs points and can break the scoring checks for that service.

    Fast path

    1. Read the README and list the services it requires (how).
    2. Open PowerShell as administrator.

    3. Disable one service (use the short service name from the table):

      Stop-Service -Name <service-name> -Force
Set-Service -Name <service-name> -StartupType Disabled

    4. Or edit and run the batch script.

    5. Confirm the must-stay-on services are running.
    6. Write each old start type in the change log so you can undo it.

    #Disable a service

    Stop-Service -Name <service-name> -Force
Set-Service -Name <service-name> -StartupType Disabled

    sc stop <service-name>
sc config <service-name> start= disabled

    Win+R > services.msc > double-click the service > Startup type = Disabled > Stop > OK.

    Commands take the short service name (RemoteRegistry); the display name ("Remote Registry") fails. Look it up with Get-Service -DisplayName "*remote*" or sc getkeyname "Remote Registry".

    Verify

    Get-Service <service-name> | Select-Object Name, Status, StartType shows Stopped and Disabled. sc qc <service-name> shows START_TYPE : 4 DISABLED.

    #Re-enable a service

    Restore the start type you wrote in the change log. Use Manual (PowerShell) or start= demand (cmd) for Manual.

    Set-Service -Name <service-name> -StartupType Automatic
Start-Service -Name <service-name>

    sc config <service-name> start= auto
sc start <service-name>

    #Services commonly disabled

    Disable only services the README does not require. "May not exist" means the service appears only when that feature or app is installed.

    Display name Service name Disable?
    Remote Registry RemoteRegistry Yes
    Telnet (server) TlntSvr Yes. Windows 11 has no Telnet Server, so it exists only if planted.
    Microsoft FTP Service ftpsvc Yes, unless an FTP server is required
    World Wide Web Publishing Service W3SVC Yes, unless a web server is required
    Web Management Service WMSvc Yes, unless IIS remote management is required
    IIS Admin Service IISADMIN Yes, unless IIS or FTP is required (may not exist)
    SNMP Service SNMP Yes (may not exist)
    SNMP Trap SNMPTrap Yes
    SSDP Discovery SSDPSRV Yes
    UPnP Device Host upnphost Yes
    Internet Connection Sharing (ICS) SharedAccess Yes
    Remote Access Auto Connection Manager RasAuto Yes
    Remote Access Connection Manager RasMan Usually leave it (VPN uses it)
    Routing and Remote Access RemoteAccess Yes
    Simple TCP/IP Services simptcp Yes (may not exist)
    Remote Desktop Services TermService Only if RDP is not required
    Remote Desktop Services UserMode Port Redirector UmRdpService Only if RDP is not required
    Remote Desktop Configuration SessionEnv Only if RDP is not required
    Windows Remote Management (WS-Management) WinRM Yes, unless required
    OpenSSH SSH Server sshd Yes, unless SSH is required (may not exist)
    Print Spooler Spooler Only if the README needs no printing
    Fax Fax Yes
    Windows Media Player Network Sharing Service WMPNetworkSvc Yes (may not exist)
    Function Discovery Resource Publication FDResPub Yes, unless file sharing is required
    Peer Name Resolution Protocol PNRPsvc Yes (may not exist)
    Peer Networking Grouping, Peer Networking Identity Manager p2psvc, p2pimsvc Yes (may not exist)
    Xbox Live Auth Manager, Xbox Live Game Save, Xbox Live Networking Service XblAuthManager, XblGameSave, XboxNetApiSvc Optional
    Xbox Accessory Management Service XboxGipSvc Optional
    Server (SMB file sharing) LanmanServer Only if no shares are needed; also removes ADMIN$ and C$
    Bluetooth Support Service bthserv Optional
    Downloaded Maps Manager MapsBroker Optional
    Retail Demo Service RetailDemo Optional
    Third-party remote tools (VNC, TeamViewer, AnyDesk) for example vncserver, uvnc_service, tvnserver, TeamViewer, AnyDesk Yes, unless authorized; also uninstall them
    Third-party servers (FileZilla Server, Apache, MySQL) for example filezilla-server, Apache2.4, MySQL80 Only if not required

    Not every disabled service scores

    Scoring usually checks a handful: Remote Registry, FTP, Telnet, SNMP, UPnP and SSDP, and RDP when it is not needed. Disabling random Windows services can break the image, so stick to the table.

    #Disable several services at once

    Edit $disable to remove anything the README requires, then paste into elevated PowerShell. For each service that exists, the script prints its current status and start type (copy that into the change log), stops it and sets it to Disabled. Missing services are skipped.

    $disable = @('RemoteRegistry','SSDPSRV','upnphost','SharedAccess','RasAuto','RemoteAccess','simptcp','SNMP','SNMPTrap','TlntSvr','ftpsvc','Fax','WMPNetworkSvc')
foreach ($s in $disable) {
  $svc = Get-Service -Name $s -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
  if ($svc) {
    "{0,-18} was {1}/{2}" -f $s, $svc.Status, $svc.StartType
    Stop-Service -Name $s -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
    Set-Service  -Name $s -StartupType Disabled
  }
}

    #Services that must stay on

    Display name Service name Should be
    Microsoft Defender Antivirus Service WinDefend Running, Automatic
    Windows Defender Firewall mpssvc Running, Automatic
    Base Filtering Engine BFE Running, Automatic
    Windows Event Log EventLog Running, Automatic
    Security Center wscsvc Running, Automatic (Delayed Start)
    Windows Security Service SecurityHealthService Running
    Windows Update wuauserv Manual or Automatic, never Disabled
    Update Orchestrator Service UsoSvc Never Disabled
    Background Intelligent Transfer Service BITS Never Disabled
    Cryptographic Services CryptSvc Running, Automatic
    Remote Procedure Call (RPC) RpcSs Running (cannot be changed)
    DNS Client Dnscache Running
    DHCP Client Dhcp Running
    Windows Management Instrumentation Winmgmt Running
    CyberPatriot or CCS Client scoring service whatever name it has Never touch it

    Check them all at once:

    Get-Service WinDefend, mpssvc, BFE, EventLog, wscsvc, wuauserv, UsoSvc, BITS, CryptSvc, Winmgmt -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Name, Status, StartType | Format-Table -AutoSize

    Fix a stopped required service, for example the event log:

    Set-Service -Name EventLog -StartupType Automatic
Start-Service -Name EventLog

    #Keep README-required services healthy

    When the README says a service is required (for example "this computer runs an FTP server" or "IIS hosts the company site"):

    1. Find the service with Get-Service | Where-Object DisplayName -match '<keyword>'.
    2. Set it to Running and Automatic.
    3. Check its firewall rule is enabled (w11-firewall).
    4. Harden its configuration instead of removing it. For IIS or FTP, that means turning off anonymous authentication and requiring SSL if the README asks.

    #Find unusual services

    Running services sorted by display name, for a quick scan:

    Get-Service | Where-Object Status -eq Running | Sort-Object DisplayName | Format-Table Name, DisplayName -AutoSize

    Services whose program is outside C:\Windows\System32 and SysWOW64. These are third-party or planted:

    Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object { $_.PathName -and $_.PathName -notmatch '(?i)\\Windows\\(System32|SysWOW64)\\' } |
  Select-Object Name, DisplayName, State, StartMode, PathName | Format-Table -AutoSize -Wrap

    Check the paths it prints with the steps in w11-malware.

    #A service will not stop

    sc queryex <service-name>
sc enumdepend <service-name>

    sc queryex shows the service's PID. sc enumdepend lists services that depend on it; stop those first, or use Stop-Service -Force, which stops dependents too. As a last resort, end the process:

    taskkill /PID <pid> /F

    #Delete a malicious service

    Only for services that are clearly planted, such as an unknown name with a program in Temp, C:\Users or ProgramData. Answer forensics questions first. In elevated cmd:

    sc stop <service-name>
sc delete <service-name>

    Then delete the program file it pointed to. Remove-Service exists only in PowerShell 6 and later. Windows 11 ships with Windows PowerShell 5.1, so use sc delete (or sc.exe delete in PowerShell).

    PreviousWindows Update and app updatesNextWindows optional features
    W11

    Windows optional features

    jump:w11-features

    Fast path

    1. Open PowerShell as administrator.

    2. Remove SMB 1.0, Telnet Client, TFTP Client and Simple TCPIP services (errors about missing features are fine):

      Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol -NoRestart
Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName TelnetClient -NoRestart
Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName TFTP -NoRestart
Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SimpleTCP -NoRestart

    3. Turn off SMB1 in the SMB server:

      Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false -Force

    4. Remove IIS only if the README needs no web or FTP server (how).

    5. Remove PowerShell 2.0 if it is still listed (how).
    6. Remove the OpenSSH Server and SNMP capabilities if not required (how).

    #Turn features off in the GUI

    Win+R > optionalfeatures (Turn Windows features on or off). Clear the box > OK. Choose not to restart yet if you have more to do.

    Clear these unless the README requires them:

    • SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support (all sub-items)
    • Telnet Client
    • TFTP Client
    • Simple TCPIP services (i.e. echo, daytime etc)
    • Internet Information Services and Internet Information Services Hostable Web Core, only if no web or FTP server is required
    • Windows PowerShell 2.0, if it is listed
    • Work Folders Client, RIP Listener and Microsoft Message Queue (MSMQ) Server, if not needed
    • Windows Subsystem for Linux and Virtual Machine Platform, only if not needed for the image's purpose

    #Remove features with PowerShell

    List what is enabled:

    Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online | Where-Object State -eq Enabled | Sort-Object FeatureName | Format-Table FeatureName, State
    GUI name FeatureName
    SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support SMB1Protocol (sub-features SMB1Protocol-Client, SMB1Protocol-Server, SMB1Protocol-Deprecation)
    Telnet Client TelnetClient
    TFTP Client TFTP
    Simple TCPIP services SimpleTCP
    Internet Information Services IIS-WebServerRole (also IIS-WebServer, IIS-FTPServer, IIS-FTPSvc, IIS-WebServerManagementTools)
    Windows PowerShell 2.0 MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2Root, MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2
    Microsoft Message Queue (MSMQ) Server MSMQ-Container
    RIP Listener RasRip
    Work Folders Client WorkFolders-Client
    Windows Subsystem for Linux Microsoft-Windows-Subsystem-Linux

    Disable a feature. Disabling a parent such as SMB1Protocol also disables its sub-features:

    Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol -NoRestart
Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName TelnetClient -NoRestart
Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName TFTP -NoRestart
Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SimpleTCP -NoRestart

    dism /online /disable-feature /featurename:SMB1Protocol /norestart
dism /online /disable-feature /featurename:TelnetClient /norestart
dism /online /disable-feature /featurename:TFTP /norestart
dism /online /disable-feature /featurename:SimpleTCP /norestart

    List enabled features with dism /online /get-features /format:table | findstr /i "Enabled".

    Remove IIS entirely, only if no web or FTP server is required:

    Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName IIS-WebServerRole -NoRestart

    An error such as "Feature name SimpleTCP is unknown" means the feature is not on this build; move on.

    Verify

    'SMB1Protocol','TelnetClient','TFTP','SimpleTCP' | ForEach-Object { Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName $_ } | Select-Object FeatureName, State shows Disabled, or DisablePending until the next restart.

    #PowerShell 2.0

    Microsoft removed Windows PowerShell 2.0 from Windows 11 version 24H2 starting with the August 2025 update, and later releases do not include it. On a patched 24H2 or newer image it will not appear in optionalfeatures. Older images, including 23H2, may still have it. Check:

    Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2Root

    If the State is Enabled, remove it:

    Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2Root -NoRestart

    If the command says the feature name is unknown, PowerShell 2.0 is already gone. Scripts that ask for version 2 then run in PowerShell 5.1.

    #Turn off SMBv1 in the SMB server

    Removing the feature is the main fix. Also turn SMB1 off in the server configuration and confirm SMB2 is on:

    Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false -Force
Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB2Protocol $true -Force
Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select-Object EnableSMB1Protocol, EnableSMB2Protocol

    You should see False and True. EnableSMB2Protocol controls both SMB2 and SMB3, so never set it to $false.

    Optional extra SMB hardening that does not break normal shares (it matches the signing options in w11-secopts):

    Set-SmbServerConfiguration -RequireSecuritySignature $true -EnableSecuritySignature $true -Force
Set-SmbClientConfiguration -RequireSecuritySignature $true -Force

    #Remove Windows capabilities

    Some components are capabilities instead of features. They appear in Settings > System > Optional features. OpenSSH Server and the SNMP Service are the ones that matter here.

    List installed capabilities:

    Get-WindowsCapability -Online | Where-Object State -eq Installed | Select-Object Name

    Remove OpenSSH Server if the README does not require SSH:

    Remove-WindowsCapability -Online -Name OpenSSH.Server~~~~0.0.1.0

    Remove the SNMP Service if the README does not require it:

    Remove-WindowsCapability -Online -Name SNMP.Client~~~~0.0.1.0

    Leave the OpenSSH Client installed; it is harmless.

    Internet Explorer

    Internet Explorer 11 is retired on Windows 11 and iexplore.exe opens Edge. Edge's IE mode is controlled at edge://settings/defaultBrowser: set "Allow sites to be reloaded in Internet Explorer mode" to Don't allow unless the README needs it.

    PreviousServicesNextFile shares and permissions
    W11

    File shares and permissions

    jump:w11-shares

    Fast path

    1. Open PowerShell as administrator (Start, type powershell, Run as administrator).

    2. List the shares:

      Get-SmbShare

    3. Leave ADMIN$, C$, IPC$ and any share the README names. print$ is also normal when a printer is shared.

    4. Remove every other share:

      Remove-SmbShare -Name "<share-name>" -Force

    5. On a share the README requires, grant only the users who need it and take Everyone off (details).

    6. Open the folder that was shared and look for prohibited files or forensics evidence (w11-files).

    #List the shares

    Get-SmbShare | Select-Object Name, Path, Description, CurrentUsers

    net share

    Win+R > fsmgmt.msc > Shared Folders > Shares.

    On a clean Windows 11 image Get-SmbShare shows only the administrative shares:

    Name   ScopeName Path       Description
----   --------- ----       -----------
ADMIN$ *         C:\Windows Remote Admin
C$     *         C:\        Default share
IPC$   *                    Remote IPC
    Share Points to Keep it?
    ADMIN$ C:\Windows Yes
    C$ (and D$ and so on) Root of each drive Yes
    IPC$ Named pipes, no folder Yes
    print$ Printer drivers Yes, when a printer is shared
    Anything else A folder someone shared Remove unless the README requires it
    Why the administrative shares stay

    Windows recreates ADMIN$ and the drive shares every time the Server service starts, so removing them does not stick. They only accept administrators, and removing them is rarely scored. Turning them off for good needs the AutoShareWks value set to 0 under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters, which can break remote management tools. Leave them alone unless the README asks.

    #Remove a share that is not required

    Remove-SmbShare -Name "<share-name>" -Force

    net share <share-name> /delete

    fsmgmt.msc > Shares > right-click the share > Stop Sharing.

    Removing the share leaves the folder and its files on disk. Open the folder and check it for media, password files and hacking tools before you move on.

    Verify

    net share lists only ADMIN$, C$, IPC$ and the shares the README requires.

    #Fix permissions on a share the README requires

    If users need the share, keep it and narrow who can use it. Show who has access now:

    Get-SmbShareAccess -Name "<share-name>"

    Grant the README users or group first, so the share is never left with nobody on it. -AccessRight takes Full, Change or Read:

    Grant-SmbShareAccess -Name "<share-name>" -AccountName "<username>" -AccessRight Change -Force

    Then take Everyone off:

    Revoke-SmbShareAccess -Name "<share-name>" -AccountName Everyone -Force

    Everyone with Full is the classic planted weakness. Guest or Anonymous Logon on the list is just as bad.

    GUI: fsmgmt.msc > Shares > right-click the share > Properties > Share Permissions.

    Verify

    Get-SmbShareAccess -Name "<share-name>" lists only the accounts the README names, with the lowest right they need for their work.

    #Check NTFS permissions with icacls

    Share permissions and NTFS (folder) permissions both apply, and the stricter one wins. Show the folder's NTFS permissions:

    icacls "<folder>"

    Example output where Everyone has full control:

    C:\Shared Everyone:(OI)(CI)(F)
          BUILTIN\Administrators:(I)(OI)(CI)(F)
          NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(I)(OI)(CI)(F)
          BUILTIN\Users:(I)(OI)(CI)(RX)

Successfully processed 1 files; Failed processing 0 files
    Code Meaning
    (F) Full control
    (M) Modify
    (RX) Read and execute
    (R) / (W) Read / write
    (OI)(CI) Applies to files and subfolders inside
    (I) Inherited from the parent folder

    Remove Everyone's explicit entries from a folder and everything under it:

    icacls "<folder>" /remove:g Everyone /t

    Give one user modify rights on a folder and its contents:

    icacls "<folder>" /grant "<username>:(OI)(CI)M"

    Reset a folder tree so it only inherits from its parent, which wipes planted custom entries:

    icacls "<folder>" /reset /t /c

    Entries marked (I) do not come off with /remove

    An inherited entry comes from the parent folder. Fix it on the parent, or stop inheritance on this folder with icacls "<folder>" /inheritance:d (copies the inherited entries as explicit ones) and then remove the entry.

    #Find folders where Everyone or Users can write

    This lists folders directly inside System32 and Program Files where Everyone, Users or Authenticated Users have write, modify or full control:

    foreach ($p in 'C:\Windows\System32','C:\Program Files','C:\Program Files (x86)') {
    Get-ChildItem $p -Directory -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | ForEach-Object {
        $d = $_
        $acl = Get-Acl $d.FullName -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
        $weak = $acl.Access | Where-Object { $_.IdentityReference -match 'Everyone|BUILTIN\\Users|Authenticated Users' -and $_.FileSystemRights -match 'FullControl|Modify|Write' -and $_.AccessControlType -eq 'Allow' }
        if ($weak) { $d.FullName }
    }
}

    Some apps give Users write access on purpose

    A few legitimate programs grant Users write on their own folder. Focus on folders that look out of place or where Everyone has FullControl. Never run icacls /reset on C:\Windows or a whole drive.

    #Take ownership of a file you cannot change

    Run in an elevated prompt. Take ownership, then give Administrators full control:

    takeown /f "<path>" /r /d y

    icacls "<path>" /grant Administrators:F /t

    /r recurses into folders and /d y answers the "do you want to replace" prompt on English systems.

    #Turn off insecure guest SMB access

    Stop the SMB client from connecting to shares without a password:

    Set-SmbClientConfiguration -EnableInsecureGuestLogons $false -Force

    Then open Settings > Network & internet > Advanced network settings > Advanced sharing settings and set:

    Profile Setting Value
    Public networks Network discovery Off
    Public networks File and printer sharing Off
    All networks Public folder sharing Off
    All networks Password protected sharing On

    SMB signing and SMBv1 are covered in Security Options and optional features.

    Verify

    Get-SmbClientConfiguration | Select-Object EnableInsecureGuestLogons shows False.

    PreviousWindows optional featuresNextRemote Desktop, Remote Assistance and WinRM
    W11

    Remote Desktop, Remote Assistance and WinRM

    jump:w11-remote

    Read the README before you turn Remote Desktop off

    If the README says users connect remotely, Remote Desktop is a required service and turning it off costs points. Harden it instead.

    Fast path

    1. Search the README for "Remote Desktop", "RDP" and "remote access".

    2. If it is not required, turn it off in elevated PowerShell:

      Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server' -Name fDenyTSConnections -Value 1

      Disable-NetFirewallRule -DisplayGroup "Remote Desktop"

    3. If it is required, turn on Network Level Authentication (details).

    4. Win+R > SystemPropertiesRemote > uncheck "Allow Remote Assistance connections to this computer" > OK.

    5. Remove anyone the README does not list from Remote Desktop Users:

      net localgroup "Remote Desktop Users"

    6. Turn off WinRM unless the README needs remote management (details).

    #Decide whether Remote Desktop is required

    Look for "Remote Desktop", "RDP", "remote access", "connect remotely" or "work from home" in the README. A user listed only in the Remote Desktop Users group is also a hint. If nothing points to it, turn it off.

    #Turn off Remote Desktop when it is not required

    1. Start > Settings > System > Remote Desktop > Off.
    2. Or Win+R > SystemPropertiesRemote > Remote Desktop > "Don't allow remote connections to this computer" > OK.
    Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server' -Name fDenyTSConnections -Value 1
Disable-NetFirewallRule -DisplayGroup "Remote Desktop"
Stop-Service TermService -Force
Set-Service TermService -StartupType Disabled

    reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server" /v fDenyTSConnections /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
netsh advfirewall firewall set rule group="Remote Desktop" new enable=No

    fDenyTSConnections = 1 means deny. It is a double negative, so 0 means Remote Desktop is allowed.

    A policy value overrides the setting

    If HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services has its own fDenyTSConnections, that value wins. Set it to 1 or delete it. The gpedit equivalent is Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Remote Desktop Services > Remote Desktop Session Host > Connections > Allow users to connect remotely by using Remote Desktop Services = Disabled.

    Verify

    reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server" /v fDenyTSConnections shows 0x1. After TermService stops, Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3389 -State Listen -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue returns nothing.

    #Remove users from Remote Desktop Users

    List the group:

    net localgroup "Remote Desktop Users"

    Remove each member the README does not authorize for remote access:

    net localgroup "Remote Desktop Users" <username> /delete

    Administrators can connect without being in this group, so the group should hold only standard users the README names.

    #Harden Remote Desktop when the README requires it

    1. Keep it on: fDenyTSConnections = 0, TermService running, the "Remote Desktop" firewall group enabled.
    2. Require Network Level Authentication: Settings > System > Remote Desktop > expand the toggle > "Require devices to use Network Level Authentication to connect" = On. In SystemPropertiesRemote it is the checkbox "Allow connections only from computers running Remote Desktop with Network Level Authentication".
    3. Keep only README-authorized users in Remote Desktop Users (above).

    4. Set NLA, TLS and high encryption in the registry (elevated cmd):

      reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp" /v UserAuthentication /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp" /v SecurityLayer /t REG_DWORD /d 2 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp" /v MinEncryptionLevel /t REG_DWORD /d 3 /f
    Value Data Meaning
    UserAuthentication 1 Network Level Authentication required
    SecurityLayer 2 TLS (shown as SSL in gpedit)
    MinEncryptionLevel 3 High (128-bit)

    The same settings in gpedit live under Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Remote Desktop Services > Remote Desktop Session Host:

    Folder Policy Setting
    Security Require user authentication for remote connections by using Network Level Authentication Enabled
    Security Require use of specific security layer for remote (RDP) connections Enabled, SSL
    Security Set client connection encryption level Enabled, High Level
    Security Always prompt for password upon connection Enabled
    Security Require secure RPC communication Enabled
    Device and Resource Redirection Do not allow drive redirection Enabled (optional)

    Verify

    reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp" /v UserAuthentication shows 0x1, and TermService is still Running in services.msc.

    #Turn off Remote Assistance connections

    Win+R > SystemPropertiesRemote > uncheck "Allow Remote Assistance connections to this computer" > OK.

    reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Remote Assistance" /v fAllowToGetHelp /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Remote Assistance" /v fAllowFullControl /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
netsh advfirewall firewall set rule group="Remote Assistance" new enable=No

    In gpedit, set Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Remote Assistance > Configure Solicited Remote Assistance = Disabled and Configure Offer Remote Assistance = Disabled.

    Verify

    Reopen SystemPropertiesRemote: the Remote Assistance box is unchecked.

    #Turn off WinRM and PowerShell remoting

    WinRM is the service behind PowerShell remoting (ports 5985 and 5986). On Windows 11 it is set to Manual and not listening unless someone enabled it. If the README does not need remote management, run in elevated PowerShell:

    Disable-PSRemoting -Force
Stop-Service WinRM -Force
Set-Service WinRM -StartupType Disabled
Disable-NetFirewallRule -DisplayGroup "Windows Remote Management" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

    Check that nothing listens on the WinRM ports:

    Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 5985,5986 -State Listen -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

    net localgroup "Remote Management Users" should list no members.

    If WinRM must stay, show its service settings:

    winrm get winrm/config/service

    AllowUnencrypted and Basic under Auth must both be false. Fix them in PowerShell (the single quotes matter):

    winrm set winrm/config/service '@{AllowUnencrypted="false"}'
winrm set winrm/config/service/auth '@{Basic="false"}'

    #Check for third-party remote access tools

    VNC (TightVNC, UltraVNC, RealVNC), TeamViewer, AnyDesk, LogMeIn, Chrome Remote Desktop, Radmin and ScreenConnect all give remote control. Uninstall them unless the README authorizes them (w11-software). Look for their ports among the listeners:

    Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Where-Object LocalPort -in 5800,5900,5938,7070 | Select-Object LocalPort, OwningProcess
    Port Usual owner
    5800, 5900 VNC server
    5938 TeamViewer
    7070 AnyDesk
    PreviousFile shares and permissionsNextUnauthorized software and hacking tools
    W11

    Unauthorized software and hacking tools

    jump:w11-software

    Check the README's required software first

    Never uninstall a program the README lists as required or that a user "needs for work". Answer forensics questions about a program before you remove it. Not every installed program is a vulnerability.

    Fast path

    1. Win+R > appwiz.cpl, then click the Installed On column so recent installs sort together.
    2. Compare the list with the README. Mark hacking tools, P2P clients, games and remote access tools (common names).
    3. Answer any forensics question that mentions one of them.

    4. Uninstall each: select it > Uninstall, or in PowerShell:

      winget uninstall --name "<program-name>"

    5. Search for portable tools that never show up in the list (details).

    6. Open Settings > Apps > Installed apps and remove Store games the README does not need.

    #List installed programs

    GUI: Win+R > appwiz.cpl (Programs and Features), or Settings > Apps > Installed apps, which also shows Store apps.

    The uninstall registry keys give the most complete list of desktop programs, 64-bit and 32-bit, machine-wide and for every signed-in user:

    Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*', 'HKLM:\Software\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*', 'Registry::HKEY_USERS\*\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object DisplayName | Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion, Publisher, InstallDate, InstallLocation | Sort-Object DisplayName | Format-Table -AutoSize

    Other views of the same thing:

    winget list

    Get-Package | Select-Object Name, Version, ProviderName | Sort-Object Name

    Store apps for the current user:

    Get-AppxPackage | Select-Object Name, Publisher | Sort-Object Name

    Per-user installs hide from your list

    A program installed for one user only appears in that user's uninstall key, which is loaded only while that user is signed in. These programs usually live in C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\Programs. Look through every user's AppData folder.

    #Uninstall a program

    appwiz.cpl > select the program > Uninstall. Or Settings > Apps > Installed apps > the three dots next to the app > Uninstall.

    Find the exact name or Id:

    winget list "<program-name>"

    Uninstall by name or by Id:

    winget uninstall --name "<program-name>"

    winget uninstall --id <package-id> -e

    Works for MSI-based installs:

    Uninstall-Package -Name "<program-name>"

    winget list also shows programs that did not come from winget. Their Id starts with ARP\Machine\ or ARP\User\ and still works with winget uninstall --id.

    #Run the vendor uninstaller when the others fail

    Show the program's uninstall command:

    Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*', 'HKLM:\Software\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*' |
    Where-Object DisplayName -match '<program-name>' | Select-Object DisplayName, UninstallString, QuietUninstallString

    Copy the UninstallString into an elevated cmd window and run it. MSI programs look like MsiExec.exe /X{GUID}; add /qn to run without prompts.

    #Winget Ids for tools that show up often

    Program winget Id
    Wireshark WiresharkFoundation.Wireshark
    Nmap Insecure.Nmap
    TeamViewer TeamViewer.TeamViewer
    TightVNC GlavSoft.TightVNC
    Tor Browser TorProject.TorBrowser
    qBittorrent qBittorrent.qBittorrent
    Steam Valve.Steam

    Ids can change. If one fails, run winget list "<program-name>" and use the Id it prints.

    Verify

    The program is gone from appwiz.cpl and its folder is gone from Program Files. If a folder with an .exe stays behind, delete it after forensics.

    #Commonly planted unwanted software

    Category Names to look for
    Packet sniffers and network scanners Wireshark, Npcap/WinPcap (installed with Wireshark), Nmap, Zenmap, Angry IP Scanner, Advanced IP Scanner, NetScanTools, SoftPerfect Network Scanner
    Password crackers and dumpers Cain & Abel, John the Ripper, Ophcrack, Hashcat, L0phtCrack, Mimikatz, pwdump, fgdump, LaZagne, THC Hydra, Medusa, Aircrack-ng, RainbowCrack
    Backdoor and remote shell tools NetCat (nc.exe, nc64.exe), Ncat, Metasploit, BeEF, PsExec in a user folder
    Remote access (when not authorized) TeamViewer, AnyDesk, LogMeIn, TightVNC, UltraVNC, RealVNC, Radmin, Chrome Remote Desktop, AmmyyAdmin, Splashtop
    P2P and torrent uTorrent, BitTorrent, qBittorrent, Vuze, Deluge, FrostWire, LimeWire, Shareaza, eMule
    Anonymizers Tor Browser (often on the Desktop or in AppData, missing from the program list), free VPN clients, proxy tools
    Games Third-party solitaire collections, Minecraft, Steam, Epic Games, Roblox, "free" game installers, Candy Crush (Store)
    Adware and PUPs Ask Toolbar, Conduit, Babylon, MyWebSearch, "PC Optimizer", "Driver Updater", registry cleaners, WebCompanion, Bonjour (if not needed)
    Old or vulnerable utilities Old CCleaner (5.33 shipped with malware), outdated Java, Adobe Flash Player, old VLC or 7-Zip (update these if required)
    Keyloggers and spyware Revealer Keylogger, Spyrix, Refog, Actual Keylogger, Kidlogger, "Free Keylogger"
    Hacking frameworks Metasploit, Armitage, Burp Suite, sqlmap, Nikto, Cheat Engine
    Servers nobody asked for FileZilla Server, Apache, XAMPP, WAMP, MySQL, TFTP servers (tftpd32/64), Python web server scripts

    Judge each tool by the README's scenario

    A tool counts as unauthorized when the company's work does not need it and it adds risk. If the README says staff do network analysis with Wireshark, keep it and update it.

    #Find portable and hidden programs

    Portable tools never appear in Programs and Features. Search the usual hiding places for programs, scripts and archives:

    $paths = @('C:\Users','C:\ProgramData','C:\Temp','C:\Windows\Temp','C:\inetpub','C:\Public','C:\Tools','C:\Downloads')
Get-ChildItem -Path $paths -Recurse -Force -File -Include *.exe,*.msi,*.bat,*.cmd,*.ps1,*.vbs,*.js,*.jar,*.py,*.zip,*.7z,*.rar -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object { $_.FullName -notmatch '\\AppData\\Local\\Microsoft\\|\\ProgramData\\Microsoft\\|\\ProgramData\\Package Cache\\' } |
    Select-Object FullName, Length, LastWriteTime | Format-Table -AutoSize

    Search the whole C: drive by tool name. It takes a few minutes, so run it in its own PowerShell window:

    $bad = 'wireshark|nmap|zenmap|^cain|^john|ophcrack|hashcat|netcat|^nc(64)?\.exe$|ncat|angry|ipscan|torrent|tor browser|keylog|mimikatz|pwdump|hydra|aircrack|metasploit|teamviewer|anydesk|vnc|psexec|lazagne|cheat ?engine'
Get-ChildItem -Path C:\ -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object { $_.Name -match $bad -and $_.FullName -notmatch '^C:\\Windows\\WinSxS' } |
    Select-Object FullName

    Places to look by hand:

    • C:\Program Files and C:\Program Files (x86): read the folder names
    • C:\ProgramData (hidden)
    • Each user's Desktop, Downloads, Documents, AppData\Local, AppData\Local\Programs and AppData\Roaming
    • C:\Users\Public and its subfolders
    • Any folder in the root of C:\ that Windows did not create (Get-ChildItem C:\ -Force)
    • The Startup folders (w11-malware)

    #Remove Microsoft Store games and apps

    Settings > Apps > Installed apps > the three dots > Uninstall. Remove games and unknown apps the README does not need. Leave system apps such as Microsoft Store, Calculator, Photos, Windows Security, Notepad and Terminal.

    To remove a Store app for every user from elevated PowerShell:

    Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers *<app-name>* | Remove-AppxPackage -AllUsers
    PreviousRemote Desktop, Remote Assistance and WinRMNextProhibited files (media, hacking files, passwords)
    W11

    Prohibited files (media, hacking files, passwords)

    jump:w11-files

    Forensics and required files first

    Do not delete the README, Forensics Question files, anything in the CyberPatriot folder, files a forensics question points to (until it is answered) or files the README calls company documents. Deleting a required file is a penalty.

    Fast path

    1. Open PowerShell as administrator.

    2. Find music and video in user folders:

      Get-ChildItem C:\Users -Recurse -Force -File -Include *.mp3,*.mp4,*.wav,*.avi,*.mkv,*.mov,*.flac,*.wma,*.wmv,*.ogg,*.m4a,*.aac -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object FullName -NotMatch '\\AppData\\' | Select-Object FullName

    3. Check each hit against the README and the forensics questions.

    4. Delete what is prohibited:

      Remove-Item "<path>" -Force

    5. Search for password files and hacking files the same way (passwords, hacking files).

    6. Empty the Recycle Bin: Clear-RecycleBin -Force.

    #Find media files in user folders

    Run in elevated PowerShell. This covers audio, video and image types and skips AppData:

    $ext = '*.mp3','*.mp4','*.m4a','*.m4v','*.wav','*.wma','*.wmv','*.flac','*.aac','*.ogg','*.avi','*.mov','*.mkv','*.flv','*.webm','*.mpg','*.mpeg','*.3gp','*.gif','*.jpg','*.jpeg','*.png','*.bmp','*.tif','*.tiff','*.heic'
Get-ChildItem -Path C:\Users -Recurse -Force -File -Include $ext -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object { $_.FullName -notmatch '\\AppData\\' } |
    Select-Object FullName, Length, LastWriteTime | Sort-Object FullName | Format-Table -AutoSize

    The same search in cmd (/a includes hidden and system files):

    dir /s /b /a C:\Users\*.mp3 C:\Users\*.mp4 C:\Users\*.wav C:\Users\*.avi C:\Users\*.mkv C:\Users\*.mov C:\Users\*.flac C:\Users\*.wma C:\Users\*.ogg C:\Users\*.m4a

    Most pictures are fine

    Wallpapers, profile pictures and company logos are legitimate. The media that scores is usually music and video the README calls non-work-related. Delete images only when they are clearly prohibited.

    #Search the whole C: drive for media

    This skips the Windows folders, which hold legitimate sounds such as C:\Windows\Media\*.wav (never delete those):

    $ext = '*.mp3','*.mp4','*.wav','*.avi','*.mkv','*.mov','*.flac','*.wma','*.ogg','*.m4a','*.wmv'
Get-ChildItem -Path C:\ -Recurse -Force -File -Include $ext -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object { $_.FullName -notmatch '^C:\\(Windows|Program Files\\WindowsApps|ProgramData\\Microsoft)\\' } |
    Select-Object FullName, Length

    #Find plaintext password files

    Search by file name:

    Get-ChildItem -Path C:\Users, C:\Temp, C:\ProgramData -Recurse -Force -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object { $_.Name -match 'pass|pwd|cred|login|secret|account|ssn|credit|card' } | Select-Object FullName

    Search inside text files for the word password:

    Get-ChildItem -Path C:\Users -Recurse -Force -File -Include *.txt,*.csv,*.xml,*.ini,*.cfg,*.conf,*.log -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object { $_.FullName -notmatch '\\AppData\\' } |
    Select-String -Pattern 'password|passwd|pwd' -List | Select-Object Path

    Office files need a manual look

    Select-String cannot read inside .docx or .xlsx files because they are zip archives. Find them by name and open the suspicious ones.

    #Find hacking-related files

    Look for packet captures (.pcap, .pcapng), wordlists (rockyou.txt, anything named wordlist), hash dumps, unauthorized password databases (.kdbx), scripts in user folders and archives that hold tools:

    Get-ChildItem -Path C:\Users, C:\ProgramData, C:\Temp -Recurse -Force -File -Include *.pcap,*.pcapng,*.cap,rockyou*,*wordlist*,*.hash,*.kdbx,*.ps1,*.bat,*.vbs,*.py,*.exe,*.zip,*.7z,*.rar -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object { $_.FullName -notmatch '\\AppData\\Local\\(Microsoft|Packages|Temp\\.*\\Microsoft)\\' } |
    Select-Object FullName, Length, LastWriteTime

    #Find hidden files and folders

    In File Explorer: View > Show > Hidden items, and View > Show > File name extensions.

    List hidden items in user folders from cmd:

    dir /a:h /s /b C:\Users

    The same in PowerShell, without the normal hidden profile files:

    Get-ChildItem -Path C:\Users -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object { $_.Attributes -match 'Hidden' -and $_.FullName -notmatch '\\AppData\\|ntuser|desktop\.ini' } | Select-Object FullName

    Show a file's attributes, then remove Hidden and System so you can see and delete it:

    attrib "<path>"

    attrib -h -s "<path>"

    #Check alternate data streams

    An alternate data stream hides data inside another file. A normal file has only the :$DATA stream, and downloaded files also carry Zone.Identifier.

    Show the streams on one file:

    Get-Item "<path>" -Stream *

    Find every file in user folders that has an extra stream:

    Get-ChildItem -Path C:\Users -Recurse -Force -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    ForEach-Object { Get-Item $_.FullName -Stream * -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue } |
    Where-Object { $_.Stream -notin ':$DATA','Zone.Identifier' } |
    Select-Object FileName, Stream, Length

    Read a stream (record it if a forensics question asks), then remove it:

    Get-Content "<path>" -Stream <stream-name>

    Remove-Item "<path>" -Stream <stream-name>

    In cmd, dir /r shows streams and more reads one:

    dir /r "<folder>"

    more < "<path>:<stream-name>"

    #Delete a file or folder

    Remove-Item "<path>" -Force

    Remove-Item "<folder>" -Recurse -Force

    del /f /a "<path>"

    rmdir /s /q "<folder>"

    If you get "Access denied", take ownership first (how). If the file is "in use", open resmon > CPU > Associated Handles, search for the file name and end that process.

    #Empty the Recycle Bin

    Files deleted in File Explorer go to the Recycle Bin and still exist. Remove-Item and del skip the bin. Empty your own bin on every drive:

    Clear-RecycleBin -Force

    Each user has a separate bin inside the hidden C:\$Recycle.Bin folder, one subfolder per user SID. List what is in all of them:

    Get-ChildItem 'C:\$Recycle.Bin' -Force -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object FullName

    Verify

    Run the searches again and nothing prohibited remains. Each scored file you removed shows up as a gain on the scoring report; the exact wording varies.

    PreviousUnauthorized software and hacking toolsNextMalware and persistence hunting
    W11

    Malware and persistence hunting

    jump:w11-malware

    Fast path

    1. Open PowerShell as administrator. The recon script covers most of these checks in one report.
    2. List listening ports with their programs (command). Anything in C:\Users, AppData, Temp or ProgramData, or named nc, is suspect.

    3. Check the Run and RunOnce keys:

      reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

    4. Check scheduled tasks outside \Microsoft\ (command).

    5. Check services that run from odd folders, the hosts file, IFEO debuggers and the Winlogon values (sections below).
    6. Record each finding for forensics, remove it, then delete its file.
    7. Run a Defender full scan: Start-MpScan -ScanType FullScan.

    #Find listening ports and their programs

    Run in elevated PowerShell:

    Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Sort-Object LocalPort | ForEach-Object {
    $p = Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
    [pscustomobject]@{ Addr = $_.LocalAddress; Port = $_.LocalPort; PID = $_.OwningProcess; Name = $p.ProcessName; Path = $p.Path }
} | Format-Table -AutoSize

    UDP endpoints:

    Get-NetUDPEndpoint | Sort-Object LocalPort | Select-Object LocalAddress, LocalPort, OwningProcess, @{n='Name';e={(Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).ProcessName}}

    The cmd equivalents. -b shows the program name and needs an elevated prompt:

    netstat -anob

    netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING

    tasklist /fi "PID eq <pid>"
    Port Normal owner on Windows 11
    135 svchost (RpcSs)
    139, 445 System (SMB, NetBIOS)
    5040 svchost (CDPSvc)
    5357 System (Web Services on Devices)
    7680 svchost (Delivery Optimization)
    49664-49670 lsass, wininit, services, svchost, spoolsv

    Suspicious: 4444, 1337, 31337, 6667, 8080 or 8888 owned by an unknown exe, 21 or 23 when the README does not need FTP or Telnet, any listener whose program sits in C:\Users, C:\Temp, AppData or ProgramData, and nc, ncat or powershell listening at all.

    Show the program behind a PID, then stop it:

    Get-Process -Id <pid> | Select-Object Id, ProcessName, Path

    Stop-Process -Id <pid> -Force

    Then remove its persistence (sections below) and delete the file after forensics.

    #Check Run and RunOnce keys

    reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce
reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer\Run

    HKCU shows only your own account. Users who are signed in have their hive under HKEY_USERS:

    Get-ChildItem Registry::HKEY_USERS | ForEach-Object {
    $k = "Registry::$($_.Name)\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"
    if (Test-Path $k) { "== $k"; Get-ItemProperty $k | Select-Object * -ExcludeProperty PS* | Format-List }
}

    For a user who is not signed in, load their hive, read it, and unload it:

    reg load HKU\Temp "C:\Users\<username>\NTUSER.DAT"
reg query HKU\Temp\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
reg unload HKU\Temp

    Remove a bad entry (use the key where you found it):

    reg delete HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run /v "<value-name>" /f

    Normal entries: SecurityHealth (SecurityHealthSystray.exe), OneDrive (in HKCU), VMware or VirtualBox tools, Edge autolaunch. Bad: anything that runs nc, powershell -enc, cmd /c, a script in Temp, AppData or Public, or an exe name you do not recognize.

    GUI: Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) > Startup apps > right-click > Disable, and regedit at the paths above.

    #Startup folders

    Open them:

    explorer shell:startup

    explorer "shell:common startup"
