    W11

    Windows troubleshooting

    jump:w11-troubleshoot

    Fast path

    1. Score went down: open your change log and undo the most recent change first.
    2. Wait 1-2 minutes and refresh the scoring report.
    3. Read the penalty line. It usually names the thing ("Critical service X stopped"); fix that exact thing (common causes).
    4. "Access denied": reopen the window with Run as administrator (details).
    5. "Running scripts is disabled": run Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Force.
    6. Report not updating: check the internet connection and the clock (details).

    #Fix a score that went down

    Undo the most recent change first and wait 1-2 minutes for the report to refresh.

    What you did Why it cost points Undo
    Deleted or demoted a README user or admin Authorized user removed Re-create the user or add them back to Administrators
    Disabled a required service (IIS, FTP, RDP, Spooler, SMB server) Critical service down Set-Service <service-name> -StartupType Automatic; Start-Service <service-name>
    Uninstalled required software Required program removed Reinstall it, for example winget install --id <package-id> -e
    Deleted a required file or company document Required file removed Restore it from the Recycle Bin (right-click > Restore)
    Removed a firewall rule a required service needs Service not reachable Re-enable the rule or rule group
    Blocked outbound traffic or broke the network Scoring cannot report Set DefaultOutboundAction to Allow and check the adapter is enabled in ncpa.cpl

    Penalties show in their own list

    The scoring report lists penalties separately from gains, and the text usually names the thing that broke. Every penalty is recoverable by undoing the change.

    #Get back in when you are locked out

    • Signed out and your password fails: type the README password exactly (case and symbols) and check Caps Lock and the keyboard layout.
    • Locked out by your own lockout policy: wait the lockout duration (30 minutes with the guide's settings), or sign in as another admin and clear the lockout in lusrmgr.msc > Users > the user > Properties > uncheck "Account is locked out".
    • Removed your own admin rights: sign in as another README admin and add yourself back. If no other admin exists, there is no fix inside the image; ask your coach about restarting the image (you lose time).

    To clear a lockout from another admin's elevated PowerShell (works on Home edition too):

    $u = [ADSI]"WinNT://./<username>,user"
$u.IsAccountLocked = $false
$u.SetInfo()

    Prevent lockouts

    Never change your own password, group membership or rights without writing it down. Never add Users or Administrators to "Deny log on locally". Keep one elevated window open while you change policy.

    #Fix PowerShell errors

    Message Fix
    "running scripts is disabled on this system" Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Force, then run the script again
    "'X' is not recognized as an internal or external command" You typed a PowerShell command in cmd (prompt starts C:\>, without PS). Type powershell first
    "The term 'X' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet" You are in PowerShell. Check the spelling. If the prompt is PowerShell 7 (pwsh), switch to Windows PowerShell (powershell.exe)
    winget is not recognized Update "App Installer" in the Microsoft Store, or use the app's own updater
    sc config does nothing or writes a file In PowerShell sc means Set-Content. Type sc.exe

    #Fix access denied

    1. Check the window is elevated: the title bar must say Administrator. If not, reopen it with right-click > Run as administrator.

    2. For a file or folder, take ownership and grant Administrators full control:

      takeown /f "<path>" /r /d y

      icacls "<path>" /grant Administrators:F /t

    3. For a registry key: regedit > right-click the key > Permissions > Advanced > Owner: Change to Administrators > Apply, then give Administrators Full Control.

    4. For Defender settings, Tamper Protection blocks changes. Turn it off in Windows Security, make the change, and turn it back on.
    5. Protected services such as WinDefend, WaaSMedicSvc and RpcSs cannot be changed in services.msc. That is normal.

    #Stop a service that will not stop

    • Set the startup type to Disabled first so nothing restarts it.
    • Stop services that depend on it: sc.exe enumdepend <service-name> lists them, or use Stop-Service <service-name> -Force.
    • Stuck in "Stopping": get its PID with sc.exe queryex <service-name>, then taskkill /PID <pid> /F.
    • It keeps coming back: in services.msc > the service > Recovery, set First, Second and Subsequent failures to Take No Action, and look for a scheduled task or Run key that restarts it (w11-malware).

    #Work without gpedit or secpol on Home edition

    Windows 11 Home has no gpedit.msc, secpol.msc or lusrmgr.msc. Check the edition with winver or:

    Get-ComputerInfo -Property WindowsProductName
    Task Use instead
    Users and groups net user, net localgroup, the PowerShell LocalAccounts cmdlets, netplwiz
    Password, lockout, audit and user rights net accounts, auditpol, and the secedit export, edit and import method (w11-passpol, w11-secopts)
    Administrative Template policies Their registry values under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies (w11-registry)

    #Scoring report not updating

    • Wait 2 minutes and refresh the page (F5).

    • Test the internet connection; TcpTestSucceeded should be True:

      Test-NetConnection www.google.com -Port 443

    • Check you did not block outbound traffic and that the hosts file does not redirect scoring sites.

    • In services.msc, find the CyberPatriot scoring service and check it is Running. If it stopped, start it. Change nothing else about it.
    • Check the clock: Settings > Time & language > Date & time > Sync now. A wrong clock breaks HTTPS.
    • If it is still stuck, ask your coach. Never reinstall or modify the scoring client.

    #Find answers in Event Viewer

    Open eventvwr.msc > Windows Logs > Security (or System). Right-click the log > Filter Current Log > type the Event IDs.

    ID Log Meaning
    4624 Security Successful logon (Logon Type 2 local, 3 network, 10 Remote Desktop)
    4625 Security Failed logon
    4634, 4647 Security Logoff
    4648 Security Logon with explicit credentials (runas)
    4672 Security Admin privileges assigned at logon
    4688 Security New process created (needs process creation auditing)
    4697 Security Service installed (needs Security System Extension auditing)
    4698 Security Scheduled task created (needs Other Object Access auditing)
    4719 Security Audit policy changed
    4720 Security User account created
    4722, 4725 Security User enabled, user disabled
    4723, 4724 Security Password change attempt, password reset attempt
    4726 Security User deleted
    4732 Security Member added to a security-enabled local group, such as Administrators
    4733 Security Member removed from a security-enabled local group
    4740 Security Account locked out
    1102 Security Security log cleared
    7045 System New service installed
    7040 System Service start type changed
    104 System An event log was cleared (System or another log)
    4104 PowerShell Operational Script block logged
    1116, 1117 Defender Operational Malware detected, action taken
    5001 Defender Operational Real-time protection turned off
    5007 Defender Operational Defender configuration changed (exclusions show up here)

    Pull the common ones from PowerShell:

    Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4720,4732} -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, @{n='Msg';e={($_.Message -split "`n")[0]}}

    Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; Id=7045} -MaxEvents 20 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Format-List TimeCreated, Message

    Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational'; Id=1116,1117,5001,5007} -MaxEvents 30 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Format-List TimeCreated, Id, Message

    Logs answer forensics questions

    Event logs often answer "which user was created", "when was the backdoor service installed" or "which account logged in remotely". Read them before you change anything, and never clear them.

    #Other quick fixes

    Problem Fix
    A Settings page says "Some settings are managed by your organization" A policy is set. Find it under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies or in gpedit (All Settings sorted by State)
    A change in secpol does not show Close and reopen secpol.msc, then run gpupdate /force
    Windows Update error 0x8024402c or 0x80244022 A planted WSUS server or proxy. Delete WUServer and UseWUServer (w11-updates) and run netsh winhttp reset proxy
    Cannot delete a file that is "in use" resmon > CPU > Associated Handles > search the file name > End Process
    Explorer crashed or the screen is black Ctrl+Shift+Esc > Run new task > explorer.exe
    Restart only Explorer Stop-Process -Name explorer -Force (it restarts itself)
    Network adapter disabled ncpa.cpl > right-click the adapter > Enable

    SRV

    Server master checklist

    jump:srv-checklist

    Work top to bottom. Items marked (DC) apply only on a domain controller. Items marked (role) apply only when that role is installed and the README needs it. Anything that works the same as on Windows 11 links to the Windows 11 section instead of repeating it here.

    Read the README first, every time

    The README decides which users are authorized, who is an admin, and which roles and services are required (for example "this server must continue to provide DNS and IIS"). Removing a required role or stopping a required service costs points and usually breaks other scoring checks too.

    #First 10 minutes on the server

    #Decide: standalone server or domain controller

    #Domain users and groups

    #Domain policy (GPO)

    #Active Directory hardening

    #Roles and features

    #Role hardening

    #Remote access

    #Services

    #Updates, Defender and firewall

    #Same as Windows 11

    #Final pass

    PreviousWindows troubleshootingNextHow Server differs from Windows 11
    SRV

    How Server differs from Windows 11

    jump:srv-differences

    Fast path

    1. Open PowerShell as administrator (Start, type powershell, Run as administrator).

    2. Read the domain role number:

      (Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem).DomainRole

    3. If it prints 4 or 5, the server is a domain controller: work from AD users and Group Policy on a domain.

    4. If it prints 2 (standalone) or 3 (member server), use the Windows 11 sections for users and local policy, then come back for roles.

    5. On a DC, record the starting health so you can tell later what you broke:

      dcdiag /q

    #Check if the server is a domain controller

    Run this in any PowerShell window. It needs no extra modules:

    (Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem).DomainRole
    Value Meaning Where users and policy live
    0 Standalone workstation Local
    1 Member workstation Local, plus domain GPOs
    2 Standalone server Local (lusrmgr.msc, secpol.msc)
    3 Member server Local users exist, but domain GPOs override local policy
    4 Backup domain controller (any DC that is not the PDC emulator) Active Directory and domain GPOs
    5 Primary domain controller (holds the PDC emulator role) Active Directory and domain GPOs

    Other confirmations if you want a second opinion. On a DC this returns the DC's details; elsewhere it errors:

    Get-ADDomainController

    The NTDS service exists only on a DC:

    Get-Service NTDS

    From cmd, dcdiag /q prints only errors, net user /domain lists domain users, and nltest finds the DC for a domain:

    dcdiag /q
net user /domain
nltest /dsgetdc:<domain-name>

    On a non-domain server, net user /domain fails with "System error 1355 has occurred. The specified domain either does not exist or could not be contacted."

    In the GUI, Server Manager > Dashboard shows an AD DS tile on a DC, and Server Manager > Tools lists Active Directory Users and Computers. Opening lusrmgr.msc on a DC shows an error saying the snap-in cannot be used on a domain controller.

    AD DS installed does not mean promoted

    Get-WindowsFeature AD-Domain-Services showing Installed only proves the role binaries are there. A server can have the role installed and never have been promoted. Trust DomainRole or Get-Service NTDS.

    Member servers

    DomainRole 3 means the server is joined to a domain but is not a DC. Local users still exist (use Windows 11 users), but GPOs from the domain override local policy. In CyberPatriot the Server image is usually standalone (2) or a DC (4 or 5).

    #What changes on a DC

    Area Windows 11 Server 2022 standalone Server 2022 domain controller
    Users lusrmgr.msc, netplwiz Same as Windows 11 dsa.msc or AD PowerShell; no local users
    Password and lockout policy secpol.msc secpol.msc Default Domain Policy GPO in gpmc.msc
    Audit, user rights, security options secpol.msc secpol.msc Default Domain Controllers Policy GPO
    Optional software optionalfeatures.exe Server Manager roles and features, Get-WindowsFeature Same as standalone
    Settings app Windows 11 layout Windows 10 layout: Settings > Update & Security Same as standalone
    Admin console Settings, Control Panel Server Manager (opens at logon), sconfig Same, plus AD consoles
    Browser Edge Edge, plus Internet Explorer 11 with IE Enhanced Security Configuration Same as standalone
    Defender Always present Removable feature Windows-Defender, automatic role exclusions Same as standalone
    Microsoft Store and consumer apps Present Not present Not present
    Built-in Administrator Disabled by default Enabled, usually the logon account Domain Administrator, usually the logon account

    #Server Manager

    Open it from Start > Server Manager (it also opens at every logon).

    • Local Server shows firewall state, Remote management (WinRM), Remote Desktop, IE Enhanced Security Configuration, Windows Update, Microsoft Defender Antivirus and time zone. Click a value to open that setting.
    • Manage > Add Roles and Features and Manage > Remove Roles and Features install and remove roles.
    • Tools launches every admin console: ADUC, DNS, DHCP, Group Policy Management, IIS Manager, Services, Event Viewer.
    • The flag icon at the top shows pending tasks and post-deployment warnings.

    #Roles and features

    A role is a server job: AD DS, DNS Server, DHCP Server, Web Server (IIS), File and Storage Services, Remote Access, Fax Server. A feature is supporting software: Telnet Client, SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support, Windows PowerShell 2.0 Engine, SNMP Service, RSAT tools. Get-WindowsFeature lists both and Uninstall-WindowsFeature removes both (removal).

    #No local users on a domain controller

    Promoting a server to DC replaces the local accounts database with Active Directory, so every user is a domain user. The only local account left is the DSRM (Directory Services Restore Mode) administrator, which is used only when you boot into DSRM (DSRM). Do all user work in ADUC or AD PowerShell (AD users).

    #Why secpol.msc changes do not stick on a DC

    Group Policy applies Local, then Site, then Domain, then OU, and the later one wins. secpol.msc and gpedit.msc edit only the Local policy, so any domain GPO that sets the same thing overrides them.

    • Password, lockout and Kerberos policy for domain accounts come only from a GPO linked at the domain root, normally the Default Domain Policy. Setting them in secpol.msc on a DC changes nothing useful.
    • User rights and many security options on DCs come from the Default Domain Controllers Policy (linked to the Domain Controllers OU).
    • A setting that no domain GPO defines does take effect from local policy, but on a DC edit the GPOs anyway so the scoring engine and gpresult agree (GPO guide).

    #Defender on Server

    • Microsoft Defender Antivirus is the removable feature Windows-Defender. If it is gone, reinstall it (how).
    • Server roles get automatic exclusions (AD database, SYSVOL, DNS, DHCP, IIS paths). They do not show in Get-MpPreference and they are normal. Remove only exclusions that Get-MpPreference lists.
    • Defender on Server does not switch itself to passive mode when another antivirus is installed.

    Everything else (real-time protection, scans, policy keys) works as on Windows 11 (Defender).

    #What IE Enhanced Security Configuration does

    Server Manager > Local Server > IE Enhanced Security Configuration. Keep it On for both Administrators and Users; turning it off is a classic planted weakness. It only affects Internet Explorer, so download any tool you need with Edge (how).

    #sconfig menu on Server 2022

    Run sconfig in an elevated PowerShell or command prompt. It starts by itself only on Server Core; on Desktop Experience you type it.

    Option Does
    1 Domain or workgroup membership
    2 Computer name
    3 Add local administrator (not used on a DC)
    4 Remote management (WinRM)
    5 Update setting: A Automatic, D Download only, M Manual
    6 Install updates: 1 all quality updates, 2 recommended quality updates, 3 feature updates
    7 Remote desktop
    8 Network settings
    9 Date and time
    10 Telemetry setting
    11 Windows activation
    12 Log off user
    13 Restart server
    14 Shut down server
    15 Exit to command line (PowerShell)

    #Server-only services you will see

    Service name Display name Belongs to
    NTDS Active Directory Domain Services DC
    Kdc Kerberos Key Distribution Center DC
    Netlogon Netlogon DC (also runs on members)
    ADWS Active Directory Web Services DC; AD PowerShell and ADAC need it
    DFSR DFS Replication DC; replicates SYSVOL
    Dfs DFS Namespace DC; serves the \\<domain-name>\SYSVOL path
    IsmServ Intersite Messaging DC
    DNS DNS Server DNS role
    DHCPServer DHCP Server DHCP role
    W3SVC and WAS World Wide Web Publishing Service, Windows Process Activation Service IIS
    ftpsvc Microsoft FTP Service IIS FTP
    WMSVC Web Management Service IIS remote management
    CertSvc Active Directory Certificate Services AD CS
    RemoteAccess Routing and Remote Access Remote Access role

    #Ports a domain controller needs open

    The AD DS and DNS roles create firewall rules for these. If you tighten the firewall on a DC, keep these inbound rules and do not delete the role rule groups.

    Port Protocol Use
    53 TCP and UDP DNS
    88 TCP and UDP Kerberos
    123 UDP Time (W32Time)
    135 TCP RPC endpoint mapper
    389 TCP and UDP LDAP
    445 TCP SMB (SYSVOL, NETLOGON, GPOs)
    464 TCP and UDP Kerberos password change
    636 TCP LDAPS
    3268 and 3269 TCP Global Catalog and Global Catalog over SSL
    9389 TCP AD Web Services
    49152-65535 TCP Dynamic RPC (replication, management)
    67 UDP DHCP (DHCP role only)
    80 and 443 TCP IIS (web role only)
    21 TCP FTP (FTP role only, plus its passive range)
    3389 TCP RDP (only if required)
    5985 and 5986 TCP WinRM HTTP and HTTPS

    Everything else about the firewall works as on Windows 11 (firewall). Never block outbound traffic.

    PreviousServer master checklistNextAD users and groups
    SRV

    AD users and groups

    jump:srv-ad-users

    This applies on a DC (or a member server with the RSAT AD tools). On a standalone server use Windows 11 users.

    The README is the only list that counts

    Remove or disable exactly the users the README does not authorize, and follow its wording ("remove" or "disable"). Never delete krbtgt, the built-in Administrator you are logged in as, or computer accounts. If the README says someone is a standard user, take them out of every admin group and keep the account.

    Fast path

    1. Open PowerShell as administrator and load the AD module:

      Import-Module ActiveDirectory

    2. List every domain user and compare with the README:

      Get-ADUser -Filter * | Sort-Object SamAccountName | Format-Table Name,SamAccountName,Enabled -AutoSize

    3. Disable a user the README does not list (or remove them if it says remove):

      Disable-ADAccount -Identity <username>

    4. List Domain Admins and remove anyone the README does not name as an admin:

      Get-ADGroupMember "Domain Admins" -Recursive | Select-Object SamAccountName

      Remove-ADGroupMember -Identity "Domain Admins" -Members <username> -Confirm:$false

    5. Check the other privileged groups (table).

    6. Disable Guest and clear the risky account flags (flags).

    #Open the ADUC and ADAC consoles

    • Active Directory Users and Computers: Win+R, type dsa.msc (or Server Manager > Tools > Active Directory Users and Computers).
    • In ADUC turn on View > Advanced Features. Without it you cannot see the Attribute Editor tab, the System container or the Object tab with deletion protection.
    • Active Directory Administrative Center: Win+R, type dsac.exe. It has a global search box and a PowerShell History pane at the bottom that shows the cmdlet behind every GUI action.
    • Users and groups live mostly in the Users and Builtin containers, but attackers also create OUs. Expand every OU.

    #List every domain user

    Get-ADUser -Filter * | Sort-Object SamAccountName | Format-Table Name,SamAccountName,Enabled -AutoSize

    All properties of one user (description, logon script, flags, group memberships):

    Get-ADUser -Identity <username> -Properties *

    Risky flags for every user in one table:

    Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties PasswordNeverExpires,PasswordNotRequired,DoesNotRequirePreAuth,AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption,CannotChangePassword,AdminCount | Format-Table SamAccountName,Enabled,PasswordNeverExpires,PasswordNotRequired,DoesNotRequirePreAuth,AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption,CannotChangePassword,AdminCount -AutoSize

    #Read the description and logon script fields

    Attackers and Forensics Questions hide passwords in the Description field and malicious logon scripts in ScriptPath (they run from \\<domain-name>\NETLOGON). List every user that has either:

    Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties Description,ScriptPath | Where-Object { $_.Description -or $_.ScriptPath } | Select-Object SamAccountName,Description,ScriptPath

    Open a script it names from C:\Windows\SYSVOL\sysvol\<domain-name>\scripts.

    #Compare AD users to the README

    Save the authorized usernames (sAMAccountName, one per line) as authorized.txt on the desktop, then list every account that is not on it. Built-in accounts are skipped:

    $authorized = Get-Content "$env:USERPROFILE\Desktop\authorized.txt" | ForEach-Object { $_.Trim() } | Where-Object { $_ }
$builtin = 'Administrator','Guest','krbtgt'
Get-ADUser -Filter * | Where-Object { $authorized -notcontains $_.SamAccountName -and $builtin -notcontains $_.SamAccountName } | Select-Object SamAccountName,Name,Enabled

    Every name it prints is not in the README. Do the same for admins with admins.txt:

    $admins = Get-Content "$env:USERPROFILE\Desktop\admins.txt" | ForEach-Object { $_.Trim() } | Where-Object { $_ }
Get-ADGroupMember "Domain Admins" -Recursive | Where-Object { $admins -notcontains $_.SamAccountName -and $_.SamAccountName -ne 'Administrator' } | Select-Object SamAccountName,objectClass

    #Check privileged group membership

    This loop prints the members of every privileged group. -Recursive expands nested groups, so a user hidden inside another group still shows up:

    $groups = 'Domain Admins','Enterprise Admins','Schema Admins','Administrators','Account Operators','Backup Operators','Server Operators','Print Operators','DnsAdmins','Group Policy Creator Owners','Remote Desktop Users','Remote Management Users','Protected Users'
foreach ($g in $groups) {
  "=== $g ==="
  try { Get-ADGroupMember -Identity $g -Recursive -ErrorAction Stop | Select-Object -ExpandProperty SamAccountName }
  catch { "  (error or group not present: $($_.Exception.Message))" }
}

    -Recursive flattens groups, so Builtin Administrators shows users only. To see which groups are nested directly inside it, drop -Recursive:

    Get-ADGroupMember -Identity Administrators | Select-Object SamAccountName,objectClass

    Expected defaults on a fresh Server 2022 domain:

    Group Container Expected members Why it matters
    Domain Admins Users Administrator plus README admins Full control of the domain
    Enterprise Admins Users (forest root only) Administrator Full control of the forest
    Schema Admins Users (forest root only) Administrator Can change the AD schema
    Administrators Builtin Administrator, Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins Full control of every DC
    Account Operators Builtin Empty Can create and change most users and groups
    Backup Operators Builtin Empty Can back up ntds.dit, which holds every password hash
    Server Operators Builtin Empty Can log on to DCs, change services, back up
    Print Operators Builtin Empty Can log on to DCs and load printer drivers
    DnsAdmins Users (exists only with the DNS role) Empty Can make the DNS service load a DLL as SYSTEM on the DC
    Group Policy Creator Owners Users Administrator Can create GPOs
    Remote Desktop Users Builtin Empty, or README RDP users RDP access
    Remote Management Users Builtin Empty WinRM and PowerShell remoting access
    Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access Builtin Authenticated Users Everyone or ANONYMOUS LOGON here allows anonymous users to read AD (fix)
    Protected Users Users Empty (optional hardening) Details

    In the GUI: dsa.msc > Users (or Builtin) > double-click the group > Members tab.

    #Remove a user from a privileged group

    Remove-ADGroupMember -Identity "Domain Admins" -Members <username> -Confirm:$false

    GUI: dsa.msc > Users > Domain Admins > Members tab > select the user > Remove > OK.

    Check Domain Admins and Builtin Administrators

    A user added directly to Builtin\Administrators is a full admin on every DC but does not appear in Domain Admins. Check Enterprise Admins and Schema Admins as well. Group changes take effect at that user's next logon.

    #Find users hidden through primary group

    A user whose primary group is Domain Admins (RID 512) does not appear in the group's member attribute. Get-ADGroupMember and ADUC still show them, but list every user whose primary group is not Domain Users to be sure:

    Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties PrimaryGroupID | Where-Object { $_.PrimaryGroupID -ne 513 -and $_.SamAccountName -ne 'Guest' } | Select-Object SamAccountName,PrimaryGroupID
    PrimaryGroupID Group
    513 Domain Users (normal)
    514 Domain Guests (normal for Guest)
    512 Domain Admins
    518 Schema Admins
    519 Enterprise Admins

    To fix one: dsa.msc > user > Member Of tab > select Domain Users > Set Primary Group, then remove the admin group.

    #Add a README-required admin

    Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "Domain Admins" -Members <username>

    If the README says "administrator" without naming a group, Domain Admins is the normal choice on a DC; it is already nested in Builtin Administrators.

    #Disable or remove an unauthorized user

    Disable the account:

    Disable-ADAccount -Identity <username>

    Or delete it, if the README says remove:

    Remove-ADUser -Identity <username> -Confirm:$false

    dsa.msc > right-click the user > Disable Account, or Delete.

    Check the result. Enabled should be False, or you get "Cannot find an object" after removal:

    Get-ADUser -Identity <username>

    If Remove-ADUser fails with "Access is denied" even as Domain Admin, the object is protected from accidental deletion. Clear the protection, then delete again:

    Get-ADUser -Identity <username> | Set-ADObject -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion $false

    In ADUC (with Advanced Features on): user > Properties > Object tab > clear Protect object from accidental deletion.

    #Disable the domain Guest account

    Disable-ADAccount -Identity Guest
Get-ADUser -Identity Guest | Select-Object Name,Enabled

    Enabled should read False.

    #The domain Administrator account

    • Do not disable the built-in Administrator if you are logged in as it or the README names it as your account.
    • Give it a strong password if the README allows changing it.
    • Rename it only if the README asks, with the GPO setting Accounts: Rename administrator account in the Default Domain Policy. You must then log in with the new name.

    #Reset a user's password

    $pw = ConvertTo-SecureString '<team-password>' -AsPlainText -Force
Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity <username> -Reset -NewPassword $pw

    GUI: dsa.msc > right-click the user > Reset Password. Use the team password unless the README gives one.

    #Reset every user's password at once

    Run this only if the README or scoring points at weak passwords. It skips you and the built-in accounts, and prints each name it changes:

    $pw = ConvertTo-SecureString '<team-password>' -AsPlainText -Force
Get-ADUser -Filter 'Enabled -eq $true' | Where-Object { $_.SamAccountName -notin @($env:USERNAME,'Administrator','krbtgt','Guest') } | ForEach-Object { Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity $_ -Reset -NewPassword $pw; $_.SamAccountName }

    The policy can reject the reset

    "The password does not meet the length, complexity, or history requirement" means the new password breaks the domain policy. An admin reset still has to meet the minimum length and complexity (minimum age and history are not checked on a reset). Use a longer password.

    #Fix dangerous account flags

    These are the Account options on dsa.msc > user > Properties > Account tab.

    Property Checkbox in ADUC Want Fix
    PasswordNeverExpires Password never expires False Set-ADUser <username> -PasswordNeverExpires $false
    PasswordNotRequired No checkbox (userAccountControl flag 32) False Set-ADUser <username> -PasswordNotRequired $false
    CannotChangePassword User cannot change password False Set-ADUser <username> -CannotChangePassword $false
    AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption Store password using reversible encryption False Set-ADUser <username> -AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption $false
    DoesNotRequirePreAuth Do not require Kerberos preauthentication False Set-ADAccountControl <username> -DoesNotRequirePreAuth $false
    UseDESKeyOnly Use only Kerberos DES encryption types for this account False Set-ADAccountControl <username> -UseDESKeyOnly $false
    AccountNotDelegated Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated True for admins Set-ADUser <username> -AccountNotDelegated $true
    TrustedForDelegation Delegation tab: Trust this user for delegation to any service False for users Set-ADAccountControl <username> -TrustedForDelegation $false

    Set-ADUser has no preauth or DES switch, which is why those two rows use Set-ADAccountControl.

    Fix every user at once. The block reads all users once, then clears each flag only where it is set. Guest and krbtgt are skipped where it matters:

    $all = Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties PasswordNeverExpires,PasswordNotRequired,DoesNotRequirePreAuth,AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption,CannotChangePassword,UseDESKeyOnly
$all | Where-Object PasswordNotRequired | Set-ADUser -PasswordNotRequired $false
$all | Where-Object DoesNotRequirePreAuth | Set-ADAccountControl -DoesNotRequirePreAuth $false
$all | Where-Object AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption | Set-ADUser -AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption $false
$all | Where-Object UseDESKeyOnly | Set-ADAccountControl -UseDESKeyOnly $false
$all | Where-Object { $_.CannotChangePassword -and $_.SamAccountName -ne 'Guest' } | Set-ADUser -CannotChangePassword $false
$all | Where-Object { $_.PasswordNeverExpires -and $_.SamAccountName -notin @('krbtgt','Guest') } | Set-ADUser -PasswordNeverExpires $false

    Verify

    Both commands should print nothing except accounts you deliberately left alone (Guest, a README service account):

    Search-ADAccount -PasswordNeverExpires -UsersOnly | Select-Object SamAccountName

    Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties PasswordNotRequired,DoesNotRequirePreAuth,AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption | Where-Object { $_.PasswordNotRequired -or $_.DoesNotRequirePreAuth -or $_.AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption } | Select-Object SamAccountName

    Before clearing Password never expires on your own account

    If your logon account's password is older than the maximum password age, you will be forced to change it at next logon. Know its password (or reset it to the team password) first. A README-listed service account may legitimately need a non-expiring password.

    Clearing PasswordNotRequired only stops future blank passwords. A user who already has a blank password keeps it, so reset the password of every user that had the flag.

    Why these flags are scored

    With DoesNotRequirePreAuth set, anyone can request an encrypted blob for that user and crack it offline (AS-REP roasting). Reversible encryption stores a recoverable password. Accounts with a service principal name (SPN) can be Kerberoasted: anyone can request a service ticket and crack it offline, so they need long passwords. DES keys are trivially broken.

    #Find accounts with SPNs (Kerberoastable)

    Get-ADUser -Filter 'ServicePrincipalName -like "*"' -Properties ServicePrincipalName | Select-Object SamAccountName,@{n='SPNs';e={$_.ServicePrincipalName -join '; '}}
    • krbtgt always has kadmin/changepw. That is normal.
    • Any other user with an SPN is a service account. If the README does not mention it, remove the SPN or at least give the account a long password:
    Set-ADUser <username> -ServicePrincipalNames @{Remove='<spn>'}

    #Find accounts that were once admins (AdminCount)

    Get-ADUser -Filter 'AdminCount -eq 1' | Select-Object SamAccountName

    AdminCount=1 is stamped on members of protected groups (Domain Admins, Administrators, Account, Backup, Server and Print Operators and others) and is not cleared when the user leaves the group. Use the list to find former admins and confirm they are out of every privileged group.

    Clearing it is optional. Clear the attribute, then turn permission inheritance back on in dsa.msc > user > Security tab > Advanced > Enable inheritance:

    Set-ADUser <username> -Clear adminCount

    #Search-ADAccount quick finds

    Find Command
    Passwords that never expire Search-ADAccount -PasswordNeverExpires -UsersOnly
    Disabled users Search-ADAccount -AccountDisabled -UsersOnly
    Locked-out users Search-ADAccount -LockedOut -UsersOnly
    Expired passwords Search-ADAccount -PasswordExpired -UsersOnly
    No logon in 90 days Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 90.00:00:00 -UsersOnly
    Expired accounts Search-ADAccount -AccountExpired -UsersOnly

    Clear the lockout on an authorized user:

    Unlock-ADAccount -Identity <username>

    Enable an authorized user who is disabled:

    Enable-ADAccount -Identity <username>

    #Create users and groups the README asks for

    Create the user with the team password, enabled. Without -Path it lands in the Users container:

    $pw = ConvertTo-SecureString '<team-password>' -AsPlainText -Force
New-ADUser -Name "<username>" -SamAccountName "<username>" -UserPrincipalName "<username>@<domain-name>" -AccountPassword $pw -Enabled $true

    To put it in an OU, add -Path "<ou-dn>", where the OU's distinguished name looks like OU=Staff,DC=corp,DC=local.

    Create a global security group and add members:

    New-ADGroup -Name "<groupname>" -GroupScope Global -GroupCategory Security
Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "<groupname>" -Members <username>

    Check it: Get-ADGroupMember "<groupname>" | Select-Object SamAccountName.

    GUI: dsa.msc > right-click Users > New > User (or Group, with scope Global and type Security).

    Copy names exactly

    Scoring checks the exact sAMAccountName and group name from the README. Copy and paste them.

    #Check computer accounts, SIDHistory and logon scripts

    List computer objects. Remove an unknown one only if it is clearly rogue (rarely scored) and never delete the DC:

    Get-ADComputer -Filter * | Select-Object Name,Enabled

    SIDHistory is an advanced backdoor and should be empty in a fresh domain:

    Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties SIDHistory | Where-Object SIDHistory | Select-Object SamAccountName,SIDHistory

    Users with a logon script. Inspect each script in C:\Windows\SYSVOL\sysvol\<domain-name>\scripts:

    Get-ADUser -Filter 'ScriptPath -like "*"' -Properties ScriptPath | Select-Object SamAccountName,ScriptPath
    PreviousHow Server differs from Windows 11NextGroup Policy on a domain
    SRV

    Group Policy on a domain

    jump:srv-gpo

    On a DC the domain GPOs hold password, lockout, Kerberos, audit, user rights and security options. secpol.msc on a DC edits only local policy, which domain GPOs override (why).

    Back up GPOs before editing

    One wrong user right in the Default Domain Controllers Policy can lock everyone out of the DC. Back up first (how) and keep an elevated PowerShell window open while you edit.

    Fast path

    1. Back up every GPO from an elevated PowerShell window:

      New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path C:\GPOBackup -Force | Out-Null
Backup-GPO -All -Path C:\GPOBackup

    2. Run gpmc.msc and open Forest > Domains > your domain. Right-click Default Domain Policy > Edit.

    3. Go to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies and set Password Policy and Account Lockout Policy from the tables below.

    4. Apply and check the result:

      gpupdate /force
Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy

    5. Set audit policy, user rights and security options in the Default Domain Controllers Policy instead (how).

    6. List every GPO and its links and look for planted ones (how).

    #Which GPO holds which setting

    Setting Edit it in Linked at
    Password policy, account lockout, Kerberos policy Default Domain Policy (or another GPO linked at the domain root) Domain root
    Audit policy, user rights assignment Default Domain Controllers Policy Domain Controllers OU
    DC security options (LDAP signing, SMB signing, NTLM) Default Domain Controllers Policy Domain Controllers OU
    Security options for every computer in the domain Default Domain Policy Domain root
    Administrative Templates (Defender, Windows Update, RDP) for DCs Default Domain Controllers Policy, or the GPO already setting it Domain Controllers OU

    Account policies set in an OU-linked GPO or in the Default Domain Controllers Policy do nothing for domain accounts. They only work from a GPO linked at the domain root.

    #Back up and restore GPOs

    Back up all GPOs (create the folder first):

    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path C:\GPOBackup -Force | Out-Null
Backup-GPO -All -Path C:\GPOBackup

    Restore one GPO from that backup:

    Restore-GPO -Name "<gpo-name>" -Path C:\GPOBackup

    #Open the Group Policy Management console

    Run gpmc.msc (or Server Manager > Tools > Group Policy Management) and expand Forest > Domains > your domain.

    • GPOs linked directly under the domain node (for example Default Domain Policy) apply to every user and computer in the domain.
    • The Domain Controllers OU has Default Domain Controllers Policy linked, which applies to DCs only.
    • The Group Policy Objects container lists every GPO, linked or not.

    To edit, right-click the GPO or its link > Edit. Every security setting is under Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings.

    #Set the domain password policy

    Path: gpmc.msc > Default Domain Policy > Edit > Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies > Password Policy.

    Setting Recommended Default in a new domain
    Enforce password history 24 passwords remembered 24
    Maximum password age 60 days (30-90 is fine) 42
    Minimum password age 1 day 1
    Minimum password length 14 characters (at least 10) 7
    Password must meet complexity requirements Enabled Enabled
    Store passwords using reversible encryption Disabled Disabled

    The editor accepts at most 14 for minimum length unless Relax minimum password length limits (same folder) is Enabled. 14 is enough for CyberPatriot. Never set a length your own team password does not meet.

    #Set the domain lockout policy

    Path: same GPO > Account Policies > Account Lockout Policy.

    Setting Recommended Default
    Account lockout threshold 5 to 10 invalid attempts (never 0) 0 (no lockout)
    Account lockout duration 30 minutes or more Not defined
    Reset account lockout counter after 30 minutes (no longer than the duration) Not defined

    Setting the threshold makes the editor offer values for the other two; accept them, then change them to the table values. Fully updated builds may also show Allow Administrator account lockout, which applies to local Administrator accounts; leave it at its default unless the README mentions it.

    #Check the Kerberos policy

    Path: same GPO > Account Policies > Kerberos Policy. These settings exist only in domain GPOs. The defaults are already secure, so scoring checks that nobody weakened them.

    Setting Secure value (default)
    Enforce user logon restrictions Enabled
    Maximum lifetime for service ticket 600 minutes
    Maximum lifetime for user ticket 10 hours
    Maximum lifetime for user ticket renewal 7 days
    Maximum tolerance for computer clock synchronization 5 minutes

    #Apply and verify the domain password policy

    gpupdate /force
net accounts

    Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy

    On a DC, net accounts shows the domain values. Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy reads them straight from the domain object. If they disagree, run gpupdate /force again after a minute.

    #Set the domain password policy with PowerShell

    This writes the domain object directly. Time spans use days.hours:minutes:seconds, so 60.00:00:00 is 60 days and 00:30:00 is 30 minutes. The observation window must not be longer than the lockout duration.

    Set-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy -Identity (Get-ADDomain).DNSRoot -MinPasswordLength 14 -PasswordHistoryCount 24 -MaxPasswordAge 60.00:00:00 -MinPasswordAge 1.00:00:00 -ComplexityEnabled $true -ReversibleEncryptionEnabled $false -LockoutThreshold 5 -LockoutDuration 00:30:00 -LockoutObservationWindow 00:30:00
Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy

    The GPO overwrites the PowerShell change

    The next time the Default Domain Policy is processed (an edit to the GPO, gpupdate /force, or the periodic security refresh), its values overwrite what Set-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy wrote. Make the GPO match, or the change silently reverts.

    #Find and fix fine-grained password policies

    Fine-grained password policies (Password Settings Objects, PSOs) override the domain policy for the users and groups they apply to. Attackers plant weak ones (length 0, no complexity, no lockout) on Domain Users or on one admin.

    List every PSO with its settings:

    Get-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy -Filter * | Format-List Name,Precedence,MinPasswordLength,ComplexityEnabled,PasswordHistoryCount,MaxPasswordAge,MinPasswordAge,LockoutThreshold,LockoutDuration,ReversibleEncryptionEnabled,AppliesTo

    See which PSO actually applies to one user. No output means the domain policy applies:

    Get-ADUserResultantPasswordPolicy -Identity <username>

    Strengthen a PSO the README wants kept:

    Set-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy -Identity "<pso-name>" -MinPasswordLength 14 -ComplexityEnabled $true -PasswordHistoryCount 24 -LockoutThreshold 5 -ReversibleEncryptionEnabled $false

    Delete a PSO the README does not mention. Clear its deletion protection first:

    Set-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy -Identity "<pso-name>" -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion $false
Remove-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy -Identity "<pso-name>" -Confirm:$false

    GUI: dsac.exe > your domain > System > Password Settings Container. When several PSOs apply to one user, the lowest Precedence number wins.

    #Settings that go in the Default Domain Controllers Policy

    gpmc.msc > Domains > your domain > Domain Controllers > Default Domain Controllers Policy > Edit. Set audit, user rights and DC security options here, not in secpol.msc.

    #Audit policy for domain controllers

    Path: Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Audit Policy. Set Success and Failure on:

    • Audit account logon events
    • Audit account management
    • Audit directory service access
    • Audit logon events
    • Audit object access
    • Audit policy change
    • Audit privilege use
    • Audit system events
    • Audit process tracking (Success at least)

    For finer control use Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Audit Policies instead. Once any advanced subcategory is configured it overrides the basic categories, because Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings is Enabled by default. Pick one approach. The categories and subcategories are the same as on Windows 11.

    Check what is in effect after gpupdate /force:

    auditpol /get /category:*

    #User rights on domain controllers

    Path: same GPO > Local Policies > User Rights Assignment. Look for anything that names Everyone, Users, Domain Users, Guests or a single user where the table does not expect it.

    Right Should contain (typical)
    Access this computer from the network Administrators, Authenticated Users, ENTERPRISE DOMAIN CONTROLLERS (Everyone and Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access are also defaults; removing them is optional hardening)
    Allow log on locally Administrators (defaults also include Account, Backup, Print and Server Operators and ENTERPRISE DOMAIN CONTROLLERS)
    Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services Administrators, plus README RDP users
    Act as part of the operating system Nobody
    Debug programs Administrators
    Take ownership of files or other objects Administrators
    Load and unload device drivers Administrators (default also has Print Operators)
    Back up files and directories, Restore files and directories Administrators, Backup Operators, Server Operators
    Create a token object Nobody
    Impersonate a client after authentication Administrators, LOCAL SERVICE, NETWORK SERVICE, SERVICE (plus IIS_IUSRS with IIS)
    Enable computer and user accounts to be trusted for delegation Administrators
    Add workstations to domain Administrators (default is Authenticated Users)
    Deny access to this computer from the network Guests
    Deny log on locally Guests
    Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services Guests

    Never put Administrators or your own account in a Deny right

    Deny log on locally or Deny access to this computer from the network containing Administrators, Authenticated Users or Everyone in the DC policy locks you out of the domain. Removing Authenticated Users from Access this computer from the network breaks Group Policy for every machine.

    #Security options for domain controllers

    Path: same GPO > Local Policies > Security Options. The AD-specific ones are in AD hardening. Generic ones (UAC, interactive logon, anonymous access) are the same settings as on Windows 11; on a DC set them in this GPO or in the Default Domain Policy.

    #Find suspicious GPOs

    #List GPOs and their links

    All GPOs with status and last change, newest first:

    Get-GPO -All | Sort-Object ModificationTime -Descending | Format-Table DisplayName,GpoStatus,ModificationTime,Id -AutoSize

    Where each GPO is linked, for the domain root and every OU:

    $targets = @((Get-ADDomain).DistinguishedName) + @(Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter * | Select-Object -ExpandProperty DistinguishedName)
foreach ($t in $targets) { (Get-GPInheritance -Target $t).GpoLinks | Select-Object Order,DisplayName,Enabled,Enforced,Target }

    A full HTML report of every setting in every GPO:

    Get-GPOReport -All -ReportType Html -Path C:\AllGPOs.html
Start-Process C:\AllGPOs.html

    #What to look for in an unknown GPO

    • Logon or startup scripts (Computer or User Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Scripts).
    • Restricted Groups, or Preferences > Control Panel Settings > Local Users and Groups, adding someone to Administrators.
    • Weak security options, Defender turned off, firewall turned off, UAC turned off.
    • Preferences > Scheduled Tasks and Preferences > Registry entries.
    • A GPO with Enforced = Yes, or a better link order than Default Domain Policy, that sets weak password or lockout values.

    Link order decides conflicts

    In gpmc.msc > your domain > Linked Group Policy Objects tab, link order 1 has the highest precedence. A planted GPO above Default Domain Policy with weaker password settings wins.

    #Disable, unlink or delete a bad GPO

    Disabling the link is the safest choice because you can undo it:

    Set-GPLink -Name "<gpo-name>" -Target "<target-dn>" -LinkEnabled No

    Remove the link:

    Remove-GPLink -Name "<gpo-name>" -Target "<target-dn>"

    Delete the GPO entirely:

    Remove-GPO -Name "<gpo-name>"

    <target-dn> is the distinguished name where it is linked, for example DC=corp,DC=local for the domain root.

    #Search SYSVOL for GPP passwords (cpassword)

    Group Policy Preferences once stored passwords encrypted with a key Microsoft published, so any cpassword value is effectively plaintext. This prints every file and line that contains one:

    Get-ChildItem "C:\Windows\SYSVOL\sysvol" -Recurse -Include *.xml -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-String -Pattern 'cpassword' | Select-Object Path,LineNumber

    To fix, delete that preference item in the GPO editor (or the XML file) and change the password of the account it referenced.

    #Run gpupdate, gpresult and rsop

    gpupdate /force
gpresult /r
gpresult /r /scope:computer
gpresult /h C:\gpresult.html
    • gpresult /r lists applied and filtered-out GPOs for the current user and computer. Run it elevated to see computer settings.
    • gpresult /h writes an HTML report that names the winning GPO for every setting.
    • rsop.msc shows the resulting policy as an MMC tree. It is older but still works.

    #Reset the two default GPOs (last resort)

    This resets Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controllers Policy to install defaults, including the weak minimum length of 7. Use it only if they are hopelessly broken, then re-apply your hardening:

    dcgpofix /target:Both
    PreviousAD users and groupsNextAdditional AD hardening
    SRV

    Additional AD hardening

    jump:srv-ad-hardening

    On a DC set these in GPOs: domain-wide items in the Default Domain Policy, DC items in the Default Domain Controllers Policy. All security options are under Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options in gpmc.msc.

    Fast path

    1. Run gpmc.msc, right-click Default Domain Controllers Policy > Edit, and open Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options.
    2. Set Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements to Require signing, and Domain controller: LDAP server channel binding token requirements to Always.
    3. Set Network security: LAN Manager authentication level to Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM, and enable Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change.
    4. Apply with gpupdate /force.

    5. In an elevated PowerShell window, stop ordinary users from joining computers and turn on the Recycle Bin:

      Set-ADDomain -Identity (Get-ADDomain) -Replace @{'ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota'='0'}
Enable-ADOptionalFeature -Identity 'Recycle Bin Feature' -Scope ForestOrConfigurationSet -Target (Get-ADForest).Name -Confirm:$false

    6. Remove Everyone and ANONYMOUS LOGON from Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access (how).

    7. Disable Print Spooler unless the README needs printing (how).

    #Priorities

    Do the Common items first. Advanced items are good practice but less often scored or riskier.

    Item Priority
    LDAP signing and channel binding, NTLMv2 only, no LM hash, SMB signing, anonymous restrictions Common
    Zerologon exception list empty, Pre-Windows 2000 group cleaned, MachineAccountQuota 0, Recycle Bin, DS Access auditing, admins not delegable, Spooler off Common
    Kerberos encryption types, NTLM session security, Protected Users, delegation review, DSRM, AdminSDHolder, SYSVOL permissions Advanced
    krbtgt password reset Leave alone unless the README says otherwise

    #Security options for domain controllers

    Policy name (Security Options) Value Registry value to verify Priority
    Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements Require signing HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Parameters LDAPServerIntegrity = 2 Common
    Domain controller: LDAP server channel binding token requirements Always ...\Services\NTDS\Parameters LdapEnforceChannelBinding = 2 (1 = When supported, 0 = Never) Common
    Network security: LDAP client signing requirements Negotiate signing (or Require signing) HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LDAP LDAPClientIntegrity = 1 (2) Advanced
    Network security: LAN Manager authentication level Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa LmCompatibilityLevel = 5 Common
    Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change Enabled ...\Control\Lsa NoLMHash = 1 Common
    Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always) Enabled (already set by default in this GPO) HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters RequireSecuritySignature = 1 Common
    Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always) Enabled ...\Services\LanmanWorkstation\Parameters RequireSecuritySignature = 1 Common
    Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always) Enabled ...\Services\Netlogon\Parameters RequireSignOrSeal = 1 Common
    Domain member: Require strong (Windows 2000 or later) session key Enabled ...\Services\Netlogon\Parameters RequireStrongKey = 1 Advanced
    Domain controller: Refuse machine account password changes Disabled ...\Services\Netlogon\Parameters RefusePasswordChange = 0 Advanced
    Domain controller: Allow server operators to schedule tasks Disabled ...\Control\Lsa SubmitControl = 0 Advanced
    Domain controller: Allow vulnerable Netlogon secure channel connections Not Defined (no accounts listed) Zerologon exception list Common
    Network access: Allow anonymous SID/Name translation Disabled Policy only Common
    Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts Enabled ...\Control\Lsa RestrictAnonymousSAM = 1 Common
    Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares Enabled ...\Control\Lsa RestrictAnonymous = 1 Common
    Network access: Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users Disabled ...\Control\Lsa EveryoneIncludesAnonymous = 0 Common
    Network access: Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares Enabled ...\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters RestrictNullSessAccess = 1 Common
    Network access: Shares that can be accessed anonymously Empty ...\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters NullSessionShares Common
    Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos AES128_HMAC_SHA1, AES256_HMAC_SHA1, Future encryption types HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\Kerberos\Parameters SupportedEncryptionTypes = 0x7FFFFFF8 Advanced
    Network security: Minimum session security for NTLM SSP based (including secure RPC) clients and servers Require NTLMv2 session security, Require 128-bit encryption ...\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0 NTLMMinClientSec and NTLMMinServerSec = 0x20080000 Advanced

    Leave the DC's anonymous named pipes alone

    On a DC, Network access: Named Pipes that can be accessed anonymously lists netlogon, samr and lsarpc by default. Domain clients need them. Do not empty that list on a DC.

    Kerberos encryption types

    Restricting Kerberos to AES can break old service accounts that only have RC4 keys. On a fresh lab domain it is fine. If authentication errors appear after the change, revert it.

    Why LDAP signing and channel binding matter

    Without signing, an attacker in the middle can relay or tamper with LDAP binds. Channel binding ties an LDAPS session to the TLS channel, which stops relaying NTLM into LDAPS. Windows clients already sign by default, so Require signing only breaks unsigned simple binds from old tools. Server 2022 does not require signing out of the box, which is why the setting is commonly scored.

    #Verify the registry values

    Run after gpupdate /force:

    Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Parameters' | Select-Object LDAPServerIntegrity,LdapEnforceChannelBinding
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa' | Select-Object LmCompatibilityLevel,NoLMHash,RestrictAnonymous,RestrictAnonymousSAM,EveryoneIncludesAnonymous
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters' | Select-Object RequireSecuritySignature,RestrictNullSessAccess,NullSessionShares

    #Disable NTLMv1 and LM hashes

    The LAN Manager authentication level = 5 and NoLMHash = 1 rows above cover this. On a DC use the GPO. On a standalone server you can set the registry directly from an elevated PowerShell window:

    Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa' -Name LmCompatibilityLevel -Value 5 -Type DWord
Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa' -Name NoLMHash -Value 1 -Type DWord

    #Clean up the Pre-Windows 2000 group

    In dsa.msc > Builtin > Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access > Members, remove Everyone and ANONYMOUS LOGON and keep Authenticated Users. With either of those two as a member, anonymous users can read most of AD.

    In PowerShell, well-known principals show up by SID, for example CN=S-1-1-0,CN=ForeignSecurityPrincipals,DC=corp,DC=local. S-1-5-11 is Authenticated Users (keep), S-1-1-0 is Everyone and S-1-5-7 is ANONYMOUS LOGON (remove). Show the raw members:

    (Get-ADGroup "Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access" -Properties member).member

    Remove Everyone and ANONYMOUS LOGON:

    $g = Get-ADGroup "Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access" -Properties member
$g.member | Where-Object { $_ -like 'CN=S-1-1-0,*' -or $_ -like 'CN=S-1-5-7,*' } | ForEach-Object { Set-ADGroup $g -Remove @{member = $_} }

    #Check Zerologon protection

    • Install updates; DCs have enforced secure Netlogon RPC since the February 2021 updates.
    • Confirm Domain controller: Allow vulnerable Netlogon secure channel connections is Not Defined in every GPO.
    • Optional registry check: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Netlogon\Parameters FullSecureChannelProtection should be 1 or absent. Patched DCs enforce secure RPC anyway, but a 0 there shows someone tried to weaken it, so set it to 1.

    #Set MachineAccountQuota to 0

    By default any domain user can join 10 computers to the domain. Set the quota to 0 and read it back:

    Set-ADDomain -Identity (Get-ADDomain) -Replace @{'ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota'='0'}
Get-ADObject (Get-ADDomain).DistinguishedName -Properties 'ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota' | Select-Object 'ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota'

    Also consider removing Authenticated Users from the Add workstations to domain user right in the Default Domain Controllers Policy.

    #Enable the AD Recycle Bin

    With the Recycle Bin you can restore a deleted user with all its attributes. It cannot be turned off once enabled, which is harmless. It needs forest functional level 2008 R2 or higher.

    Enable-ADOptionalFeature -Identity 'Recycle Bin Feature' -Scope ForestOrConfigurationSet -Target (Get-ADForest).Name -Confirm:$false
Get-ADOptionalFeature -Filter 'Name -like "Recycle Bin Feature"' | Select-Object Name,EnabledScopes

    EnabledScopes is no longer empty once it is on. GUI: dsac.exe > right-click the domain > Enable Recycle Bin.

    #Restore a deleted user

    Get-ADObject -Filter 'isDeleted -eq $true -and samAccountName -eq "<username>"' -IncludeDeletedObjects | Restore-ADObject

    #Audit directory service access

    In the Default Domain Controllers Policy, set either the basic Audit directory service access to Success and Failure, or the advanced Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Audit Policies > DS Access > Audit Directory Service Access and Audit Directory Service Changes to Success and Failure. Check it:

    auditpol /get /category:"DS Access"

    #Add admins to Protected Users

    Members cannot use NTLM, DES or RC4 for Kerberos, cannot be delegated, and their credentials are not cached. It suits README admin accounts other than your own:

    Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "Protected Users" -Members <username>

    Do not add the account you are logged in with

    Protected Users breaks NTLM logons (RDP by IP address, some tools) and cached logons, so you can lock yourself out. Add only other admin accounts, never computer or service accounts.

    #Mark admin accounts as sensitive

    Set Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated on every Domain Admin, then list the result for every account that has been privileged:

    Get-ADGroupMember "Domain Admins" -Recursive | Where-Object objectClass -eq 'user' | ForEach-Object { Set-ADUser $_ -AccountNotDelegated $true }
Get-ADUser -Filter 'AdminCount -eq 1' -Properties AccountNotDelegated | Select-Object SamAccountName,AccountNotDelegated

    GUI: dsa.msc > user > Properties > Account tab > Account options > Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated.

    #Find unconstrained delegation

    Computers trusted for delegation. DCs always appear here, which is normal:

    Get-ADComputer -Filter 'TrustedForDelegation -eq $true' | Select-Object Name

    Users trusted for delegation. There should be none:

    Get-ADUser -Filter 'TrustedForDelegation -eq $true' | Select-Object SamAccountName

    Constrained delegation targets:

    Get-ADObject -Filter 'msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo -like "*"' -Properties msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo | Select-Object Name,msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo

    Remove delegation from a user:

    Set-ADAccountControl <username> -TrustedForDelegation $false

    Remove it from a non-DC computer. Never remove it from a DC:

    Get-ADComputer <hostname> | Set-ADAccountControl -TrustedForDelegation $false

    #Leave krbtgt alone

    • Never delete, enable or rename krbtgt. It is disabled by design.
    • Resetting its password invalidates every Kerberos ticket (the fix after a Golden Ticket attack). The correct procedure is two resets about 10 hours apart. In competition, leave it alone unless the README says otherwise.

    #Secure the DSRM administrator

    The Directory Services Restore Mode password belongs to a separate local admin account on each DC. DsrmAdminLogonBehavior under HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa should be absent or 0; a value of 2 allows the DSRM account to log on over the network at any time, which is a backdoor.

    Check the value:

    Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa' -Name DsrmAdminLogonBehavior -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

    Remove it:

    Remove-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa' -Name DsrmAdminLogonBehavior -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

    Reset the DSRM password from an elevated cmd window. Type the new password twice when prompted:

    ntdsutil "set dsrm password" "reset password on server null" quit quit

    #Check AdminSDHolder permissions

    List who has rights on the AdminSDHolder object:

    Import-Module ActiveDirectory
$dn = "CN=AdminSDHolder,CN=System," + (Get-ADDomain).DistinguishedName
(Get-Acl "AD:$dn").Access | Select-Object IdentityReference,ActiveDirectoryRights,AccessControlType -Unique | Sort-Object IdentityReference | Format-Table -AutoSize

    Every 60 minutes the permissions on AdminSDHolder (CN=AdminSDHolder,CN=System,DC=corp,DC=local in a domain named corp.local) are copied onto all protected accounts and groups, so an entry planted there gives an attacker control of admin accounts again automatically.

    Expected identities are built-in: SYSTEM, Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Administrators, Authenticated Users (read), Everyone (limited), SELF, Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access, Cert Publishers, Windows Authorization Access Group, Terminal Server License Servers. A named ordinary user with GenericAll or WriteDacl is a backdoor. Remove it in dsa.msc (Advanced Features on) > System > AdminSDHolder > Properties > Security > Advanced.

    #Check SYSVOL and NETLOGON permissions

    net share
icacls C:\Windows\SYSVOL\sysvol
icacls C:\Windows\SYSVOL\sysvol\<domain-name>\scripts
    • net share on a DC must list SYSVOL and NETLOGON. If either is missing, Group Policy is broken (fix).
    • Normal NTFS rights: Administrators, SYSTEM and CREATOR OWNER full; Authenticated Users and Server Operators read and execute. Everyone, Users or Authenticated Users with Modify or Full allows any user to plant a logon script or edit GPO files. Remove those write rights.
    • Do not change the SYSVOL and NETLOGON share permissions themselves.
    • Look in the scripts folder (NETLOGON) for unknown .bat, .ps1 and .vbs files.

    #Disable the print spooler on DCs

    PrintNightmare and printer-bug coercion attacks target the Spooler on DCs. Unless the README requires printing from this server, stop and disable it from an elevated PowerShell window:

    Stop-Service Spooler -Force
Set-Service Spooler -StartupType Disabled

    More services to keep or disable are in Server services.

    PreviousGroup Policy on a domainNextRemove roles and features
    SRV

    Remove roles and features

    jump:srv-roles

    Never remove README-required roles

    If the README says the server provides DNS, DHCP, web, FTP or file sharing, that role and its service stay. On a DC never remove AD-Domain-Services, DNS, RSAT-AD-PowerShell or GPMC. Removing AD DS means demoting the DC, which destroys a single-DC domain.

    Fast path

    1. Open PowerShell as administrator and list what is installed:

      Get-WindowsFeature | Where-Object Installed | Format-Table Name,DisplayName,InstallState -AutoSize

    2. Compare with the README and the table of usual removals. Delete from the list below anything the README needs.

    3. Remove the rest:

      $remove = 'FS-SMB1','Telnet-Client','TFTP-Client','PowerShell-V2','SNMP-Service','Simple-TCPIP','Fax','PNRP'
Get-WindowsFeature $remove | Where-Object Installed | Uninstall-WindowsFeature

    4. Check the result. Each should read Available, or UninstallPending until you reboot:

      Get-WindowsFeature $remove | Format-Table Name,InstallState

    5. Reboot when it is convenient if the output said Restart Needed: Yes.

    #List installed roles and features

    Get-WindowsFeature | Where-Object Installed | Format-Table Name,DisplayName,InstallState -AutoSize

    GUI: Server Manager > Manage > Remove Roles and Features > Next > select the server. Checked boxes on the Server Roles page and the Features page are installed.

    #Remove a role or feature

    Remove one feature:

    Uninstall-WindowsFeature -Name <feature-name>

    Several at once:

    Uninstall-WindowsFeature -Name Telnet-Client,TFTP-Client,PowerShell-V2

    Server Manager > Manage > Remove Roles and Features > Server Roles or Features page > clear the box > Next > Remove.

    Some removals need a reboot to finish. The output then shows Restart Needed: Yes and Get-WindowsFeature <feature-name> shows UninstallPending until you restart. Add -Restart only when you are ready for the reboot.

    Do not use -Remove

    Uninstall-WindowsFeature -Remove also deletes the feature's files from the component store, so reinstalling needs the install media. Plain Uninstall-WindowsFeature is enough for scoring.

    #Usually unneeded features and their exact names

    Feature (display name) Name for PowerShell Notes
    SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support FS-SMB1 Subfeatures FS-SMB1-CLIENT and FS-SMB1-SERVER. Almost always remove. Needs a restart
    Telnet Client Telnet-Client Remove
    TFTP Client TFTP-Client Remove
    Windows PowerShell 2.0 Engine PowerShell-V2 Remove (attackers downgrade to it to bypass logging). Keep PowerShell and PowerShell-ISE
    SNMP Service SNMP-Service Also SNMP-WMI-Provider. Remove unless the README requires SNMP
    Simple TCP/IP Services Simple-TCPIP Remove (echo, chargen, daytime, qotd)
    Fax Server (role) Fax Remove
    Peer Name Resolution Protocol PNRP Remove
    Web Server (IIS) Web-Server Remove only if the README needs no website or FTP
    FTP Server Web-Ftp-Server Subfeatures Web-Ftp-Service and Web-Ftp-Ext. Remove if FTP is not required
    WebDAV Publishing Web-DAV-Publishing Remove unless required
    Directory Browsing (IIS) Web-Dir-Browsing Removing it makes directory listings impossible
    IIS Management Service Web-Mgmt-Service Remote IIS management (WMSVC); remove if not needed
    Remote Access (role) RemoteAccess Role services DirectAccess-VPN, Routing, Web-Application-Proxy. Remove unless the README needs VPN or routing
    SMTP Server SMTP-Server Remove unless required
    Windows Deployment Services WDS Remove unless required
    Wireless LAN Service Wireless-Networking Remove on a server without Wi-Fi
    Print and Document Services Print-Services Remove on a DC unless the README requires printing
    Internet Printing Client Internet-Print-Client Remove if listed
    Remote Assistance Remote-Assistance Remove unless required
    Telnet Server Not available on Server 2022 A telnet server you find is third-party software; uninstall it

    After removing FS-SMB1, also confirm the server config with Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select-Object EnableSMB1Protocol (False) (SMB).

    #Reinstall a role you removed by mistake

    Install-WindowsFeature -Name <feature-name> -IncludeManagementTools

    Then restore its configuration (sites, shares, scopes), because removing IIS, DHCP or DNS can delete it. Set its services back to Automatic and start them (recovery).

    #Third-party software

    FTP servers like FileZilla Server, VNC, Wireshark, games and hacking tools are programs, not features. Remove them as on Windows 11 with appwiz.cpl or Settings > Apps (software).

    PreviousAdditional AD hardeningNextIIS web server hardening
    SRV

    IIS web server hardening

    jump:srv-iis

    Only harden IIS if the README requires a website

    If no website is required, remove the role instead with Uninstall-WindowsFeature Web-Server (roles).

    Fast path

    1. Open PowerShell as administrator, load the IIS module and list the sites:

      Import-Module WebAdministration
Get-Website | Format-Table Name,ID,State,PhysicalPath -AutoSize

    2. Turn off directory browsing server-wide:

      Set-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST' -Filter 'system.webServer/directoryBrowse' -Name enabled -Value $false

    3. Run every application pool as ApplicationPoolIdentity:

      Get-ChildItem IIS:\AppPools | ForEach-Object { Set-ItemProperty "IIS:\AppPools\$($_.Name)" -Name processModel.identityType -Value ApplicationPoolIdentity }

    4. Turn on logging for every site:

      Get-Website | ForEach-Object { Set-ItemProperty "IIS:\Sites\$($_.Name)" -Name logFile.enabled -Value $true }

    5. Check web root permissions with icacls C:\inetpub\wwwroot (fix).

    6. Hunt for web shells (how) and remove WebDAV unless required.

    #Open IIS Manager and load the PowerShell module

    Run inetmgr (or Server Manager > Tools > Internet Information Services (IIS) Manager). The left pane has the server node (server-wide settings), then Sites, then each site. Feature icons are in the middle and the Actions pane is on the right.

    The WebAdministration module comes with the IIS management scripts and tools (Web-Scripting-Tools). List sites, bindings and app pools with their identities:

    Import-Module WebAdministration
Get-Website | Format-Table Name,ID,State,PhysicalPath -AutoSize
Get-WebBinding | Format-Table protocol,bindingInformation -AutoSize
Get-ChildItem IIS:\AppPools | Select-Object Name,State,@{n='Identity';e={$_.processModel.identityType}},@{n='User';e={$_.processModel.userName}}

    The command-line tool is %windir%\system32\inetsrv\appcmd.exe, for example appcmd list site and appcmd list apppool.

    #IISAdministration equivalents

    Server 2022 also ships the newer IISAdministration module. Either module works; the commands on this page use WebAdministration.

    Task WebAdministration IISAdministration
    List sites Get-Website Get-IISSite
    Stop a site Stop-Website -Name "<site-name>" Stop-IISSite -Name "<site-name>" -Confirm:$false
    Start a site Start-Website -Name "<site-name>" Start-IISSite -Name "<site-name>"
    Delete a site Remove-Website -Name "<site-name>" Remove-IISSite -Name "<site-name>" -Confirm:$false
    List app pools Get-ChildItem IIS:\AppPools Get-IISAppPool
    List bindings Get-WebBinding Get-IISSiteBinding -Name "<site-name>"

    #Turn off directory browsing

    inetmgr > server node > Directory Browsing > Actions: Disable. Repeat on each site.

    Server-wide default:

    Import-Module WebAdministration
Set-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST' -Filter 'system.webServer/directoryBrowse' -Name enabled -Value $false

    One site (this writes the site's web.config, so it also overrides a planted setting there):

    Set-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'IIS:\Sites\<site-name>' -Filter 'system.webServer/directoryBrowse' -Name enabled -Value $false

    %windir%\system32\inetsrv\appcmd set config "<site-name>" /section:directoryBrowse /enabled:false

    Verify

    This should print False, and browsing to http://localhost/<path>/ for a folder with no default page should return 403:

    Get-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'IIS:\Sites\<site-name>' -Filter 'system.webServer/directoryBrowse' -Name enabled

    #Check web.config does not turn it back on

    A directoryBrowse enabled="true" element in a site's web.config overrides the server setting. Search for it:

    Select-String -Path C:\inetpub\wwwroot\web.config,C:\inetpub\wwwroot\*\web.config -Pattern directoryBrowse

    #Review authentication

    GUI: inetmgr > site > Authentication. A public site normally has Anonymous Authentication Enabled and everything else Disabled. Intranet or admin pages have Anonymous Disabled and Windows Authentication Enabled. Basic Authentication sends passwords in clear text unless the site is HTTPS only.

    Check the anonymous identity: select Anonymous Authentication > Edit. It should be Specific user: IUSR, or Application pool identity. An administrator account here means every visitor runs as admin.

    Read the anonymous settings for a site:

    Get-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST' -Location '<site-name>' -Filter 'system.webServer/security/authentication/anonymousAuthentication' -Name enabled
Get-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST' -Location '<site-name>' -Filter 'system.webServer/security/authentication/anonymousAuthentication' -Name userName

    Turn off anonymous authentication on a site:

    Set-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST' -Location '<site-name>' -Filter 'system.webServer/security/authentication/anonymousAuthentication' -Name enabled -Value $false

    Turn off basic authentication on a site:

    Set-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST' -Location '<site-name>' -Filter 'system.webServer/security/authentication/basicAuthentication' -Name enabled -Value $false

    Do not break the required site

    Turning off anonymous authentication on a public website makes it ask every visitor for a password. If the README says the site is public, leave anonymous on and confirm the identity is IUSR.

    #Stop or remove unused sites

    If the README names one site, stop or remove the others, including Default Web Site if it is not the required one.

    Stop a site and keep it from starting at boot:

    Stop-Website -Name "<site-name>"
Set-ItemProperty "IIS:\Sites\<site-name>" -Name serverAutoStart -Value $false

    Delete a site (its content folder stays on disk):

    Remove-Website -Name "<site-name>"

    Delete an unused application pool:

    Remove-WebAppPool -Name "<pool-name>"

    GUI: inetmgr > Sites > right-click the site > Manage Website > Stop (or Remove).

    #Set the application pool identity

    Every pool should run as ApplicationPoolIdentity, never LocalSystem or an admin user. Check, change and recycle one pool:

    Get-ChildItem IIS:\AppPools | Select-Object Name,@{n='Identity';e={$_.processModel.identityType}}
Set-ItemProperty "IIS:\AppPools\<pool-name>" -Name processModel.identityType -Value ApplicationPoolIdentity
Restart-WebAppPool -Name "<pool-name>"

    GUI: inetmgr > Application Pools > select the pool > Advanced Settings > Process Model > Identity > ApplicationPoolIdentity.

    #Add an HTTPS binding

    Do this only if the README asks for HTTPS or a certificate already exists. Create a self-signed certificate, add the binding and attach the certificate:

    $cert = New-SelfSignedCertificate -DnsName "<hostname>" -CertStoreLocation Cert:\LocalMachine\My
New-WebBinding -Name "<site-name>" -Protocol https -Port 443
(Get-WebBinding -Name "<site-name>" -Protocol https).AddSslCertificate($cert.Thumbprint, "My")

    GUI: inetmgr > site > Bindings > Add > Type https, Port 443, choose the SSL certificate.

    Remove the http binding only if the README does not need plain HTTP; scoring often checks the site still answers on its original URL.

    #Require SSL

    GUI: inetmgr > site > SSL Settings > Require SSL. PowerShell:

    Set-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST' -Location '<site-name>' -Filter 'system.webServer/security/access' -Name sslFlags -Value 'Ssl'

    #Disable TLS 1.0 and 1.1

    SSL 2.0 and 3.0 are already off on Server 2022; TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are still on by default. This turns off the server side of both through the SCHANNEL registry keys. It needs a reboot and is rarely scored:

    foreach ($p in 'TLS 1.0','TLS 1.1') {
  $k = "HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL\Protocols\$p\Server"
  if (-not (Test-Path $k)) { New-Item $k -Force | Out-Null }
  New-ItemProperty $k -Name Enabled -Value 0 -PropertyType DWord -Force | Out-Null
  New-ItemProperty $k -Name DisabledByDefault -Value 1 -PropertyType DWord -Force | Out-Null
}

    #Request filtering

    GUI: inetmgr > site > Request Filtering.

    • Edit Feature Settings: clear Allow double escaping, and set Maximum allowed content length sensibly. Clear Allow unlisted verbs only if you then list the allowed verbs.
    • HTTP Verbs tab: Deny Verb TRACE (and TRACK).
    • File Name Extensions tab: .config, .cs, .mdb and similar are denied by default. Keep them, and add Deny for extensions the site should never serve.
    • Hidden Segments: web.config, bin and App_Data are hidden by default. Keep them.

    Deny TRACE server-wide:

    Add-WebConfigurationProperty -PSPath 'MACHINE/WEBROOT/APPHOST' -Filter 'system.webServer/security/requestFiltering/verbs' -Name '.' -Value @{verb='TRACE';allowed='false'}
