    less <file> Scroll a file; /text searches, n next match, q quits
    cat <file> Print a short file
    grep -n 'text' <file> Lines containing text, with line numbers
    grep -rni 'text' <path> Recursive, case-insensitive search
    grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' <file> Hide comment and blank lines
    grep -E 'a|b' <file> Match a or b
    find / -name '<file>' 2>/dev/null Find files by name, hide permission errors
    find /home -iname '*.mp3' Case-insensitive wildcard search
    head -n 20 <file>, tail -n 20 <file> First or last 20 lines
    tail -f /var/log/auth.log Follow a log live (Ctrl+C stops)
    wc -l <file> Count lines
    sort, uniq Sort, remove duplicates

    A pipe (|) sends one command's output into the next, for example ps aux | grep ssh.

    #Use tab completion and history

    • Press Tab to complete a command or path; press it twice to list the choices.
    • Press Up to recall earlier commands.
    • Press Ctrl+R and type part of an old command to search history. Enter runs it, Ctrl+C cancels.
    • Run history | grep ufw to list earlier ufw commands.
    • Ctrl+C stops a running command, Ctrl+L clears the screen, and q leaves pagers such as less and man.

    #Copy and paste in the terminal

    Keys Action
    Ctrl+Shift+C Copy selected text
    Ctrl+Shift+V Paste
    Shift+Insert Paste
    Select text, then middle-click Paste the selection

    Ctrl+C in a terminal stops the running command. It does not copy.

    #Fix permission denied errors

    • Put sudo in front of the command, or run it in the root shell.

    • sudo echo x > /etc/<file> fails because the > redirect runs as you. Write through tee instead, which overwrites the file (tee -a appends):

      echo 'x' | sudo tee /etc/<file>

    • If even root gets "Operation not permitted", the file may be immutable. Check with lsattr <file> and clear the flag with sudo chattr -i <file>.

    PreviousLinux Mint master checklistNextREADME and Forensics on Linux
    LNX

    README and Forensics on Linux

    jump:lin-readme

    Answer Forensics before you fix

    Deleting a user, file or package can destroy the evidence a Forensics Question asks about. Answer first, then fix.

    Fast path

    1. Double-click the README shortcut on the desktop and read all of it.
    2. Write down authorized admins, authorized users, required services, required and forbidden software, and special instructions.

    3. List the Forensics Question files:

      ls ~/Desktop

    4. Open each one without sudo, type the answer after ANSWER:, and save with Ctrl+S:

      xed ~/Desktop/'Forensics Question 1.txt'

    5. Check the scoring report on the desktop for the points.

    #Read the README first

    The README is a desktop shortcut that opens a web page in Firefox. Write these down before you change anything:

    • Authorized administrators (they must be in the sudo group) and any passwords given.
    • Authorized standard users (they must exist and must not be in sudo).
    • Critical or required services, for example "SSH is a critical service" or "this machine is an FTP server".
    • Required and forbidden software, for example "no hacking tools" or "games are not allowed".
    • Special instructions, such as "create user X", "add group Y" or "user Z must use bash".

    Required means required

    Removing or breaking a service the README lists as critical costs points, and so does removing an authorized user. If you are unsure, leave it and ask the team.

    The scoring report is another desktop shortcut. Refresh it after each batch of changes; points can take a minute or two to appear.

    #Answer the Forensics questions

    The files are on the desktop: Forensics Question 1.txt, Forensics Question 2.txt, and so on. Each holds the question and a line that starts with ANSWER:. Replace only the placeholder text after ANSWER: and keep the prefix. A finished line looks like this:

    ANSWER: /home/user1/Music/hidden/song.mp3
    • If there are several ANSWER: lines, fill each one.
    • Match the format the question asks for: full path, username only, lowercase hash, and so on.
    • Do not rename, move or change the owner of the file. Open it without sudo.
    • Copy the evidence (path, port, user, file content) into your changelog too. Another question may ask about the same thing after you have removed it.

    #Find files and evidence

    Goal Command
    Find a file by name sudo find / -iname '*secret*' 2>/dev/null
    Find files owned by a user sudo find / -user <username> -type f 2>/dev/null
    Files changed in the last 3 days sudo find /home /etc -type f -mtime -3 2>/dev/null
    Search inside files for text sudo grep -rnI 'text' /home 2>/dev/null
    Fast name search from a database sudo updatedb && locate <file> (install plocate if missing)
    What kind of file this is file <file>
    Readable text inside a binary strings <file> | less
    Size, owner, permissions, timestamps stat <file>
    Permissions in octal stat -c '%a %U:%G %n' <file>
    Hidden files ls -la <path>
    A user's UID and groups id <username>
    Recent logins and failures last, sudo lastb, lastlog
    Which package owns a file dpkg -S <path>
    What is listening on a port sudo ss -tulpn
    MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 hash md5sum <file>, sha1sum <file>, sha256sum <file>

    #Decode base64, hex, ROT13 and binary

    Base64 text uses letters, digits, + and /, and often ends in = or ==. Decode a string:

    echo 'Q3liZXJQYXRyaW90' | base64 -d; echo

    Decode a whole file:

    base64 -d <file>

    Turn a hex string back into text (install with sudo apt install xxd if xxd is missing):

    echo '48656c6c6f' | xxd -r -p; echo

    Show a hex dump of a file:

    xxd <file> | less

    Decode ROT13:

    echo 'Uryyb' | tr 'A-Za-z' 'N-ZA-Mn-za-m'

    Turn 8-bit binary groups, separated by spaces, into text:

    for b in 01001000 01101001; do printf "\\x$(printf %x $((2#$b)))"; done; echo

    Decode URL-encoded text such as a%20b:

    python3 -c 'import sys,urllib.parse;print(urllib.parse.unquote(sys.argv[1]))' 'a%20b'

    #Common Forensics Question types

    Question asks How
    Path of a hidden media or MP3 file sudo find /home -iname '*.mp3' 2>/dev/null
    Which user has UID X or is in group Y getent passwd or getent group <groupname>
    Port a backdoor listens on sudo ss -tulpn, then check the program
    Program that runs from cron sudo crontab -l -u <username>, cat /etc/crontab, ls /etc/cron.d
    Hash of a file sha256sum <file> (copy it exactly, lowercase)
    Decode a message base64, hex or ROT13 commands above
    Who logged in last, and when last -n 20
    Which package provides a program dpkg -S "$(command -v <program>)"; if it says "no path found", try /bin/<program> or /sbin/<program>, because many 22.04 packages register /bin paths
    Content of a deleted file that is still running sudo ls -l /proc/<pid>/exe, then sudo cp /proc/<pid>/exe /root/recovered
    Permissions of a file in octal stat -c '%a' <file>
    GID of a group getent group <groupname> (third field)
    Shell of a user getent passwd <username> (last field)
    SSH key comment or owner cat /home/<username>/.ssh/authorized_keys (the last field is the comment)
    Image metadata strings <file> | head, or sudo apt install libimage-exiftool-perl then exiftool <file>
    PreviousTerminal survival on MintNextUsers and groups
    LNX

    Users and groups

    jump:lin-users

    Answer Forensics before deleting accounts

    Home folders often hold Forensics evidence. Never delete an authorized user, including your own account.

    Fast path

    1. List human users and compare with the README:

      awk -F: '$3>=1000 && $3<65534 {print $1}' /etc/passwd

    2. List admins and compare with the README admin list:

      getent group sudo

    3. Delete each unauthorized user (after Forensics): sudo deluser <username>.

    4. Remove each unauthorized admin: sudo gpasswd -d <username> sudo.
    5. Add each missing admin: sudo usermod -aG sudo <username>.

    6. Check for extra root accounts; only root may print:

      awk -F: '$3==0 {print $1}' /etc/passwd

    7. Set the team password on every user (details).

    #List users and admins

    Open Menu > Administration > Users and Groups (cinnamon-settings-users) and enter your password. The left list shows human accounts. Account type "Administrator" means the user is in the sudo group; "Standard" means they are not. The Groups tab lists groups and their members. System accounts and UID 0 tricks do not show here, so finish with the terminal checks.

    List human users with UID, home and shell:

    awk -F: '$3>=1000 && $3<65534 {print $1, $3, $6, $7}' /etc/passwd

    List every account that has a real login shell:

    grep -vE '(nologin|false|sync)$' /etc/passwd

    List admin and sensitive groups:

    getent group sudo admin adm lpadmin sambashare root shadow

    Show one user's full membership, including the primary group:

    id <username>

    Primary group membership does not show in /etc/group

    A user whose primary GID (fourth field of /etc/passwd) is 27, the sudo group on Mint, has sudo rights but is missing from getent group sudo. Find them with awk -F: '$4==27 {print $1}' /etc/passwd. id <username> shows both kinds of membership.

    Group Grants Who belongs in it
    sudo Full root through sudo Only README admins
    admin Full root through the legacy %admin sudoers line Nobody; the group normally does not exist
    adm Read system logs Admins only
    lpadmin Manage printers Admins only
    sambashare Create Samba user shares Admins, or as the README says
    root (GID 0) Group access to root-group files Only root
    shadow Read /etc/shadow No user accounts

    The first account created at install is normally in adm, cdrom, sudo, dip, plugdev, lpadmin and sambashare. Accounts created later as Standard are in none of the admin groups.

    #Read /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and /etc/group

    A line from /etc/passwd (mode 644) has seven fields, name:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell:

    user1:x:1001:1001:User One,,,:/home/user1:/bin/bash
    • UID 0 means root powers whatever the name is. Only root may have UID 0.
    • UIDs 1000 to 60000 are normal users, below 1000 are system accounts, and 65534 is nobody.
    • x means the hash is in /etc/shadow. A hash or an empty field here is a vulnerability.
    • System accounts should use /usr/sbin/nologin or /bin/false. The exceptions are root (/bin/bash) and sync (/bin/sync).

    A line from /etc/shadow (mode 640, owner root:shadow) has the fields name:hash:lastchange:min:max:warn:inactive:expire::

    user1:$y$j9T$...:19650:1:90:7:::
    Hash field starts with Meaning
    $y$ yescrypt (Mint 21 default, good)
    $6$ SHA-512 (good)
    $5$ SHA-256 (acceptable)
    $1$ MD5 (weak, reset the password)
    ! or * Locked, no password login
    empty No password at all: anyone can log in. Fix now.

    A line from /etc/group (mode 644) is groupname:x:GID:member1,member2:

    sudo:x:27:user1,user2

    /etc/gshadow (mode 640, root:shadow) mirrors /etc/group with group passwords and group admins.

    #Delete an unauthorized user

    End the user's processes, then delete the account and keep the home folder:

    sudo pkill -KILL -u <username>

    sudo deluser <username>

    After Forensics are answered, you can remove the home folder too:

    sudo deluser --remove-home <username>

    The low-level equivalents are sudo userdel <username> and sudo userdel -r <username>. Check it worked: getent passwd <username> prints nothing.

    #Add a user or group

    In Users and Groups click +, pick Standard or Administrator, type the username, and click Add. Select the new user and click the password field to set a password. Use the Groups tab to add a group and tick its members.

    Create a user interactively (sets the password and creates the home folder):

    sudo adduser <username>

    Create a group:

    sudo groupadd <groupname>

    Add a user to a group. Keep the -a: without it, usermod -G removes the user from every group not listed:

    sudo usermod -aG <groupname> <username>

    Remove a user from a group:

    sudo gpasswd -d <username> <groupname>

    Delete a group:

    sudo groupdel <groupname>

    sudo gpasswd -a <username> <groupname> and sudo deluser <username> <groupname> also add and remove members.

    Group changes apply at the user's next login. Check with getent group <groupname> or id <username>.

    #Add or remove an administrator

    In Users and Groups select the user and change Account Type to Administrator or Standard.

    Make a README admin an administrator:

    sudo usermod -aG sudo <username>

    Demote an unauthorized admin to a standard user, and take away log and printer admin rights:

    sudo gpasswd -d <username> sudo
sudo gpasswd -d <username> adm
sudo gpasswd -d <username> lpadmin

    gpasswd -d prints "is not a member" when the user was not in that group; that is fine. Also remove any personal sudoers line for the user (sudoers).

    #Set passwords for every user

    Set one user's password interactively:

    sudo passwd <username>

    Set one user's password without prompts:

    printf '%s:%s\n' '<username>' '<team-password>' | sudo chpasswd

    Set the same password on several users. Replace user1 user2 user3 with the README names and keep the single quotes around the password:

    PW='Cyb3rP@tri0t!2026'
for u in user1 user2 user3; do
  printf '%s:%s\n' "$u" "$PW" | sudo chpasswd && echo "set $u"
done

    chpasswd goes through PAM (/etc/pam.d/chpasswd includes common-password), so once you add enforce_for_root or password history it can refuse a password (why). Setting passwords before tightening PAM avoids that.

    Your own account

    Change the password of the account you are logged in as only if the README says to, and write the new password down. sudo and the screen lock will then want the new one.

    #Lock the root account

    sudo passwd -l root

    Check it: sudo passwd -S root prints L in the second field. On Mint root is normally locked already. Do not delete root or change its shell.

    #Remove extra UID 0 accounts

    List accounts with UID 0 and accounts whose primary group is root. Each command must print only root:

    awk -F: '$3==0 {print $1}' /etc/passwd
awk -F: '$4==0 {print $1}' /etc/passwd

    userdel and usermod -u usually refuse a UID 0 account ("user is currently used by process 1"), because every root process counts as that user. Edit the files with the locking editors instead:

    sudo vipw

    sudo vipw -s
    • Unauthorized UID 0 account: answer Forensics first, then delete its line in vipw (/etc/passwd) and its line in vipw -s (/etc/shadow).
    • Authorized user who was given UID 0: in vipw, change the third field from 0 to a free UID (check one with getent passwd 1050, which must print nothing) and the fourth field to that user's own GID. Then give the home folder back: sudo chown -R <username>:<username> /home/<username>.

    Check it worked: the UID 0 command prints only root, and sudo pwck -r shows no new errors.

    #Find empty or weak password hashes

    sudo awk -F: '$2=="" {print "EMPTY:", $1}' /etc/shadow
sudo awk -F: '$2 ~ /^\$1\$/ {print "MD5:", $1}' /etc/shadow
awk -F: '$2!="x" {print "hash in passwd:", $1}' /etc/passwd

    Show the password status of every account (P usable password, L locked, NP no password):

    sudo passwd -S -a

    Fix a user who should log in with sudo passwd <username>. Lock an account that should not log in with sudo passwd -l <username>. If /etc/passwd holds anything other than x in the second field, run sudo pwconv to move it to shadow, then reset that user's password.

    #Fix system accounts with login shells

    List accounts below UID 1000 that can log in:

    awk -F: '$3<1000 && $7 !~ /(nologin|false|sync)$/ {print $1, $3, $7}' /etc/passwd

    Only root should print. Service accounts of README-required software may legitimately have a shell (for example postgres gets /bin/bash when PostgreSQL is installed); leave those. For anything else (for example games, www-data, or a fake backup2 with /bin/bash), remove the shell and lock the password:

    sudo usermod -s /usr/sbin/nologin <username>
sudo passwd -l <username>

    An account that is not a real package or system account (unknown name, recently added, UID near 999) is a planted user. Answer Forensics, then delete it.

    #Find hidden users

    • AccountsService can hide a user from the login screen with SystemAccount=true. Search for it with sudo grep -r SystemAccount /var/lib/AccountsService/users/.
    • A home folder outside /home shows up in field 6 of /etc/passwd.
    • Duplicate UIDs: cut -d: -f3 /etc/passwd | sort -n | uniq -d. Duplicate names: cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd | sort | uniq -d.
    • A read-only consistency report: sudo pwck -r and sudo grpck -r.

    Verify

    awk -F: '$3>=1000 && $3<65534 {print $1}' /etc/passwd matches the README user list exactly, getent group sudo lists only README admins, and awk -F: '$3==0 {print $1}' /etc/passwd prints only root.

    PreviousREADME and Forensics on LinuxNextsudoers and sudo rights
    LNX

    sudoers and sudo rights

    jump:lin-sudo

    Always use visudo

    A syntax error in /etc/sudoers or any file in /etc/sudoers.d/ breaks sudo for everyone. visudo checks the syntax before saving. Keep your root shell open while you edit; if sudo is already broken, see troubleshooting (pkexec visudo).

    Fast path

    1. Search every sudoers file for risky rules:

      sudo grep -rnE 'NOPASSWD|!authenticate|ALL' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/

    2. Edit the main file and delete anything not in the clean file:

      sudo visudo

    3. List the drop-in files and edit or remove unknown ones: sudo ls -la /etc/sudoers.d/, then sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/<file>.

    4. Check the whole configuration parses:

      sudo visudo -c

    5. Confirm a standard user has no sudo rights: sudo -l -U <username>.

    #Edit sudoers safely with visudo

    Edit the main file:

    sudo visudo

    Edit a drop-in file:

    sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/<file>

    visudo opens nano on Mint. If it opens vi instead, run sudo EDITOR=nano visudo.

    If you save a file with an error, visudo asks "What now?". Press e to edit again or x to exit without saving. Never press Q: it saves the broken file.

    sudo visudo -c checks every file and prints parsed OK for each one.

    #What a clean Mint 21 sudoers file looks like

    These are the only active lines in a stock /etc/sudoers. Defaults use_pty is present on current 22.04 builds and may be missing on older images:

    Defaults        env_reset
Defaults        mail_badpass
Defaults        secure_path="/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/snap/bin"
Defaults        use_pty

root    ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL
%admin ALL=(ALL) ALL
%sudo   ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL

@includedir /etc/sudoers.d
    • %sudo means "members of the group sudo". Leave that line alone and control admins through group membership.
    • @includedir (or the older #includedir) is a directive, even though the old form starts with #. It loads every file in /etc/sudoers.d/ whose name has no . and does not end in ~.

    #Check the files in /etc/sudoers.d

    sudo ls -la /etc/sudoers.d/

    A stock Mint 21 folder holds README and 0pwfeedback (Defaults pwfeedback, which shows asterisks while you type a password). For every other file, ask dpkg who owns it:

    dpkg -S /etc/sudoers.d/<file>

    A package name means a package installed it. "no path found" means someone added it by hand; read it closely. Note a malicious file's name and content in your changelog, then delete it:

    sudo rm /etc/sudoers.d/<file>

    #Remove dangerous sudoers entries

    Entry Why it is bad Fix
    <username> ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL for a non-admin Gives root to an unauthorized user Delete the line
    %users ALL=(ALL) ALL or ALL ALL=(ALL) ALL Every user is root Delete the line
    NOPASSWD: anywhere sudo without a password Remove NOPASSWD:
    Defaults !authenticate or Defaults:<username> !authenticate No password prompt Delete the line
    A user allowed /bin/bash, /bin/sh, /usr/bin/vim, /usr/bin/find, /usr/bin/python3 or /usr/bin/less Each of these can open a root shell Delete the line
    Defaults !env_reset or env_keep+=LD_PRELOAD Users can inject code into root programs Delete the line
    Defaults timestamp_timeout=-1 sudo never asks again Delete it or set 5
    Defaults !use_pty or other negated logging options Weakens logging Delete the line
    A group line such as %games ALL=(ALL) ALL Root for every member of that group Delete the line
    An include pointing at an unusual folder Hides rules somewhere else Read that folder

    #Add hardening Defaults

    Run sudo visudo and add these under the existing Defaults lines:

    Defaults        use_pty
Defaults        logfile="/var/log/sudo.log"
Defaults        passwd_tries=3
Defaults        timestamp_timeout=5

    use_pty runs commands in a pseudo-terminal so background processes cannot outlive the session, and logfile keeps a dedicated sudo log. passwd_tries=3 is already the default; writing it out satisfies checklists that look for it.

    #Check what a user can run with sudo

    Show the rules that apply to one user:

    sudo -l -U <username>

    Show your own rules with sudo -l. A standard user should print:

    User <username> is not allowed to run sudo on <hostname>.

    #Remove a user's sudo rights

    1. Remove the user from the groups: sudo gpasswd -d <username> sudo (and from admin if that group exists).
    2. Delete any line naming the user in /etc/sudoers or /etc/sudoers.d/*, using visudo.
    3. Delete a whole malicious drop-in with sudo rm /etc/sudoers.d/<file> after noting it for Forensics.

    #Check polkit rules

    Mint's graphical admin tools use pkexec and polkit, which treat members of sudo (and admin) as administrators. Mint 21 ships polkit 0.105, which reads .pkla rule files. List them:

    sudo ls -la /etc/polkit-1/localauthority/50-local.d/ /etc/polkit-1/localauthority.conf.d/ /var/lib/polkit-1/localauthority/

    Remove any rule that gives ResultAny=yes, ResultInactive=yes or ResultActive=yes to unauthorized users or groups. 51-ubuntu-admin.conf in localauthority.conf.d is stock: it names unix-group:sudo;unix-group:admin as admins.

    Verify

    sudo visudo -c reports parsed OK for every file, sudo grep -rnE 'NOPASSWD|!authenticate' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/ prints nothing, and sudo -l -U <username> says a standard user is not allowed to run sudo.

    PreviousUsers and groupsNextPassword policy (login.defs, pwquality, history)
    LNX

    Password policy (login.defs, pwquality, history)

    jump:lin-passpol

    Keep a root shell open while editing PAM

    Before you touch anything in /etc/pam.d/, open a terminal, run sudo -i, and leave it open. Back up once with sudo mkdir -p /root/cp-backup && sudo cp -an /etc/pam.d /root/cp-backup/ (without the mkdir, cp puts the files straight into /root/cp-backup and the restore path below is wrong). After every change, test in a SECOND terminal with su - <username> and sudo -k; sudo true. If logins break, restore from the root shell with cp -a /root/cp-backup/pam.d/. /etc/pam.d/. Do not log out, lock the screen or reboot until a test login works.

    Fast path

    1. Open a root shell (sudo -i) and leave it open; back up /etc/pam.d as above.
    2. Set every user's password first (how).

    3. Set aging for new accounts:

      sudo sed -i -E 's/^PASS_MAX_DAYS.*/PASS_MAX_DAYS\t90/; s/^PASS_MIN_DAYS.*/PASS_MIN_DAYS\t1/; s/^PASS_WARN_AGE.*/PASS_WARN_AGE\t7/' /etc/login.defs

    4. Apply aging to existing users with the chage loop.

    5. Install pwquality and set the rules in /etc/security/pwquality.conf (how).
    6. Add remember=5 to the pam_unix line in /etc/pam.d/common-password (how).
    7. Remove nullok from /etc/pam.d/common-auth (how).
    8. Test su - <username> in the second terminal.

    #Set password aging in login.defs

    Open the file and press Ctrl+W, type PASS_MAX, Enter:

    sudo nano /etc/login.defs

    The Mint defaults are PASS_MAX_DAYS 99999, PASS_MIN_DAYS 0 and PASS_WARN_AGE 7. Change the three lines to:

    PASS_MAX_DAYS   90
PASS_MIN_DAYS   1
PASS_WARN_AGE   7

    The sed command in the fast path makes the same change in one step. Check the result:

    grep -E '^PASS_(MAX|MIN|WARN)' /etc/login.defs

    PASS_MIN_DAYS 1 is enough for scoring; some checklists use 7. Optional extras in the same file are UMASK 027 (new files are not world-readable) and LOGIN_RETRIES 3. ENCRYPT_METHOD SHA512 is usually already set; it is used by tools such as chpasswd -c that hash outside PAM, while normal password changes are hashed by the yescrypt option on the pam_unix line.

    #Apply aging to existing users with chage

    login.defs only applies to accounts created after the change. Existing users need chage. Set passwords first, then age one user:

    sudo chage -M 90 -m 1 -W 7 <username>

    Age every human user at once:

    for u in $(awk -F: '$3>=1000 && $3<65534 {print $1}' /etc/passwd); do
  sudo chage -M 90 -m 1 -W 7 "$u" && echo "aged $u"
done

    Check one user:

    sudo chage -l <username>

    You should see Minimum number of days between password change : 1, Maximum number of days between password change : 90 and Number of days of warning before password expires : 7.

    Old passwords expire the moment you set -M 90

    Set the new passwords with chpasswd BEFORE applying aging; that resets the last-change date. To reset only the date, run sudo chage -d "$(date +%F)" <username>. If chage -l shows a "Last password change" more than 90 days ago, chage -M 90 expires that password immediately, and the user (including your own account in sudo and at the screen lock) is forced to change it at the next authentication. Never run chage -d 0 on your own account or an account the scoring engine logs in with; it forces a change at next login and can lock you out of the desktop.

    #Turn on password complexity with pwquality

    Install the PAM module (it may already be installed) and check that it is in the password stack:

    sudo apt install libpam-pwquality

    grep pwquality /etc/pam.d/common-password

    Expected output:

    password        requisite                       pam_pwquality.so retry=3

    If the grep prints nothing, add the pwquality line yourself directly above the pam_unix line and add use_authtok try_first_pass to pam_unix (full file). Normally installing the package runs pam-auth-update, which adds that line and changes the pam_unix line to pam_unix.so obscure use_authtok try_first_pass yescrypt. If common-password was already edited by hand, pam-auth-update prints "Local modifications to /etc/pam.d/common-*, not updating" and adds nothing.

    Set the rules. Every line in the stock /etc/security/pwquality.conf is a comment, so you can append yours at the end:

    sudo nano /etc/security/pwquality.conf

    minlen = 12
ucredit = -1
lcredit = -1
dcredit = -1
ocredit = -1
difok = 3
maxrepeat = 3
usercheck = 1
dictcheck = 1
enforce_for_root
retry = 3
    Setting Meaning
    minlen = 12 Minimum length (use 14 if a checklist asks)
    ucredit = -1 At least 1 uppercase letter (a negative value is a required count)
    lcredit = -1 At least 1 lowercase letter
    dcredit = -1 At least 1 digit
    ocredit = -1 At least 1 symbol
    minclass = 3 Alternative to the credits: at least 3 of the 4 character classes
    difok = 3 New password must differ from the old one in 3 characters
    maxrepeat = 3 No more than 3 identical characters in a row
    usercheck = 1 Reject passwords containing the username
    dictcheck = 1 Reject dictionary words
    enforce_for_root Apply the rules when root sets a password too
    retry = 3 Prompts before passwd gives up

    Some scoring checks read the PAM line instead of the conf file, so you can also put the options on the line itself:

    password        requisite                       pam_pwquality.so retry=3 minlen=12 ucredit=-1 lcredit=-1 dcredit=-1 ocredit=-1 difok=3 enforce_for_root

    Test it: as a normal user run passwd and try password1. It must be rejected with a "BAD PASSWORD" message. If passwd says "You must wait longer to change your password", the minimum age you set is blocking the test; it says nothing about pwquality.

    enforce_for_root also blocks root's chpasswd

    Without enforce_for_root, root running passwd <username> or chpasswd only sees a warning for a weak password and the change goes through. With it, root's changes must pass every rule, because chpasswd uses /etc/pam.d/common-password. A failing password prints BAD PASSWORD: ..., then pam_chauthtok() failed ... Have exhausted maximum number of retries for service and password not changed. The example team password Cyb3rP@tri0t!2026 passes all the rules above. Checks that compare old and new passwords (difok) are skipped for root, because root is not asked for the old password.

    #Set password history

    The quickest history setting is remember=5 on the pam_unix line of /etc/pam.d/common-password:

    sudo nano /etc/pam.d/common-password

    The stock active lines on Mint 21 with pwquality installed:

    password        requisite                       pam_pwquality.so retry=3
password        [success=1 default=ignore]      pam_unix.so obscure use_authtok try_first_pass yescrypt
password        requisite                       pam_deny.so
password        required                        pam_permit.so
password        optional                        pam_gnome_keyring.so

    After the change, only the pam_unix line is different:

    password        requisite                       pam_pwquality.so retry=3
password        [success=1 default=ignore]      pam_unix.so obscure use_authtok try_first_pass yescrypt remember=5
password        requisite                       pam_deny.so
password        required                        pam_permit.so
password        optional                        pam_gnome_keyring.so

    Without libpam-pwquality the pam_unix line is pam_unix.so obscure yescrypt. Never add use_authtok to pam_unix unless a pam_pwquality (or pam_cracklib) line sits above it: with nothing to supply the new password, every change fails with "Authentication token manipulation error".

    pam_pwhistory is the alternative. Insert one line between pwquality and pam_unix. Use requisite: with required, a rejected password only fails after pam_unix has already saved it. Leave success=1 unchanged, because it counts the lines after pam_unix:

    password        requisite                       pam_pwquality.so retry=3
password        requisite                       pam_pwhistory.so remember=5 use_authtok enforce_for_root
password        [success=1 default=ignore]      pam_unix.so obscure use_authtok try_first_pass yescrypt remember=5

    Either one alone satisfies a history check, and using both is harmless. The old hashes are stored in /etc/security/opasswd, which should be mode 600, owner root:root. On Mint 21 (PAM 1.4) pam_pwhistory takes its options on the PAM line only; the pwhistory.conf file arrived in a later PAM release.

    History blocks re-using the team password

    With pam_pwhistory ... enforce_for_root, root setting a password that is already in that user's history is refused with "Password has been already used. Choose another." and chpasswd prints password not changed. Set the team password once per user, or set passwords before you turn on history. pam_unix's own remember= check does not apply when root sets the password.

    #Check the hashing algorithm

    grep -n 'pam_unix' /etc/pam.d/common-password

    Mint 21 uses yescrypt on the pam_unix line, and sha512 is also acceptable. If the line says md5, bigcrypt or names no method, change it to yescrypt and reset every user's password so the hashes are rewritten.

    #Remove nullok

    With nullok, accounts that have an empty password can log in. Find it:

    grep -n nullok /etc/pam.d/common-auth /etc/pam.d/common-password

    The stock common-auth line on Mint 21 is:

    auth    [success=1 default=ignore]      pam_unix.so nullok

    Change it to:

    auth    [success=1 default=ignore]      pam_unix.so

    Remove nullok and the older nullok_secure from both files in one step:

    sudo sed -i 's/ nullok_secure//; s/ nullok//' /etc/pam.d/common-auth /etc/pam.d/common-password

    If you already added pam_faillock, the pam_unix line reads success=2; the sed works the same way.

    Fix empty passwords before removing nullok

    After nullok is gone, any account with an empty password can no longer log in at all, at the login screen, in su, or at the screen lock. Run sudo awk -F: '$2=="" {print $1}' /etc/shadow first and give those accounts passwords (or lock them if they are not authorized).

    #Avoid pam-auth-update overwrites

    /etc/pam.d/common-* are generated by pam-auth-update. Without --force it refuses to overwrite files you edited by hand, so your edits survive package installs. Never run sudo pam-auth-update --force after manual changes: it rebuilds the files from the profiles and drops your faillock, history and nullok edits. After installing any libpam-* package, re-check your lines:

    grep -nE 'pwquality|pwhistory|faillock|remember|nullok' /etc/pam.d/common-*
    What the stock PAM files look like on Mint 21

    Mint 21 uses Ubuntu 22.04's PAM 1.4. These are the active lines of a fresh install; a desktop with home-folder encryption also has pam_ecryptfs.so lines.

    /etc/pam.d/common-auth:

    auth    [success=1 default=ignore]      pam_unix.so nullok
auth    requisite                       pam_deny.so
auth    required                        pam_permit.so
auth    optional                        pam_cap.so

    /etc/pam.d/common-account:

    account [success=1 new_authtok_reqd=done default=ignore]        pam_unix.so
account requisite                       pam_deny.so
account required                        pam_permit.so

    /etc/pam.d/common-password is shown under password history. The [success=N default=ignore] control means "on success skip the next N lines". In each file a successful pam_unix jumps over pam_deny.so and lands on pam_permit.so; a failure falls into pam_deny.so.

    Verify

    Run these and compare:

    grep -E '^PASS_' /etc/login.defs
sudo chage -l <username>
grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/security/pwquality.conf
grep -nE 'pwquality|pam_unix|pwhistory' /etc/pam.d/common-password
grep -n nullok /etc/pam.d/common-* || echo "no nullok"

    Expect PASS values 90, 1 and 7; chage showing 90, 1 and 7; your pwquality settings; pam_pwquality and remember=5 in common-password; and "no nullok".

    Previoussudoers and sudo rightsNextAccount lockout (pam_faillock)
    LNX

    Account lockout (pam_faillock)

    jump:lin-lockout

    Highest-risk edit on the image

    A wrong line in /etc/pam.d/common-auth can stop every login, including sudo and the screen lock. Keep a root shell open (sudo -i), back up /etc/pam.d (how), and test with su - <username> in a second terminal before you close anything. pam_tally2 does not exist on Mint 21; guides that use it are outdated.

    Fast path

    1. Open a root shell and back up PAM:

      sudo -i

      mkdir -p /root/cp-backup && cp -an /etc/pam.d /etc/security /root/cp-backup/

    2. Append the lockout values (run once; every stock line in this file is a comment):

      printf 'deny = 5\nfail_interval = 900\nunlock_time = 900\n' | sudo tee -a /etc/security/faillock.conf

    3. Edit /etc/pam.d/common-auth so it matches the finished file.

    4. Append the account line (run once):

      echo 'account required                        pam_faillock.so' | sudo tee -a /etc/pam.d/common-account

    5. In the second terminal, log in with su - <username>, then test the lockout.

    Ubuntu 22.04 ships no pam-auth-update profile for faillock, so these edits are made by hand.

    #Set the lockout values in faillock.conf

    sudo nano /etc/security/faillock.conf

    Uncomment and set these lines, or append them at the end:

    deny = 5
fail_interval = 900
unlock_time = 900
    Setting Meaning Default when not set
    deny = 5 Lock after 5 consecutive failures 3
    fail_interval = 900 Count failures within 15 minutes 900
    unlock_time = 900 The lock ends by itself after 15 minutes (0 means never; avoid that on a competition image) 600
    even_deny_root Lock root too (leave it off; it is risky) off
    audit Log the username for unknown users off
    silent Do not tell the user they are locked off
    dir = /var/run/faillock Where failure records are kept /var/run/faillock

    The records live on tmpfs, so a reboot clears them.

    #Add pam_faillock to common-auth

    sudo nano /etc/pam.d/common-auth

    The stock active lines on Mint 21:

    auth    [success=1 default=ignore]      pam_unix.so nullok
auth    requisite                       pam_deny.so
auth    required                        pam_permit.so
auth    optional                        pam_cap.so

    The finished file, with nullok removed and pam_faillock added:

    auth    requisite                       pam_faillock.so preauth
auth    [success=2 default=ignore]      pam_unix.so
auth    [default=die]                   pam_faillock.so authfail
auth    requisite                       pam_deny.so
auth    required                        pam_permit.so
auth    optional                        pam_cap.so

    The three changes:

    1. A new first line, pam_faillock.so preauth, refuses accounts that are already locked before the password is checked.
    2. success=1 becomes success=2. On a correct password pam_unix now skips two lines (authfail and pam_deny) and lands on pam_permit.
    3. A new line right after pam_unix, [default=die] pam_faillock.so authfail, records the failure and stops.

    Type the lines in nano to match the finished file, save, and test.

    This rewrites the stock pam_unix line into the three faillock lines. Run it once, only on an unmodified file, then compare the result with the finished file:

    sudo sed -i -E 's/^(auth\s+)\[success=1 default=ignore\](\s+pam_unix\.so.*)$/auth\trequisite\t\t\tpam_faillock.so preauth\n\1[success=2 default=ignore]\2\nauth\t[default=die]\t\t\tpam_faillock.so authfail/' /etc/pam.d/common-auth

    grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/pam.d/common-auth

    It keeps nullok if it was there; remove it with the nullok step.

    Count the lines if your file is different

    success=N means "skip the next N lines". If you add authfail but leave pam_unix at success=1, a correct password lands on pam_deny.so and every login fails. If your common-auth has extra modules between pam_unix and pam_deny (for example pam_sss, pam_winbind or pam_ecryptfs), pick N so a successful pam_unix lands exactly on pam_permit.so.

    #Add pam_faillock to common-account

    Append this line at the end of /etc/pam.d/common-account:

    account required                        pam_faillock.so

    It clears the user's failure count after a successful login, so only consecutive failures count toward the lock.

    #Test the lockout without logging out

    Do this in the second (normal) terminal. In the root shell su never asks for a password, so a test there proves nothing. Log in with the correct password, then type exit:

    su - <username>

    Run su - <username> again five times with a wrong password, then look at the records:

    sudo faillock --user <username>

    You should see five lines with V (valid) in the last column. A sixth su - <username> with the correct password must now fail. Clear the lock and confirm the login works again:

    sudo faillock --user <username> --reset

    Also run sudo -k; sudo true with your own password to confirm sudo still works.

    #Clear a locked account

    Clear one user's failures:

    sudo faillock --user <username> --reset

    Show every user's failure records with sudo faillock. A locked user who tries to log in sees "The account is locked due to 5 failed logins" with the minutes left.

    The authsucc variant you may find in a file

    Some guides use this layout instead: pam_unix at success=1, then [default=die] pam_faillock.so authfail, then sufficient pam_faillock.so authsucc, then requisite pam_deny.so. It also works, as long as pam_deny.so still follows the authsucc line. A common broken version replaces pam_deny and pam_permit with the authfail and authsucc lines. On Ubuntu 22.04 that version admits a locked user who types the correct password (Launchpad bug 1966416), because a failing sufficient line is ignored and a later optional module succeeds. If you find that layout, put pam_deny.so and pam_permit.so back or switch to the layout above. Do not mix the two.

    Verify

    grep -n faillock /etc/pam.d/common-auth /etc/pam.d/common-account
grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/security/faillock.conf

    Expect two faillock lines in common-auth (preauth before pam_unix, authfail right after it, pam_unix at success=2), one in common-account, and deny = 5, fail_interval = 900, unlock_time = 900 in faillock.conf.

    PreviousPassword policy (login.defs, pwquality, history)NextFirewall (ufw / gufw)
    LNX

    Firewall (ufw / gufw)

    jump:lin-firewall

    Never block outbound traffic

    Keep the outgoing default at allow. The scoring engine and the README web page need outbound connections.

    Fast path

    1. Set the defaults:

      sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing

    2. Allow each README-required service, for example SSH (table):

      sudo ufw allow OpenSSH

    3. Turn the firewall on and answer y if asked:

      sudo ufw enable

    4. Turn on logging:

      sudo ufw logging on

    5. Check the result with sudo ufw status verbose.

    #Turn on the firewall

    Open the menu and type firewall to start Firewall Configuration (gufw). If it is missing, install it with sudo apt install gufw. Enter your password, set Status ON, Incoming Deny and Outgoing Allow. Add rules on the Rules tab with +.

    ufw is installed on Mint but turned off by default. Install it if it was removed:

    sudo apt install ufw

    sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status verbose

    Expected output:

    Status: active
Logging: on (low)
Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing), disabled (routed)

    #Allow README-required services

    Service Rule
    SSH sudo ufw allow OpenSSH or sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
    SSH on a custom port sudo ufw allow <port>/tcp
    Apache or nginx sudo ufw allow 80/tcp and sudo ufw allow 443/tcp (or sudo ufw allow 'Apache Full')
    FTP (vsftpd) sudo ufw allow 20:21/tcp plus the passive range, for example sudo ufw allow 40000:40100/tcp
    Samba sudo ufw allow Samba (137,138/udp and 139,445/tcp)
    MySQL remote access (rare) sudo ufw allow from <ip-address> to any port 3306 proto tcp
    DNS server (bind9) sudo ufw allow 53
    Mail (postfix, dovecot) sudo ufw allow 25/tcp, plus 143/tcp and 993/tcp (IMAP) or 110/tcp and 995/tcp (POP3) as needed
    CUPS printing from the network (rare) sudo ufw allow 631/tcp

    List the application profiles with sudo ufw app list. A profile appears only after its package is installed.

    #Remove or deny rules

    List rules with numbers:

    sudo ufw status numbered

    Delete one by number. The list renumbers after each delete, so list again before the next one:

    sudo ufw delete <rule-number>

    Delete a rule by its text:

    sudo ufw delete allow 23/tcp

    Add explicit denies, for example telnet and NFS:

    sudo ufw deny 23/tcp
sudo ufw deny 2049

    Look for planted allow rules for telnet (23), FTP (21) when FTP is not required, VNC (5900-5910), backdoor ports (4444, 1337, 31337, 6666), rsh (512-514), SNMP (161) and RDP (3389).

    #Turn on logging

    sudo ufw logging on

    on means level low. Use sudo ufw logging medium if a checklist asks for more. Logs go to /var/log/ufw.log.

    #Rate-limit SSH

    Block an address that opens 6 or more connections within 30 seconds:

    sudo ufw limit OpenSSH

    #Reset a sabotaged firewall

    If the rules are a mess or /etc/ufw/*.rules was tampered with, reset and rebuild. The reset turns ufw off and saves the old rules as backup files:

    sudo ufw --force reset

    sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow <port>/tcp
sudo ufw enable

    Do not install firewalld next to ufw; they conflict. If sudo iptables -S shows many odd ACCEPT rules that ufw did not create, reset and re-enable ufw.

    ufw config files

    /etc/default/ufw should contain IPV6=yes and DEFAULT_INPUT_POLICY="DROP". /etc/ufw/ufw.conf should contain ENABLED=yes after you enable the firewall. /etc/ufw/sysctl.conf can override kernel settings; check it if kernel values keep reverting.

    Verify

    sudo ufw status verbose shows Status: active, Logging: on (low) and Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing), and systemctl is-enabled ufw prints enabled.

    PreviousAccount lockout (pam_faillock)NextUpdates and repositories
    LNX

    Updates and repositories

    jump:lin-updates

    Fast path

    1. Check the package sources for planted repos (how):

      grep -rvE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/apt/sources.list /etc/apt/sources.list.d/

    2. Start the upgrade early in its own terminal and keep working elsewhere:

      sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y

    3. Open Update Manager > Edit > Preferences and turn on auto-refresh and every Automation option (how).

    4. Set daily automatic updates in /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades (how).
    5. Afterwards, check every required service with systemctl status <service-name>.

    #Install updates

    Open Menu > Administration > Update Manager (mintupdate). Click Refresh, then Install Updates. If Update Manager offers an update to itself first, install that, then refresh again.

    sudo apt update
sudo apt full-upgrade -y

    A full upgrade can take 10-40 minutes. Do not run two apt commands at once, and do not run apt while Update Manager is installing.

    Keep your config when asked

    Upgrades can restart services; check required services afterward with systemctl status <service-name>. If dpkg asks whether to replace a config file you modified, choose the default (N, keep your currently-installed version) so your hardening is not overwritten.

    #Check repositories for bad sources

    On Mint the real list is in /etc/apt/sources.list.d/; /etc/apt/sources.list is normally empty or only comments.

    Open Menu > Administration > Software Sources (mintsources). Check Official repositories, PPAs and Additional repositories, and remove anything the README does not need. The Maintenance tab has "Fix MergeList problems" and "Purge residual configuration" for a broken apt.

    Show every active source line with its file name:

    grep -rvE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/apt/sources.list /etc/apt/sources.list.d/

    ls -la /etc/apt/sources.list.d/

    Move a bad repo file out of the folder:

    sudo mv /etc/apt/sources.list.d/<file> /root/cp-backup/

    A legitimate Mint 21.x /etc/apt/sources.list.d/official-package-repositories.list looks like this. The Mint codename is vanessa (21.0), vera (21.1), victoria (21.2) or virginia (21.3), and mirror hostnames may differ:

    deb http://packages.linuxmint.com virginia main upstream import backport

deb http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu jammy main restricted universe multiverse
deb http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu jammy-updates main restricted universe multiverse
deb http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu jammy-backports main restricted universe multiverse

deb http://security.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ jammy-security main restricted universe multiverse

    Red flags:

    • A line with another Ubuntu codename (focal, bionic, noble), Debian, Kali, or a random IP address or domain.
    • [trusted=yes] or [allow-insecure=yes] in a deb line.
    • No jammy-security line, which means no security updates. Add it back.
    • Unknown PPA files in sources.list.d/ that the README does not need.
    • Held packages that block security updates. List them with apt-mark showhold and release one with sudo apt-mark unhold <package>.
    • Pin files in /etc/apt/preferences.d/ that block updates. Mint ships its own (official-package-repositories.pref, and nosnap.pref, which blocks snapd on purpose); look for unknown ones with a negative Pin-Priority.

    Search apt's config for proxies, unauthenticated installs and hook scripts:

    grep -rniE 'proxy|unauth|invoke|insecure' /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/

    Acquire::http::Proxy pointing somewhere odd, AllowUnauthenticated "true", or DPkg::Pre-Invoke / Post-Invoke running unknown scripts are all planted. Move the file to /root/cp-backup/.

    #Turn on Update Manager automation

    Open Update Manager > Edit > Preferences.

    Tab Setting
    Auto-refresh "Refresh the list of updates automatically" on, with a short interval (for example daily)
    Automation "Apply updates automatically" on (asks for your password)
    Automation "Remove obsolete kernels and dependencies" on
    Automation "Update Cinnamon spices automatically" and "Update Flatpaks automatically" on

    Turn on automatic updates and automatic removal of old kernels:

    sudo mintupdate-automation upgrade enable
sudo mintupdate-automation autoremove enable

    The spices, Flatpak and auto-refresh options are set in the GUI only.

    Check the timers:

    systemctl list-timers --all | grep -i mintupdate

    You should see mintupdate-automation-upgrade.timer (and mintupdate-automation-autoremove.timer when kernel cleanup is on). Automatic runs log to /var/log/mintupdate.log.

    #Configure unattended-upgrades

    Mint's own automation is Update Manager. Some scoring checks look for Ubuntu's unattended-upgrades as well, and it may not be installed on Mint. Install it and turn it on (answer Yes):

    sudo apt install unattended-upgrades
sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades

    Set /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades to these lines ("1" means every day, "0" turns it off):

    APT::Periodic::Update-Package-Lists "1";
APT::Periodic::Download-Upgradeable-Packages "1";
APT::Periodic::AutocleanInterval "7";
APT::Periodic::Unattended-Upgrade "1";

    apt reads the files in apt.conf.d in name order and a later file wins, so look for a planted file sorting after 20auto-upgrades (for example 99-noupdates) that sets the same keys to "0":

    grep -rn 'APT::Periodic' /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/

    Open /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades with sudo nano and add the Ubuntu origins inside the Unattended-Upgrade::Allowed-Origins { block, above the closing };:

            "Ubuntu:jammy-security";
        "Ubuntu:jammy-updates";

    The stock origins are "${distro_id}:${distro_codename}" and "${distro_id}:${distro_codename}-security". On Mint ${distro_id} is Linuxmint and ${distro_codename} is the Mint codename (for example virginia), so neither matches Ubuntu's archives and nothing gets installed without these two lines.

    Check which origins it will use:

    sudo unattended-upgrade --dry-run --debug 2>&1 | grep -i 'allowed origins'

    Expected output includes o=Ubuntu,a=jammy-security. The run log is in /var/log/unattended-upgrades/.

    #Update specific packages and the kernel

    Upgrade single packages without a full upgrade:

    sudo apt install --only-upgrade firefox
sudo apt install --only-upgrade openssh-server sudo openssl bash

    List what is still waiting, and compare installed and available versions of one package:

    apt list --upgradable
apt policy <package>

    Kernel updates arrive with sudo apt full-upgrade or Update Manager. Update Manager > View > Linux Kernels shows installed and available kernels; do not switch kernel series during a round. A new kernel only runs after a reboot, so plan the reboot late in the round and check uname -r afterward.

    #Fix broken apt or dpkg

    Error Fix
    Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend Another apt or Update Manager is running. Wait, or find it with ps aux | grep -E 'apt|dpkg'. Only if nothing is running: sudo rm /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend /var/lib/dpkg/lock /var/cache/apt/archives/lock /var/lib/apt/lists/lock
    dpkg was interrupted, you must manually run 'sudo dpkg --configure -a' sudo dpkg --configure -a
    Unmet dependencies sudo apt --fix-broken install
    NO_PUBKEY or signature errors on an official repo sudo apt install --reinstall linuxmint-keyring ubuntu-keyring
    NO_PUBKEY on an unknown repo Remove that repo
    Hash sum mismatch sudo rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*, then sudo apt update
    Temporary failure resolving Check the network, and check /etc/hosts and /etc/resolv.conf for tampering

    Verify

    sudo apt update ends with "All packages are up to date", apt list --upgradable is empty or nearly so, and cat /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades shows "1" for the periodic keys.

    PreviousFirewall (ufw / gufw)NextServices and open ports
    LNX

    Services and open ports

    jump:lin-services

    Remove only what the README does not require

    If the README says the machine is a web server, Apache stays and gets hardened. Never stop or remove anything named CyberPatriot or CCS.

    Fast path

    1. List listening ports and the program behind each:

      sudo ss -tulpn

    2. List running services:

      systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running

    3. For each server you do not recognize, check the README. If it is not required, purge its package (table):

      sudo apt purge <package>

    4. For a base-system service you cannot remove, stop and disable it: sudo systemctl disable --now <service-name>.

    5. Confirm each required service still runs: systemctl is-active <service-name>.

    #List listening ports and services

    sudo ss -tulpn

    systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running

    List what starts at boot:

    systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled

    Socket units can start a service on demand, so list them too:

    systemctl list-units --type=socket

    For each required service, systemctl is-active <service-name> must print active.

    #Read ss output

    Example output:

    Netid State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port Process
tcp   LISTEN 0      32           0.0.0.0:21         0.0.0.0:*     users:(("vsftpd",pid=812,fd=3))
tcp   LISTEN 0      4096   127.0.0.53%lo:53         0.0.0.0:*     users:(("systemd-resolve",pid=511,fd=14))
    • 0.0.0.0, [::] or * means reachable from the network. 127.0.0.1 or ::1 means local only, which is lower risk.
    • Normal on Mint: systemd-resolve on 127.0.0.53:53, cupsd on 127.0.0.1:631, cups-browsed on UDP 0.0.0.0:631, avahi-daemon on UDP 5353, and the DHCP client on UDP 68.
    • Find the package behind a program with dpkg -S "$(sudo readlink -f /proc/<pid>/exe)" (without sudo, readlink cannot see root's processes).
    • Alternatives: sudo lsof -i -P -n | grep LISTEN, or sudo netstat -tulpn (needs the net-tools package).

    #Stop, disable, mask or purge a service

    Stop and disable a service in one step:

    sudo systemctl disable --now <service-name>

    Block it from starting at all, even manually or as a dependency, and undo that later if needed:

    sudo systemctl mask <service-name>

    sudo systemctl unmask <service-name>

    Remove the program and its config, then clean up the leftovers:

    sudo apt purge <package>
sudo apt autoremove --purge

    Purge unauthorized server software; scoring usually checks that the package is gone. Use disable or mask for base-system services you cannot remove or are unsure about. Socket-activated services also need their socket disabled, or they start again on the next connection. For printing that is sudo systemctl disable --now cups.service cups.socket cups.path cups-browsed.service, and for mDNS sudo systemctl disable --now avahi-daemon.service avahi-daemon.socket.

    #Commonly planted services

    Service (unit) Package to purge Port Notes
    vsftpd vsftpd 21 FTP server
    proftpd proftpd-basic (or proftpd-core) 21 FTP server
    pure-ftpd pure-ftpd 21 FTP server
    telnet through inetd telnetd, inetutils-telnetd, telnetd-ssl 23 Plaintext login. Purge the telnet client too if policy says so
    apache2 apache2 apache2-bin apache2-data apache2-utils 80, 443 Web server
    nginx nginx nginx-common nginx-core 80, 443 Web server
    lighttpd lighttpd 80 Web server
    smbd, nmbd samba (leave samba-libs and smbclient alone) 139, 445 File sharing
    nfs-server nfs-kernel-server 2049 NFS exports
    rpcbind rpcbind 111 Only NFS needs it
    avahi-daemon avahi-daemon 5353/udp mDNS, part of the desktop. Prefer disabling the service and socket
    cups, cups-browsed cups, cups-browsed 631 Printing. Disable only if the README says no printing
    snmpd snmpd 161/udp SNMP agent
    xinetd, inetd xinetd, openbsd-inetd, inetutils-inetd many Super-servers; read /etc/inetd.conf and /etc/xinetd.d/
    ypbind nis varies Old directory service
    rsh, rlogin rsh-server, rsh-redone-server, rsh-client 512-514 Plaintext remote shell
    talk talkd, talk, inetutils-talkd 517-518/udp Old chat
    tftpd-hpa tftpd-hpa, tftpd, atftpd 69/udp No authentication
    named bind9 53 DNS server
    isc-dhcp-server isc-dhcp-server 67/udp DHCP server
    squid squid 3128 Proxy
    postfix postfix 25 Mail server (removing it may pull in another MTA; that is fine)
    dovecot dovecot-core dovecot-imapd dovecot-pop3d 110, 143, 993, 995 Mail server
    mysql, mariadb mysql-server, mariadb-server 3306 Database
    postgresql postgresql 5432 Database
    VNC x11vnc, vino, tigervnc-standalone-server, tightvncserver 5900+ Remote desktop
    xrdp xrdp 3389 Remote desktop
    ssh openssh-server 22 Only if SSH is not required
    netcat listeners netcat-traditional, ncat any See malware
    any other web port none 8080 and others Check ss output for every web port

    Purge several at once. Edit the list to match what you found and what the README allows, and read apt's removal list before you answer Y:

    sudo apt purge vsftpd telnetd inetutils-telnetd rsh-server talkd tftpd-hpa xinetd openbsd-inetd snmpd nis

    Then clean up dependencies, again reading the list first. Answer n if it includes cinnamon, mint or xserver packages:

    sudo apt autoremove --purge

    apt purge with a package that is installed nowhere only prints a notice. A misspelled or unknown package name makes the whole command fail with "Unable to locate package"; remove that name and run it again.

    #Services that are normal on Mint 21

    Leave these alone: accounts-daemon, acpid, anacron, apparmor, avahi-daemon (optional), bluetooth, colord, cron, cups (optional), dbus, kerneloops, lightdm, ModemManager, NetworkManager, openvpn (inactive), polkit, rsyslog, rtkit-daemon, systemd-*, thermald, ubuntu-system-adjustments, udisks2, ufw, upower, wpa_supplicant, and unattended-upgrades if installed.

    #Find services added by an attacker

    systemctl list-unit-files --type=service --state=enabled
ls -la /etc/systemd/system/ /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/
systemctl list-timers --all

    Show a unit's file and its ExecStart line:

    systemctl cat <service-name>

    A unit file stored directly in /etc/systemd/system/ (a regular file, not a symlink) with an odd name, or an ExecStart that points at /tmp, /dev/shm, /var/tmp, a home folder, nc or bash -i, is a backdoor. Handle it as described in malware.

    Verify

    sudo ss -tulpn shows only README-required listeners plus the normal local ones, and systemctl is-active <service-name> prints active for each required service.

    PreviousUpdates and repositoriesNextSSH server hardening
    LNX

    SSH server hardening

    jump:lin-ssh

    Only if the README requires SSH

    "Remote access" in a README usually means SSH. If SSH is not required, remove it instead of hardening it.

    Fast path

    1. Back up the SSH config: sudo mkdir -p /root/cp-backup && sudo cp -an /etc/ssh /root/cp-backup/.

    2. Look for drop-in files that override the main file:

      sudo grep -rn . /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/

    3. Edit the main file and set the recommended values:

      sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config

    4. Check the syntax and restart:

      sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl restart ssh

    5. Confirm the effective settings:

      sudo sshd -T | grep -iE 'permitrootlogin|passwordauthentication|permitemptypasswords|x11forwarding|maxauthtries|allowusers'

    The service unit is ssh on Mint and Ubuntu. sshd is only an alias that exists while the service is enabled, so use ssh in systemctl commands.

    #Recommended sshd_config settings

    Edit the existing line (delete the leading #) instead of adding a second copy. If a keyword appears twice, sshd uses the first one.

    Setting Value Why
    PermitRootLogin no The stock default is prohibit-password, which still allows root with a key
    PasswordAuthentication yes or no per README Set no only if users have keys set up; otherwise you lock them out
    PermitEmptyPasswords no Blocks blank-password logins
    PubkeyAuthentication yes Keys allowed
    X11Forwarding no Ubuntu's file sets this to yes; change that line
    MaxAuthTries 3 (or 4) Limits guesses per connection (default 6)
    LoginGraceTime 60 Drops slow unauthenticated sessions (default 120)
    ClientAliveInterval 300 Probes idle clients every 5 minutes
    ClientAliveCountMax 2 Disconnects after 2 failed probes. Some checklists say 0, but on OpenSSH 8.9 0 turns the idle disconnect off
    UsePAM yes Needed for PAM policies such as faillock
    HostbasedAuthentication no No host-based trust
    IgnoreRhosts yes Ignores .rhosts
    PermitUserEnvironment no Users cannot inject environment variables
    KbdInteractiveAuthentication no Ubuntu's file already sets this (older name: ChallengeResponseAuthentication)
    LogLevel VERBOSE Logs key fingerprints
    AllowTcpForwarding no (if not needed) No tunnels
    Banner /etc/issue.net Optional warning banner
    AllowUsers README users, space-separated Only listed users may log in. Forgetting one locks them out
    Protocol leave out SSH-1 is gone in OpenSSH 8.9 and the keyword is ignored; adding Protocol 2 is harmless
    Port 22 unless the README says otherwise A changed port needs a matching ufw rule

    The lines to set, as they should read in the file:

    PermitRootLogin no
PermitEmptyPasswords no
X11Forwarding no
MaxAuthTries 3
LoginGraceTime 60
ClientAliveInterval 300
ClientAliveCountMax 2
HostbasedAuthentication no
IgnoreRhosts yes
PermitUserEnvironment no
LogLevel VERBOSE

    #Check drop-in files in sshd_config.d

    sudo grep -rn . /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/

    Drop-in files override the main file

    Ubuntu's /etc/ssh/sshd_config starts with Include /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf, above every setting. sshd keeps the FIRST value it reads for each keyword, so a planted /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/<file>.conf with PermitRootLogin yes beats your edit further down the main file. Fix or delete the drop-in.

    The folder is empty on a stock Mint install, and only files ending in .conf are read. Also check the end of the main file for Match blocks: settings after a Match User or Match Address line apply only to those connections and can quietly re-enable root or password logins. sudo sshd -T -C user=<username>,host=localhost,addr=127.0.0.1 shows the settings a specific user would get.

    #Test and restart SSH

    Check the syntax. No output means it is fine:

    sudo sshd -t

    sudo systemctl restart ssh
systemctl status ssh --no-pager

    Test a real login (type yes to the host key prompt):

    ssh <username>@localhost

    If sshd -t prints an error, fix the named line before you restart. A failed restart leaves SSH down, which costs points when it is required. "Missing privilege separation directory: /run/sshd" means the service is stopped; sudo systemctl start ssh creates the folder.

    sshd -T prints the effective settings in lowercase. Trust it over what you see in the file.

    #Review authorized_keys

    List and print every authorized_keys file on the disk:

    sudo find / -xdev \( -name authorized_keys -o -name authorized_keys2 \) -exec ls -la {} \; -exec cat {} \; 2>/dev/null

    Check whether the key file location was changed:

    sudo grep -ri AuthorizedKeysFile /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/
    • Remove keys the README did not authorize, especially in /root/.ssh/authorized_keys and for unauthorized users. Note the key comment for Forensics first.
    • Look for unexpected command= or from= options at the start of a key line.
    • An AuthorizedKeysFile pointing at an odd path (for example /tmp/keys) is a backdoor.
    • ~/.ssh should be 700 and authorized_keys 600, owned by the user.

    Fix the permissions for one user:

    sudo chmod 700 /home/<username>/.ssh
sudo chmod 600 /home/<username>/.ssh/authorized_keys
sudo chown -R <username>:<username> /home/<username>/.ssh

    #Check other SSH files

    • /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*_key must be 600 root:root, and the *.pub files 644.
    • /etc/hosts.equiv, ~/.rhosts and ~/.shosts should not exist.
    • /etc/ssh/sshrc and ~/.ssh/rc run at every login and should not exist unless you know why.
    • ~/.ssh/environment is only used with PermitUserEnvironment yes; delete planted ones.

    Pair SSH with the firewall: allow it before enabling ufw, consider sudo ufw limit OpenSSH (firewall), and set up fail2ban (how).

    #Remove SSH when it is not required

    Answer any Forensics Question about SSH keys or logins first, then purge the server. The openssh-client package (the ssh command) can stay:

    sudo apt purge openssh-server

    Check that nothing listens on port 22: sudo ss -tlnp | grep ':22 ' prints nothing.

    Verify

    sudo sshd -T | grep -iE 'permitrootlogin|permitemptypasswords|x11forwarding|maxauthtries' prints permitrootlogin no, permitemptypasswords no, x11forwarding no and maxauthtries 3, and systemctl is-active ssh prints active.

    PreviousServices and open portsNextHardening required services (FTP, Apache, Samba, MySQL, PHP, nginx, mail)
    LNX

    Hardening required services (FTP, Apache, Samba, MySQL, PHP, nginx, mail)

    jump:lin-required-services

    Never remove a service the README calls critical

    A required service that stops, gets purged or fails its functional check costs points every scoring cycle. Harden it in place, test the config, and confirm it is still running after every change.

    Fast path

    1. Find which server services are installed and running:

      systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running | grep -E 'vsftpd|proftpd|pure-ftpd|apache2|nginx|smbd|nmbd|mysql|mariadb|php|postfix|dovecot'

    2. Compare with the README. Keep and harden the ones it requires; the rest belong in Services and open ports.

    3. Back up the service's config folder (paths in the table below):

      sudo cp -a <path> /root/

    4. Set the values from that service's subsection on this page.

    5. Run the service's syntax test from the table, then restart it:

      sudo systemctl restart <service-name>

    6. Confirm it is running and still works:

      systemctl is-active <service-name>

    #Config files and test commands

    Service systemd unit Main config Syntax test
    vsftpd vsftpd /etc/vsftpd.conf none; read journalctl -u vsftpd after restart
    ProFTPD proftpd /etc/proftpd/proftpd.conf sudo proftpd -t
    Pure-FTPd pure-ftpd /etc/pure-ftpd/conf/ (one file per option) read journalctl -u pure-ftpd
    Apache apache2 /etc/apache2/ sudo apache2ctl configtest
    nginx nginx /etc/nginx/ sudo nginx -t
    PHP 8.1 apache2 or php8.1-fpm /etc/php/8.1/ php -l <file> for scripts
    Samba smbd, nmbd /etc/samba/smb.conf testparm -s
    MySQL 8.0 mysql /etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/mysqld.cnf sudo mysqld --validate-config
    MariaDB 10.6 mariadb /etc/mysql/mariadb.conf.d/50-server.cnf read journalctl -u mariadb
    Postfix postfix /etc/postfix/main.cf sudo postfix check
    Dovecot dovecot /etc/dovecot/conf.d/ sudo doveconf -n

    Ubuntu 22.04 ships PHP 8.1, MySQL 8.0, MariaDB 10.6, Samba 4.15, Apache 2.4.52, nginx 1.18, vsftpd 3.0.5 and Postfix 3.6. Mint 21 uses the same packages.

    #Harden vsftpd (FTP)

    Back up and open the config:

    sudo cp -a /etc/vsftpd.conf /root/vsftpd.conf.bak
sudo nano /etc/vsftpd.conf

    Set these lines (change the existing line if it is there, add it if not):

    anonymous_enable=NO
anon_upload_enable=NO
anon_mkdir_write_enable=NO
local_enable=YES
write_enable=NO
chroot_local_user=YES
xferlog_enable=YES
ssl_enable=YES
allow_anon_ssl=NO
force_local_logins_ssl=YES
force_local_data_ssl=YES
rsa_cert_file=/etc/ssl/certs/ssl-cert-snakeoil.pem
rsa_private_key_file=/etc/ssl/private/ssl-cert-snakeoil.key
    Setting Why
    anonymous_enable=NO No anonymous FTP (already NO in the Ubuntu default file, but planted images flip it)
    write_enable YES only if the README says users upload files; otherwise NO
    chroot_local_user=YES Users are locked into their home directory
    allow_writeable_chroot=YES Add only if chroot plus a writable home is needed (see "If it fails" below)
    ssl_enable=YES and the two force_local_* lines Encrypt logins and data with TLS
    rsa_cert_file / rsa_private_key_file The snakeoil certificate from the ssl-cert package; these two lines are already in the default file
    xferlog_enable=YES Log transfers to /var/log/vsftpd.log

    To allow only listed users, also add userlist_enable=YES, userlist_deny=NO and userlist_file=/etc/vsftpd.userlist, then put one username per line in that file.

    /etc/ftpusers is the opposite list: users who may never use FTP. It is read through PAM (/etc/pam.d/vsftpd) and root is in it by default; keep it there. The same PAM file also requires the user's shell to be listed in /etc/shells, so an FTP user whose shell you set to nologin can no longer log in to FTP.

    Check that the certificate exists before turning on TLS:

    ls -l /etc/ssl/certs/ssl-cert-snakeoil.pem /etc/ssl/private/ssl-cert-snakeoil.key

    If either file is missing, install the package and generate it:

    sudo apt install ssl-cert
sudo make-ssl-cert generate-default-snakeoil --force-overwrite

    Restart and confirm:

    sudo systemctl restart vsftpd
systemctl is-active vsftpd

    If it fails: 500 OOPS: vsftpd: refusing to run with writable root inside chroot() means the user's home is writable while chroot_local_user=YES. Add allow_writeable_chroot=YES and restart. If ssl_enable=YES makes the README's FTP clients fail, set it back to NO (one lost item is better than a broken required service).

    #Other FTP servers

    ProFTPD: in /etc/proftpd/proftpd.conf keep the <Anonymous ~ftp> block commented out or deleted, and set:

    DefaultRoot ~
ServerIdent off
RequireValidShell on

    Test with sudo proftpd -t, then sudo systemctl restart proftpd. TLS settings live in /etc/proftpd/tls.conf.

    Pure-FTPd keeps one option per file. Turn off anonymous logins and lock users into their homes:

    echo yes | sudo tee /etc/pure-ftpd/conf/NoAnonymous
echo yes | sudo tee /etc/pure-ftpd/conf/ChrootEveryone
sudo systemctl restart pure-ftpd

    #Harden Apache2

    Back up the whole config folder:

    sudo cp -a /etc/apache2 /root/apache2.bak

    Open /etc/apache2/conf-available/security.conf (it is enabled by default) and set these three lines. The Ubuntu defaults are ServerTokens OS and ServerSignature On.

    ServerTokens Prod
ServerSignature Off
TraceEnable Off

    In /etc/apache2/apache2.conf, find the <Directory /var/www/> block. Ubuntu ships it with Options Indexes FollowSymLinks, which lists folder contents to anyone. Change it to:

    <Directory /var/www/>
    Options -Indexes +FollowSymLinks
    AllowOverride None
    Require all granted
</Directory>

    Leave AllowOverride None unless the site needs .htaccess files. The <Directory /> block above it must stay Require all denied; a planted image may have changed it to granted.

    Optional security headers go in security.conf. They need the headers module:

    sudo a2enmod headers

    Header set X-Content-Type-Options: "nosniff"
Header set X-Frame-Options: "sameorigin"

    Enable the security config (it is on by default; this puts it back if someone disabled it):

    sudo a2enconf security

    Disable modules the site does not use. autoindex and status are on by default; -f skips the "essential module" prompt for autoindex:

    sudo a2dismod -f autoindex status

    If the README's site is a different virtual host, disable the default one:

    sudo a2dissite 000-default

    Test, then restart. The test must print Syntax OK:

    sudo apache2ctl configtest
sudo systemctl restart apache2

    #Clean up the web root

    After answering forensics questions, remove files in /var/www/html that are not part of the site (phpinfo.php, shell.php, backup.zip, a .git folder). Search for web shells:

    sudo grep -rlE 'eval\(|base64_decode|system\(|shell_exec|passthru' /var/www

    Make the site files owned by root, so www-data can read them but not change them. Skip this if the README says the site accepts uploads into a folder; that folder must stay writable by www-data.

    sudo chown -R root:root /var/www/html
sudo find /var/www/html -type d -exec chmod 755 {} +
sudo find /var/www/html -type f -exec chmod 644 {} +

    Apache must run as www-data, never root. Check /etc/apache2/envvars:

    grep -E 'APACHE_RUN_(USER|GROUP)' /etc/apache2/envvars

    You should see www-data on both lines. To turn on HTTPS when the README asks for it:

    sudo a2enmod ssl
sudo a2ensite default-ssl
sudo systemctl reload apache2

    #Harden nginx

    In /etc/nginx/nginx.conf, inside the http { block, the Ubuntu file has server_tokens off; commented out. Uncomment it or add these lines:

    server_tokens off;
autoindex off;

    Remove any autoindex on; lines:

    sudo grep -rn 'autoindex on' /etc/nginx/

    Optional headers, inside the same http { block or a server { block:

    add_header X-Frame-Options SAMEORIGIN;
add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff;

    Test and reload:

    sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx

    #Harden PHP

    Each way of running PHP has its own php.ini. Edit the one the web server uses:

    Used by File
    Apache module (libapache2-mod-php8.1) /etc/php/8.1/apache2/php.ini
    PHP-FPM (usual with nginx) /etc/php/8.1/fpm/php.ini
    Command line only /etc/php/8.1/cli/php.ini 
    ls /etc/php/*/

    Set these values:

    Setting Value Ubuntu default
    expose_php Off Off
    display_errors Off Off
    log_errors On On
    allow_url_fopen Off if the site does not fetch URLs On
    allow_url_include Off Off
    file_uploads Off if the site has no upload form On
    disable_functions exec,passthru,shell_exec,system,proc_open,popen,pcntl_exec empty
    session.cookie_httponly 1 empty
    session.use_strict_mode 1 0

    Test the site after setting disable_functions; some applications call exec.

    Restart whichever runs PHP:

    sudo systemctl restart apache2

    sudo systemctl restart php8.1-fpm

    #Harden Samba

    Back up and edit:

    sudo cp -a /etc/samba/smb.conf /root/smb.conf.bak
sudo nano /etc/samba/smb.conf

    In [global] set these. Ubuntu's file ships with map to guest = bad user and usershare allow guests = yes, both of which you are replacing:

    map to guest = never
restrict anonymous = 2
server min protocol = SMB2
usershare allow guests = no
server signing = mandatory
server smb encrypt = desired

    server smb encrypt is the current name; older guides write smb encrypt, which Samba 4.15 still accepts. server min protocol already defaults to SMB2_02 on this Samba version, but writing it out satisfies checks that read the file.

    In each share the README requires (for example [shared]):

    guest ok = no
browseable = yes
read only = yes
valid users = @<groupname> <username>
create mask = 0660
directory mask = 0770

    Use read only = no only if the README says users write to the share.

    Check the config and restart:

    testparm -s
sudo systemctl restart smbd nmbd

    #Remove extra shares and Samba users

    • Delete shares the README does not mention, and any share of /, /etc, /root or a home directory with write access.
    • [printers] and [print$] are in the default file; remove them if printing is not required. [homes] is commented out by default; remove or restrict it if someone enabled it.

    • Look for shares users created themselves:

      ls -la /var/lib/samba/usershares/

    Samba keeps its own password database. List Samba users:

    sudo pdbedit -L

    Remove an unauthorized one, or set a password for an authorized one:

    sudo smbpasswd -x <username>

    sudo smbpasswd -a <username>

    #Harden the MySQL or MariaDB server

    Run the secure installation script with sudo (without sudo it cannot log in, because root uses socket authentication):

    sudo mysql_secure_installation

    Answers, in order:

    1. VALIDATE PASSWORD component: y, then 1 (MEDIUM). It only checks passwords set from now on.
    2. On current Ubuntu 22.04 builds the script prints Skipping password set for root as authentication with auth_socket is used by default. That is correct; root logs in through sudo mysql and has no password to set.
    3. Remove anonymous users: y.
    4. Disallow root login remotely: y.
    5. Remove test database: y.
    6. Reload privilege tables: y.
    sudo mariadb-secure-installation

    sudo mysql_secure_installation runs the same script. Answers:

    1. Current root password: press Enter.
    2. Switch to unix_socket authentication: n (root already uses it on Ubuntu).
    3. Change the root password: y, then the team password unless the README gives one.
    4. Remove anonymous users, disallow root login remotely, remove test database, reload privilege tables: y to each.

    Older MySQL builds loop on the root password

    MySQL 8.0 builds from mid 2022 (around 8.0.29) loop forever on SET PASSWORD has no significance for user 'root'@'localhost'. Press Ctrl+C and do the same cleanup with the SQL commands below. Updating the package fixes the script.

    #Check database accounts by hand

    List every account and how it logs in:

    sudo mysql -e "SELECT user,host,plugin FROM mysql.user;"

    Expected on a clean MySQL 8.0: root@localhost with auth_socket, plus debian-sys-maint, mysql.infoschema, mysql.session and mysql.sys, all on localhost. Leave those system accounts alone.

    Remove anonymous accounts and remote root:

    sudo mysql -e "DROP USER IF EXISTS ''@'localhost';"
sudo mysql -e "DROP USER IF EXISTS ''@'<hostname>';"
sudo mysql -e "DROP USER IF EXISTS 'root'@'%';"

    Remove an account the README does not mention:

    sudo mysql -e "DROP USER '<username>'@'localhost';"

    See what an application account can do:

    sudo mysql -e "SHOW GRANTS FOR '<username>'@'localhost';"

    GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* or WITH GRANT OPTION on an application account is too much. Changing an application account's password breaks the site unless you also update the password in the site's config file, so only do it when the README asks.

    #Set the server options

    In /etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/mysqld.cnf (MySQL) or /etc/mysql/mariadb.conf.d/50-server.cnf (MariaDB), under [mysqld]:

    bind-address = 127.0.0.1
local-infile = 0
