    NET

    Module 6 data link layer

    jump:net-m6-datalink

    #Purpose of the data link layer

    The data link layer (Layer 2) handles communication between NICs on the same network. It:

    • Allows upper layers to access the media without knowing what media is used.
    • Accepts Layer 3 packets (IPv4 or IPv6) and encapsulates them into Layer 2 frames.
    • Controls how data is placed on and received from the media.
    • Exchanges frames between endpoints over the network media.
    • Receives encapsulated data and directs it to the right upper-layer protocol.
    • Performs error detection and rejects any corrupt frame.

    Layer 2 standards come from the IEEE, ITU, ISO and ANSI. The IETF does not write them.

    #LLC and MAC sublayers

    Sublayer Standard Position Job
    LLC (Logical Link Control) IEEE 802.2 Upper sublayer, between networking software and device hardware Puts information in the frame that identifies which network layer protocol is used, so IPv4 and IPv6 can share one interface and media
    MAC (Media Access Control) IEEE 802.3 (Ethernet), 802.11 (WLAN), 802.15 (WPAN) Lower sublayer, implemented in hardware (the NIC) Data encapsulation (frame delimiting, addressing, error detection) and media access control

    Memory aid

    LLC talks up to Layer 3 (software). MAC talks down to Layer 1 (hardware).

    #IEEE 802 standards to know

    Standard Technology
    802.2 Logical Link Control (LLC)
    802.3 Ethernet (wired LAN)
    802.11 WLAN (Wi-Fi)
    802.15 WPAN (Bluetooth; Zigbee is 802.15.4)
    802.16 WiMAX
    802.1Q VLAN tagging (802.1 covers bridging and management)

    #The data link layer at every hop

    At each router the packet crosses, the router:

    1. Accepts the frame from the medium.
    2. De-encapsulates the frame (removes the Layer 2 header and trailer) to get the packet.
    3. Re-encapsulates the packet into a new frame for the next medium.
    4. Forwards the new frame.

    The Layer 3 packet stays the same. The Layer 2 frame and its MAC addresses are rebuilt at every hop, and each link can use a different Layer 2 protocol (Ethernet, serial WAN, wireless).

    #Topologies

    • Physical topology: the physical connections, meaning how devices and cables are wired.
    • Logical topology: the virtual connections, meaning how frames travel from node to node. The data link layer uses the logical topology when it controls media access.

    #WAN topologies

    Topology Description Notes
    Point-to-point Permanent link between two endpoints Simplest and most common WAN topology; the two nodes do not share the media, so the frame needs little addressing
    Hub and spoke Central site connects branch sites over point-to-point links WAN version of a star; branches reach each other only through the hub
    Mesh Every system connected to every other system High availability, but high administrative and physical cost
    Hybrid Combination of topologies Partial mesh connects only some sites

    #LAN topologies

    Topology Description Notes
    Star End devices connect to a central switch Easy to install, scale and troubleshoot; most common today
    Extended star Star networks linked together Larger LANs
    Bus All devices chained on one cable, terminated at each end Legacy coax Ethernet; no switch needed
    Ring Each device connected to its neighbors in a ring Legacy FDDI and Token Ring; not terminated

    #Half-duplex and full-duplex

    Mode Behavior Where
    Half-duplex Both devices can send and receive, but only one at a time WLANs, legacy bus topologies with Ethernet hubs
    Full-duplex Both devices send and receive at the same time Ethernet switches by default (half-duplex only when connected to a hub)

    Duplex must match

    Both ends of a link must use the same duplex. A mismatch causes inefficiency, collisions and latency. See duplex mismatch.

    #Media access control methods

    Access type Also called Examples How it works
    Contention-based Non-deterministic CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA All half-duplex nodes compete for the medium
    Controlled Deterministic, scheduled Legacy Token Ring, legacy ARCNET Each node gets its own turn; inefficient because a node waits even when the medium is idle
    Method Full name Used by How it works
    CSMA/CD Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection Legacy bus-topology Ethernet and Ethernet hubs (half-duplex) Listen, send when quiet; on a detected collision, senders stop and retry later
    CSMA/CA Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance IEEE 802.11 WLANs Listen; the sender includes the time it needs the medium; the receiver returns an acknowledgment; no ACK means retry
    Why wireless avoids instead of detects

    A radio cannot reliably detect a collision while it transmits, so CSMA/CA tries to avoid collisions by announcing how long the medium will be busy. Legacy CSMA/CD also sends a jam signal after a collision and waits a random backoff time before retrying. Full-duplex switched Ethernet has no collisions, so it needs neither method. FDDI also used token passing, but the course lists only Token Ring and ARCNET as controlled access examples.

    #Data link frame

    Field Part Purpose
    Frame start Header Marks the beginning of the frame
    Addressing Header Source and destination nodes on the media
    Type Header Identifies the Layer 3 protocol in the data field
    Control Header Special flow control services such as QoS
    Data Payload The packet (packet header, segment header and data)
    Error detection Trailer FCS (frame check sequence) holding a CRC value
    Frame stop Trailer Marks the end of the frame
    • Header = frame start, addressing, type, control. Trailer = error detection and frame stop.
    • No single frame format fits all media. A WLAN frame carries more control information than an Ethernet frame because of collision avoidance.

    #How FCS and CRC error detection works

    1. The sender runs a cyclic redundancy check (CRC) on the frame and puts the result in the FCS field.
    2. The receiver runs the same calculation.
    3. If the values match, the frame is accepted. If not, the frame is discarded. Layer 2 does not resend it; upper layers such as TCP handle retransmission.

    #Layer 2 addresses

    • A Layer 2 address is a physical address (the MAC address in Ethernet).
    • It is used only for local delivery on the same network.
    • Routers replace the Layer 2 addresses at every hop. The IP addresses stay the same.

    #Common Layer 2 protocols

    Protocol Where
    Ethernet (802.3) Wired LANs
    802.11 wireless WLANs
    PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) Point-to-point WAN links
    HDLC (High-Level Data Link Control) Point-to-point WAN links; default on Cisco serial interfaces
    Frame Relay Legacy WAN service

    LAN protocols need more addressing because many hosts share the network. Point-to-point WAN protocols need little or none because only two devices are on the link. Older WAN protocols such as ATM and X.25 are being replaced by Ethernet in the WAN.

    PreviousModule 5 number systems, binary, decimal and hexNextModule 7 Ethernet switching
    NET

    Module 7 Ethernet switching

    jump:net-m7-ethernet

    #Ethernet basics

    Fact Value
    Standards IEEE 802.2 (LLC) and 802.3 (Ethernet); wireless LANs are 802.11
    Layers Data link and physical (Layers 2 and 1)
    Speeds in the course 10 Mbps, 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, 40 Gbps, 100 Gbps
    MAC sublayer jobs Data encapsulation (frame, addressing, error detection) and media access control
    Media access Legacy half-duplex hubs use CSMA/CD; full-duplex switched links do not need it

    #Ethernet frame fields

    Field Bytes Purpose
    Preamble 7 Alternating 1s and 0s that synchronize sender and receiver
    Start Frame Delimiter (SFD) 1 Ends the synchronization pattern and marks the start of the frame
    Destination MAC address 6 Intended recipient: unicast, multicast or broadcast
    Source MAC address 6 Sending NIC; always a unicast address
    Type/Length (EtherType) 2 Upper-layer protocol in the data field
    Data 46 to 1500 Encapsulated packet; padding is added when it is under 46 bytes
    Frame Check Sequence (FCS) 4 CRC value used to detect errors 
    | Preamble 7 | SFD 1 | Dest MAC 6 | Src MAC 6 | Type 2 | Data 46-1500 | FCS 4 |
|<-- not counted -->|<---------------- 64 to 1518 bytes ----------------->|

    #Frame size rules

    Fact Value
    Minimum frame 64 bytes (6+6+2+46+4)
    Maximum frame 1518 bytes (6+6+2+1500+4)
    Counted from Destination MAC through FCS; preamble and SFD (8 bytes) are not counted
    Under 64 bytes Collision fragment or runt frame; automatically discarded
    More than 1500 bytes of data Jumbo or baby giant frame
    Outside 64 to 1518 without special support Dropped by the receiver
    With an 802.1Q VLAN tag 1522 bytes maximum (tag adds 4 bytes; covered in the next course)

    #Type field values

    Value Meaning
    0x0800 IPv4
    0x86DD IPv6
    0x0806 ARP
    0x8100 802.1Q VLAN tag follows
    1500 (0x05DC) or less The field is a length (IEEE 802.3 frame with LLC)
    1536 (0x0600) or more The field is a type (Ethernet II)

    #MAC addresses

    Fact Value
    Length 48 bits = 6 bytes = 12 hex digits
    OUI First 24 bits (6 hex digits), assigned to the vendor by the IEEE
    Vendor-assigned part Last 24 bits, unique for every NIC with that OUI
    Other names Physical address, burned-in address (BIA, stored in ROM); software can override it
    Format Example Used by
    Dashes 00-60-2F-3A-07-BC Windows (ipconfig /all)
    Colons 00:60:2F:3A:07:BC Linux, macOS
    Dots, three groups of 4 0060.2F3A.07BC Cisco IOS

    #Unicast, broadcast and multicast MAC addresses

    Type Destination MAC Notes
    Unicast One receiving NIC Source MAC is always unicast; found with ARP (IPv4) or ND (IPv6)
    Broadcast FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF (all 48 bits = 1) Every device on the LAN processes it; switches flood it; routers do not forward it; used by ARP requests and DHCPv4
    IPv4 multicast Starts with 01-00-5E For IPv4 multicast addresses 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255; the rest comes from the low 23 bits of the IP
    IPv6 multicast Starts with 33-33 For IPv6 multicast addresses in FF00::/8

    When a NIC receives a frame, it passes it up if the destination MAC is its own, the broadcast address, or a multicast group the host joined. Otherwise it discards the frame (unless it is capturing in promiscuous mode).

    #The MAC address table

    A Layer 2 switch forwards using only Layer 2 MAC addresses, stored in the MAC address table (also called the CAM table, content addressable memory). The table is empty when the switch powers on.

    #How a switch learns from the source MAC

    1. A frame enters a port.
    2. The switch reads the source MAC address.
    3. If the MAC is not in the table, the switch adds it with the incoming port number.
    4. If it is already there, the switch resets its aging timer. If it was listed on a different port, the entry moves to the new port.

    #How a switch forwards by the destination MAC

    Destination MAC Switch action
    Known unicast on another port Forwards out that one port
    Known unicast on the same port it arrived on Filters (drops) the frame
    Unknown unicast Floods out all ports except the incoming port
    Broadcast Floods out all ports except the incoming port (same VLAN)
    Multicast Floods out all ports except the incoming port, unless multicast snooping is on

    Learn and forward

    Learn from the source, forward by the destination. A switch never learns from a destination address.

    #MAC table aging and other facts

    • Dynamic entries are removed after 5 minutes (300 seconds) without activity, the default on Cisco Catalyst switches.
    • One port can hold several MAC addresses when it connects to another switch.
    • Hosts do not address frames to the switch; it is transparent to them.
    • Each switch port is its own collision domain. All ports in one VLAN form one broadcast domain.

    #MAC address table commands

    Show every learned MAC address (privileged EXEC):

    show mac address-table

    You should see entries like:

              Mac Address Table
-------------------------------------------

Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
----    -----------       --------    -----
   1    0060.2f3a.07bc    DYNAMIC     Fa0/1

    Show only dynamic entries, or look up one address:

    show mac address-table dynamic
show mac address-table address <mac-address>

    Clear the dynamic entries:

    clear mac address-table dynamic

    Show the aging time:

    show mac address-table aging-time

    Verify learning

    Ping between two PCs, then run show mac address-table. Both PC MACs appear with their port numbers and type DYNAMIC.

    #Switch forwarding methods

    Method Forwarding starts Error checking Latency
    Store-and-forward After the entire frame arrives Computes the CRC and compares it to the FCS; discards bad frames Highest
    Cut-through: fast-forward Right after reading the destination MAC None; can forward bad frames Lowest; the typical form of cut-through
    Cut-through: fragment-free After the first 64 bytes Checks the first 64 bytes, where most collisions and errors happen Between the two
    Why store-and-forward

    Store-and-forward is required for QoS analysis on converged networks, where frames must be classified for traffic priority. It drops damaged frames, which saves bandwidth, and it buffers frames so ports of different speeds can exchange them. Some switches run cut-through per port until a user-defined error threshold is reached, then switch to store-and-forward automatically.

    #Memory buffering on switches

    Method Description
    Port-based memory Frames wait in queues linked to specific incoming and outgoing ports. A frame leaves only after every frame ahead of it, so one busy destination port can delay the whole queue even when other ports are free.
    Shared memory All frames go into one common buffer shared by all ports, allocated dynamically. It holds larger frames with fewer drops and supports asymmetric switching (ports of different speeds, such as a 10 Gbps server port and 1 Gbps PC ports).

    #Duplex and speed settings

    Fact Value
    Duplex modes Full-duplex (both ends send at once) and half-duplex (one at a time)
    Autonegotiation Optional feature on most switches and NICs; picks full-duplex and the highest common speed when both ends support it
    Gigabit Ethernet ports Full-duplex only
    10/100 ports Full or half
    Course best practice Configure both switch ports as full-duplex

    #Duplex mismatch

    • A duplex mismatch means one end runs full-duplex and the other half-duplex. It is one of the most common causes of poor performance on 10/100 Mbps links.
    • It happens when a port reset leaves autonegotiation with different results, or when someone changes one side of a link and forgets the other.
    • Symptoms: a slow link, errors, and late collisions on the half-duplex side.

    Change both ends together

    Both sides should have autonegotiation on, or both should have it off. Setting one side manually and leaving the other on auto is the classic way to create a mismatch.

    #Set speed and duplex

    Hard-code a port to 100 Mbps full-duplex, from privileged EXEC:

    configure terminal
interface <interface>
duplex full
speed 100
end

    Return the port to autonegotiation:

    configure terminal
interface <interface>
duplex auto
speed auto
end

    Verify

    show interfaces <interface> shows a line such as "Full-duplex, 100Mb/s". show interfaces status lists speed and duplex for every port ("a-full" means autonegotiated full-duplex).

    #Auto-MDIX

    • Auto-MDIX (automatic medium-dependent interface crossover) detects whether a straight-through or crossover cable is attached and configures the port to work with it.
    • It is on by default on switches running Cisco IOS 12.2(18)SE or later, but it can be disabled. The course says to use the correct cable anyway.
    • On some switches, speed and duplex must be set to auto for auto-MDIX to work.

    Re-enable auto-MDIX on a port, from privileged EXEC:

    configure terminal
interface <interface>
duplex auto
speed auto
mdix auto
end

    On a real Catalyst switch, check the auto-MDIX state (Packet Tracer may not support this command):

    show controllers ethernet-controller <interface> phy | include MDIX

    #Ethernet standards and speeds

    Standard Speed Media Max distance
    10BASE-T 10 Mbps Cat3 or better UTP 100 m
    100BASE-TX (Fast Ethernet) 100 Mbps Cat5 or better UTP 100 m
    100BASE-FX 100 Mbps Multimode fiber About 2 km
    1000BASE-T (Gigabit) 1 Gbps Cat5e or better UTP, all 4 pairs 100 m
    1000BASE-SX 1 Gbps Multimode fiber (short wavelength) About 220 to 550 m
    1000BASE-LX 1 Gbps Single-mode (about 5 km) or multimode (about 550 m) (long wavelength) About 5 km on SMF
    10GBASE-T 10 Gbps Cat6a (100 m) or Cat6 (about 55 m) 100 m
    10GBASE-SR / 10GBASE-LR 10 Gbps Multimode / single-mode fiber About 300 to 400 m / 10 km

    These are general Ethernet facts for context. The ITN course itself lists only the speeds.

    Reading an Ethernet standard name

    The number is the speed in Mbps (10, 100, 1000) or G for gigabit. BASE means baseband signaling. The suffix gives the media: T or TX = twisted-pair copper, FX = fiber, S (SX, SR) = short-wavelength fiber (multimode), L (LX, LR) = long-wavelength fiber (often single-mode).

    #Bits and bytes

    Fact Value
    Bit A single 1 or 0; the smallest unit of data
    Byte 8 bits; 256 values (0-255)
    Text encoding ASCII uses one byte per character ("A" = 65 = 01000001); Unicode covers more characters
    Signals Electrical (copper), light pulses (fiber), radio or microwave (wireless)
    Units Speeds in bits per second; storage in bytes (KB, MB, GB)

    #Wireless and mobile technologies

    Technology What to know
    Cellular (4G, 5G) Wide-area mobile data and voice through cell towers
    GPS Satellites determine the device's location; receive-only
    Wi-Fi 802.11 WLAN on 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz (6 GHz on Wi-Fi 6E and 7)
    Bluetooth Short-range, low-power device-to-device (WPAN) with pairing
    NFC (Near Field Communication) A few centimeters; contactless payments and tags
    Airplane mode Turns off the cellular, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios

    Lower frequency gives longer range and better wall penetration. Higher frequency gives more bandwidth and shorter range. Wi-Fi uses unlicensed bands.

    #Home network components

    Component Job
    Home wireless router (integrated router) Router to the ISP, small switch (often 4 LAN ports), wireless AP, DHCP server, NAT and firewall in one box
    Internet (WAN) port Connects to the ISP modem
    Ethernet (LAN) ports Wired home devices
    Modem Converts the ISP signal (cable, DSL, fiber ONT) to Ethernet
    Wireless clients Laptops, phones and IoT devices with wireless NICs

    2.4 GHz uses channels 1-11 in the US, with 1, 6 and 11 as the non-overlapping set. 5 GHz has many non-overlapping channels. Pick the least crowded channel to reduce interference.

    #Wireless security for home and small office

    Setting What it does Strength
    Change the default admin username and password Stops anyone using the factory login Do first
    Change the default SSID The SSID (Service Set Identifier) is the network name; defaults reveal the router brand Basic
    Disable SSID broadcast Hides the name from casual scans Weak, still discoverable with tools
    MAC address filtering Allows only listed MAC addresses Weak, MACs can be spoofed
    WEP Original encryption Insecure, do not use
    WPA Interim replacement using TKIP Deprecated
    WPA2 AES (CCMP) encryption; Personal uses a pre-shared key, Enterprise uses 802.1X with a RADIUS server Good, minimum acceptable
    WPA3 SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) replaces the pre-shared key handshake in Personal mode; resists password guessing Best
    Disable WPS The Wi-Fi Protected Setup PIN is easy to brute-force Recommended
    Update firmware Patches router vulnerabilities Recommended

    Quiz answer pattern

    "Most secure wireless encryption" = WPA3, or WPA2 with AES when WPA3 is not offered. "Authentication with a server" = WPA2 or WPA3 Enterprise with RADIUS (802.1X).

    #The access layer

    Hierarchical layer Job
    Access Where end devices connect: switches and wireless APs (hubs in legacy networks)
    Distribution Interconnects access-layer networks; policy and routing between them
    Core High-speed backbone connecting distribution layers and the internet

    #Hubs and switches compared

    Hub Switch
    OSI layer Layer 1 Layer 2
    Forwards based on Nothing; repeats bits out all ports Destination MAC in the MAC address table
    Collision domains One shared collision domain Each port is its own
    Broadcast domains One One per VLAN
    Duplex Half-duplex Full-duplex

    #Broadcast domains

    • A broadcast domain is the set of devices that receive each other's broadcast frames.
    • Switches flood broadcasts, so all switch ports in one VLAN form one broadcast domain.
    • Routers do not forward broadcasts, so each router interface is a separate broadcast domain. Splitting a network with routers or VLANs contains broadcasts.

    #DHCP basics

    DHCP automatically gives hosts an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS server. It uses UDP port 67 (server) and 68 (client), and addresses are leased for a set time and renewed.

    Step Message Sent by Notes
    1 Discover Client Broadcast; the client has no IP yet
    2 Offer Server Offers an address
    3 Request Client Broadcast; accepts one offer
    4 Acknowledgment (ACK) Server Confirms the lease

    Servers, printers and network devices usually get static addresses. Client PCs and phones usually use DHCP. A Windows host that cannot reach a DHCP server assigns itself an APIPA address (169.254.x.x).

    #ARP basics

    ARP finds the MAC address for a known IPv4 address on the local network.

    1. The host checks its ARP cache for the IP.
    2. If it is missing, the host sends an ARP request as a broadcast (destination MAC FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF).
    3. The owner of that IP sends a unicast ARP reply with its MAC.
    4. The sender stores the mapping in its ARP cache. Entries time out.

    For a remote destination, the host ARPs for the default gateway's MAC. IPv6 does not use ARP; it uses ICMPv6 Neighbor Discovery (NS and NA messages).

    Where View the ARP cache
    Windows arp -a
    Linux ip neigh
    Cisco IOS show ip arp or show arp

    Networking glossary A to Z

    jump:net-glossary

    #Glossary A to F

    Term Meaning
    Access method Rule that decides when a device may send on the media
    ACL (access control list) Ordered list of permit and deny statements that filters traffic
    Application layer OSI Layer 7 and the top TCP/IP layer; interface between applications and the network
    ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) Maps a known IPv4 address to a MAC address on the local network
    Attenuation Loss of signal strength over distance
    Auto-MDIX Port feature that detects straight-through or crossover cabling and adjusts
    Autonegotiation Two Ethernet ports agree on the best common speed and duplex
    AUX port Legacy router port for remote access through a modem
    Bandwidth Capacity of a medium to carry data, in bits per second
    Binary Base-2 number system using only 0 and 1
    Bit Smallest unit of data, a single 0 or 1; the Layer 1 PDU
    Broadcast One-to-all delivery on the local network; Ethernet broadcast MAC is FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF
    Broadcast domain Devices that receive each other's broadcasts; bounded by routers
    BYOD Bring your own device; users reach company resources from personal devices
    Byte 8 bits
    CAM table Content addressable memory; another name for the switch MAC address table
    Cladding Glass layer around a fiber core that reflects light back into the core
    Coaxial cable Copper cable with a center conductor and braided shield; cable internet and antennas
    Collision domain Segment where simultaneous transmissions can collide; each switch port is one
    Console port Out-of-band management port on Cisco devices, reached with a rollover cable
    Converged network One network that carries voice, video and data
    CRC (cyclic redundancy check) Calculation that produces the FCS value
    Crossover cable T568A on one end, T568B on the other; connects like devices
    Crosstalk Interference from the signal on a neighboring wire
    CSMA/CA Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance; 802.11 wireless
    CSMA/CD Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection; legacy half-duplex Ethernet
    Cut-through switching Switch starts forwarding before the whole frame arrives (fast-forward or fragment-free)
    Data link layer OSI Layer 2; frames, MAC addressing, media access, error detection
    De-encapsulation Removing headers and trailers as data moves up the layers at the receiver
    Default gateway Router interface address hosts use to reach other networks
    DHCP Automatically assigns IP settings to hosts (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledgment)
    Dispersion Spreading of a light pulse over time in fiber; limits distance
    DNS Translates domain names into IP addresses
    DoS (denial of service) Attack that makes a service or device unavailable
    DSL Internet access over telephone lines
    Duplex mismatch Two ends of a link with different duplex settings; poor performance
    EIA Electronic Industries Alliance; electrical wiring, connectors and 19-inch racks
    EMI Electromagnetic interference that distorts signals on copper
    Encapsulation Adding headers (and a trailer at Layer 2) as data moves down the layers
    Encoding Converting bits into a predefined code of signals (Manchester, 4B/5B)
    End device Host that is the source or destination of a message
    EtherType 2-byte frame field naming the upper-layer protocol (0x0800 IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6, 0x0806 ARP)
    Extranet Controlled access to an organization's network for outside partners
    Fault tolerance Keeps working after a failure, using redundancy
    FCS (frame check sequence) 4-byte Ethernet trailer field holding the CRC value
    Fiber-optic cable Carries light through glass; immune to EMI and RFI
    Flooding Switch sends a frame out all ports except the incoming one
    Flow control Managing how much data is sent and how fast
    Fragment-free Cut-through method that checks the first 64 bytes before forwarding
    Frame The Layer 2 PDU
    Full-duplex Sending and receiving at the same time

    #Glossary G to M

    Term Meaning
    Goodput Usable data delivered over time: throughput minus overhead
    Half-duplex Sending or receiving, one direction at a time
    HDLC High-Level Data Link Control; Layer 2 protocol for point-to-point WAN links
    Hexadecimal Base-16 number system (0-9, A-F); one digit = 4 bits
    Hextet A 16-bit block of an IPv6 address (4 hex digits)
    Hub Layer 1 device that repeats signals out all ports; one collision domain
    IANA Internet Assigned Numbers Authority; manages IP addresses, domain names and protocol identifiers for ICANN
    ICANN Coordinates IP address allocation and domain names; based in the US
    ICMP Internet Control Message Protocol; error and diagnostic messages such as ping
    IEEE Standards body for the 802 family (Ethernet, Wi-Fi)
    IETF Develops and maintains internet and TCP/IP standards, published as RFCs
    Interface Network port on a router or switch
    Intermediary device Connects end devices and moves data (switch, router, AP, firewall)
    Intranet Private network open only to an organization's members
    IPS Intrusion prevention system; detects and blocks attacks
    Jumbo frame Ethernet frame carrying more than 1500 bytes of data
    LAN Network in a small area, usually owned by one organization
    Latency Time, including delays, for data to travel from one point to another
    LC connector Small-form-factor fiber connector
    LLC Logical Link Control (802.2); upper data link sublayer that identifies the Layer 3 protocol
    Logical topology How frames travel between nodes; diagram shows devices, ports and addressing
    MAC address 48-bit Layer 2 address written as 12 hex digits
    MAC address table Switch table mapping MAC addresses to ports
    MAC sublayer Lower data link sublayer; frame encapsulation and media access control in hardware
    MAN Network spanning a city or campus
    Manchester encoding 10 Mbps Ethernet encoding with a voltage transition in the middle of each bit
    Mesh topology Every site connected to every other site; partial mesh connects only some
    MIMO Multiple-input multiple-output; multiple antennas (802.11n and later)
    Multicast One-to-a-group delivery; MAC starts 01-00-5E (IPv4) or 33-33 (IPv6)
    Multimode fiber (MMF) Larger-core fiber with an LED source; up to 550 m
    Multiplexing Interleaving many conversations on the same network

    #Glossary N to Z

    Term Meaning
    NAT Network Address Translation; maps private IPv4 addresses to public ones
    NIC Network interface card; gives a device its network connection and MAC address
    NVRAM Non-volatile memory that stores the startup-config
    OSI model 7-layer reference model developed by ISO and ITU
    OUI First 24 bits of a MAC address, identifying the vendor
    Packet The Layer 3 PDU
    PAN Personal area network, such as Bluetooth devices around one person
    PDU Protocol data unit; the name for data at each layer
    Peer-to-peer Network where each computer is both client and server, with no dedicated server
    Physical layer OSI Layer 1; transmits bits as signals over media
    Physical topology Physical layout of devices and cables
    Point-to-point Permanent link between two endpoints; simplest WAN topology
    PPP Point-to-Point Protocol; Layer 2 WAN protocol
    Preamble 7-byte alternating pattern that synchronizes Ethernet receivers
    Presentation layer OSI Layer 6; formatting, compression, encryption
    Protocol suite Group of protocols that work together, such as TCP/IP
    QoS Quality of Service; prioritizes time-sensitive traffic
    RFC Request for Comments; documents that define internet standards
    RFI Radio frequency interference
    RJ-45 8-pin connector for UTP Ethernet
    Rollover cable Console cable from a PC to a Cisco console port
    Router Layer 3 device that forwards packets between networks and separates broadcast domains
    Running-config Active configuration held in RAM
    Runt Ethernet frame under 64 bytes; discarded
    SAN Storage area network
    SC connector Square push-pull fiber connector
    Scalability A network grows without losing service for existing users
    Segment The Layer 4 (transport) PDU
    Sequencing Numbering segments so they can be reassembled in order
    Session layer OSI Layer 5; organizes dialogues and manages data exchange
    SFD Start Frame Delimiter; 1 byte marking the start of an Ethernet frame
    Shared memory buffering Switch buffer shared by all ports; supports asymmetric switching
    Single-mode fiber (SMF) Small-core fiber with a laser source; long distances
    SSH Secure Shell; encrypted remote CLI access
    SSID Wireless network name
    ST connector Round bayonet (twist-on) fiber connector
    Startup-config Saved configuration in NVRAM, loaded at boot
    Store-and-forward Switch receives the whole frame and checks the FCS before forwarding
    STP (shielded twisted pair) Twisted-pair cable with shielding against EMI
    Straight-through cable Same wiring standard on both ends; connects unlike devices
    SVI Switch virtual interface; the VLAN interface that gives a switch an IP address
    Switch Layer 2 device that forwards frames by destination MAC address
    T568A, T568B TIA/EIA-568 pin color standards for RJ-45 termination
    TCP Reliable, connection-oriented transport protocol
    Telnet Unencrypted remote CLI access
    Throughput Measured transfer of bits over a period of time
    TIA Telecommunications Industry Association; radio, cellular towers, VoIP, satellite and cabling standards
    Trailer Data added at the end of a frame (the FCS)
    Transport layer OSI Layer 4; segments, ports, reliability, flow control
    UDP Connectionless, best-effort transport protocol
    Unicast One-to-one delivery
    UTP Unshielded twisted pair; most common LAN cable
    WAN Network connecting LANs across large distances
    WISP Wireless internet service provider
    WLAN Wireless LAN (802.11)
    WPA2, WPA3 Wi-Fi security standards; WPA2 uses AES, WPA3 adds SAE

    Networking flashcards for self-test

    jump:net-flashcards

    Click a card to reveal the answer. These are original practice items written for this guide, not real quiz questions.

    #Module 3 flashcards: protocols and models

    Q: Name the five message rules that network protocols define.

    Encoding, formatting and encapsulation, size, timing, and delivery options.

    Q: Which three things make up message timing?

    Flow control, response timeout, and access method.

    Q: Which delivery option sends to a selected group of hosts?

    Multicast.

    Q: Which IP version has no broadcast?

    IPv6. It uses multicast instead.

    Q: Which protocol function labels segments so they can be put back in order?

    Sequencing.

    Q: Loading a web page, which protocol carries the frame from NIC to NIC on the LAN?

    Ethernet.

    Q: Which protocol manages each conversation and guarantees delivery for HTTP?

    TCP.

    Q: Which organization publishes RFCs?

    The IETF.

    Q: Which organization creates the 802.3 and 802.11 standards?

    The IEEE.

    Q: Which organization is known for 19-inch rack and electrical wiring standards?

    The EIA.

    Q: Which organization handles DSL, IPTV and video compression standards?

    ITU-T.

    Q: Which body manages IP addresses, domain names and protocol identifiers on behalf of ICANN?

    IANA.

    Q: Which group does long-term research on internet and TCP/IP protocols?

    The IRTF.

    Q: List the OSI layers from 1 to 7.

    Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

    Q: Which OSI layer handles compression and encryption?

    Layer 6, Presentation.

    Q: Which OSI layer organizes the dialogue and manages data exchange?

    Layer 5, Session.

    Q: Which TCP/IP layer maps to OSI Layers 1 and 2?

    Network Access.

    Q: Is OSI a protocol model or a reference model?

    A reference model. TCP/IP is a protocol model.

    Q: What is the PDU at the network layer?

    Packet.

    Q: What is the PDU at the transport layer?

    Segment.

    Q: Which layer adds a trailer during encapsulation?

    The data link layer (the FCS).

    Q: Give the two benefits of segmenting data.

    Speed, because many conversations can be multiplexed, and efficiency, because only lost segments are resent.

    Q: Which address stays the same from source to final destination, IP or MAC?

    The IP address.

    Q: A host sends to a server on another network. Whose MAC is the destination in the frame?

    The host's default gateway router interface.

    Q: In which TCP/IP layer does the course list ARP?

    Network Access.

    Q: In which TCP/IP layer does the course list NAT and ICMPv6 ND?

    Internet.

    Q: Which routing protocol runs between ISPs on the internet?

    BGP.

    #Module 4 flashcards: physical layer

    Q: What three areas do physical layer standards cover?

    Physical components, encoding, and signaling.

    Q: Which encoding has a transition in the middle of every bit, low to high for a 1?

    Manchester encoding.

    Q: How does goodput differ from throughput?

    Throughput is the measured transfer of bits. Goodput is only the usable data, after overhead is removed.

    Q: Which term means the time for data to travel, including delays?

    Latency.

    Q: How does UTP limit crosstalk without shielding?

    Cancellation, by twisting wire pairs with different twist rates.

    Q: What is the maximum length of a UTP segment?

    100 meters.

    Q: Which UTP category does the course call the minimum acceptable today, at 1000 Mbps?

    Cat5e.

    Q: Which UTP category adds a separator between pairs?

    Cat6.

    Q: Which organization's standard (568) defines UTP cable types, lengths, connectors and testing?

    TIA/EIA.

    Q: What colors are on pins 1 and 2 in T568B?

    White/orange and orange.

    Q: What colors are on pins 1 and 2 in T568A?

    White/green and green.

    Q: Which cable connects a PC to a switch?

    Straight-through.

    Q: Which cable connects two switches without auto-MDIX?

    Crossover.

    Q: Which cable connects a PC directly to a router Ethernet port?

    Crossover.

    Q: Which cable connects a PC serial port to a router console port?

    Rollover (console) cable.

    Q: Which copper cable type is used for cable internet and antenna connections?

    Coaxial cable.

    Q: Which media is completely immune to EMI and RFI?

    Fiber-optic cable.

    Q: Which fiber uses a laser and a very small core for long distances?

    Single-mode fiber.

    Q: Which fiber uses LEDs and reaches up to 550 m at 10 Gbps?

    Multimode fiber.

    Q: What jacket color marks a single-mode patch cord?

    Yellow. Multimode is orange or aqua.

    Q: Which fiber connector is square with a push-pull latch?

    SC.

    Q: Which fiber connector uses a twist-on bayonet lock?

    ST.

    Q: Which part of a fiber cable acts like a mirror?

    The cladding.

    Q: Why do users on a WLAN share bandwidth?

    Wireless is a shared medium that runs half-duplex.

    Q: Which IEEE standard is Bluetooth?

    802.15.

    Q: Which IEEE standard is Zigbee?

    802.15.4.

    Q: Which IEEE standard is WiMAX?

    802.16.

    Q: Which 802.11 standard uses MIMO on both 2.4 and 5 GHz at 150 to 600 Mbps?

    802.11n (Wi-Fi 4).

    Q: Which 802.11 standard is called High-Efficiency Wireless?

    802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6).

    Q: Which two Wi-Fi standards top out at 54 Mbps?

    802.11a (5 GHz) and 802.11g (2.4 GHz).

    #Module 5 flashcards: number systems

    Q: What are the eight binary place values of an octet, left to right?

    128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.

    Q: Convert 11100000 to decimal.

    224.

    Q: Convert 252 to binary.

    11111100.

    Q: How many bits does one hex digit represent?

    4.

    Q: Convert 0xFE to decimal.

    254.

    Q: Convert 168 to hex.

    A8.

    Q: How many bits are in an IPv6 address, and how many hextets?

    128 bits in 8 hextets of 16 bits.

    Q: How many hex digits are in a MAC address?

    12 (48 bits).

    #Module 6 flashcards: data link layer

    Q: Which data link sublayer identifies the network layer protocol in the frame?

    LLC (IEEE 802.2).

    Q: Which data link sublayer handles media access and frame encapsulation in hardware?

    MAC.

    Q: Name the four standards bodies the course lists for the data link layer.

    IEEE, ITU, ISO and ANSI.

    Q: What happens to the Layer 2 frame when a router forwards a packet?

    The router strips it and builds a new frame for the next link.

    Q: Which WAN topology is the simplest?

    Point-to-point.

    Q: Which topology gives high availability but costs the most because every node links to every other?

    Full mesh.

    Q: Which access method does 802.11 wireless use?

    CSMA/CA.

    Q: Which access method did legacy hub-based Ethernet use?

    CSMA/CD.

    Q: Give the two course examples of controlled access.

    Legacy Token Ring and legacy ARCNET.

    Q: Which frame field carries the CRC result?

    The FCS in the trailer (error detection field).

    Q: Which generic frame field identifies the Layer 3 protocol?

    The type field.

    Q: Name two Layer 2 protocols used on point-to-point WAN links.

    PPP and HDLC.

    #Module 7 flashcards: Ethernet switching

    Q: What are the minimum and maximum Ethernet frame sizes?

    64 bytes and 1518 bytes.

    Q: Which fields are left out when counting Ethernet frame size?

    The preamble and SFD.

    Q: How long is the Ethernet FCS field?

    4 bytes.

    Q: What is the size range of the Ethernet data field?

    46 to 1500 bytes.

    Q: What is a frame smaller than 64 bytes called?

    A runt or collision fragment.

    Q: Which Type value indicates IPv6?

    0x86DD.

    Q: Which Type value indicates ARP?

    0x0806.

    Q: How many bits are in the OUI?

    24 bits.

    Q: What is the Ethernet broadcast MAC address?

    FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF.

    Q: Which prefix begins an IPv4 multicast MAC address?

    01-00-5E.

    Q: Which prefix begins an IPv6 multicast MAC address?

    33-33.

    Q: Which address does a switch use to build its MAC table?

    The source MAC address.

    Q: What does a switch do with a frame whose destination MAC is not in its table?

    Floods it out all ports except the one it arrived on.

    Q: How long does a dynamic MAC table entry last by default?

    5 minutes (300 seconds) without activity.

    Q: Which switching method checks the FCS before forwarding?

    Store-and-forward.

    Q: Which switching method is required for QoS analysis?

    Store-and-forward.

    Q: Which switching method has the lowest latency?

    Fast-forward (cut-through).

    Q: Which switching method waits for the first 64 bytes?

    Fragment-free.

    Q: Which buffering method allows asymmetric switching?

    Shared memory buffering.

    Q: In which duplex mode do Gigabit Ethernet ports operate?

    Full-duplex only.

    Q: What is the usual symptom of a duplex mismatch?

    Poor performance, with late collisions on the half-duplex side.

    Q: What interface command re-enables auto-MDIX?

    mdix auto

    Q: Which command shows the MAC addresses a switch has learned?

    show mac address-table

    Q: Which Ethernet standard runs Gigabit over Cat5e copper?

    1000BASE-T.

    Q: Which Gigabit fiber standard uses short-wavelength multimode fiber?

    1000BASE-SX.

    PreviousNetworking glossary A to ZNextPacket Tracer challenge strategy
    PT

    Packet Tracer challenge strategy

    jump:pt-strategy

    Fast path

    1. Read every page of the instructions window (Next/Previous) before you touch a device.
    2. Copy every exact value into a scratch text file: hostnames, passwords, banner text, IPs, masks, gateways, SSIDs, passphrases, usernames, domain name, descriptions.
    3. Hover over each device and write down its model. Interface names depend on the model (table).
    4. Do cabling, modules and power first (which cable).
    5. Configure one device at a time, using a template where one fits, and check the completion percentage after each device.

    6. Save every router and switch before you leave it:

      write memory

    7. Save the activity file and submit the way the round instructions say.

    The Packet Tracer (PT) activity is graded automatically by comparing your devices against a hidden answer network. Points come from exact matches: a hostname of s1 when the task says S1 earns nothing. Read carefully once, then type from your list.

    Exact spelling and case are graded

    Hostnames, passwords, usernames, SSIDs, passphrases, banner text and domain names are case-sensitive and checked character by character. Copy them from the instructions instead of retyping from memory. An extra space, a missing period or a wrong capital letter in a banner can cost the item.

    #Workflow checklist for the activity

    #Do not change things the task did not ask for

    The grader may also check items you were never told about: existing IPs, existing VLAN membership, existing cables. Do not "clean up" devices, rename display labels, delete devices, move cables or re-address anything outside the instructions.

    Never click Reset Activity

    Reset Activity reloads the original file and wipes all of your work.

    #How grading and Check Results work

    • A .pka activity contains an answer network. Each graded item (for example S1 > Hostname or S1 > Ports > Vlan1 > IP Address) is compared against your network.
    • If the author left feedback on, the bottom of the instructions window shows a completion percentage and a Check Results button. Check Results opens a window with an Assessment Items tab (a tree of items marked correct or incorrect) and sometimes a Connectivity Tests tab (pings the grader runs).
    • The author can hide feedback. If you see only a percentage, or nothing, verify each requirement yourself with show commands.
    • Some activities compare the saved startup-config, so save every device.
    • Some activities show a countdown timer in the instructions window. The CyberPatriot round rules set the overall time window; read them before the round.

    Use the percentage as a tripwire

    Check the percentage after every device. If it did not move after you finished a requirement, re-read that requirement while it is fresh. A typo in a value, the wrong interface or the wrong device are the usual causes (why the score is stuck).

    #Time management

    Phase Share of time What to do
    Read and plan 10% Read every instruction page, copy all values, note device models
    Physical and cabling 10% Add modules, connect cables, power on
    Device configuration 55% One device at a time, save each
    Verification 15% Pings, show commands, Check Results
    Buffer 10% Fix red items, final save, submit
    • Do the items you are sure of first. Park anything confusing and come back after the easy points are banked.
    • Do not spend more than a few minutes stuck on one item.
    • Build configs in a text editor (Notepad, or a PC's Desktop > Text Editor), fill in the values, then paste.

    #Paste configs into the CLI tab

    1. Write the commands in a plain text editor with the exact values filled in, or start from a template.
    2. Copy them.
    3. In PT, open the device, click the CLI tab, click in the console window and press Enter until you see a prompt.
    4. Get to the prompt the block expects (usually Switch# or Router#, after enable).
    5. Click the Paste button below the console window. Keyboard paste also works in most versions.
    6. Scroll back and read every line that starts with %, then verify with show running-config.

    Pasted commands that ask a question

    A command that prompts for input takes the next pasted line as its answer. Keep these out of pasted blocks, or put them last:

    • copy running-config startup-config asks Destination filename [startup-config]?. Use write memory in pasted blocks.
    • crypto key generate rsa with no options asks for the modulus. Use crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 1024.
    • If RSA keys already exist, even the full command asks Do you really want to replace them? [yes/no]:. Check first with show ip ssh; if SSH is already enabled, type the command by hand and answer yes.
    • reload and erase startup-config ask for confirmation. Never paste them.

    To run a show command or save without leaving configuration mode, put do in front of it (details).

    #Verify each requirement as you go

    Requirement type Verify with
    Hostname, passwords, banner, lines show running-config
    Interface IP and up/down state show ip interface brief
    IPv6 addresses show ipv6 interface brief
    SSH show ip ssh, then ssh -l <admin-username> <ip-address> from a PC
    Default gateway on a switch show running-config, look for ip default-gateway
    PC addressing PC > Desktop > Command Prompt > ipconfig /all
    End-to-end connectivity ping from the PC Command Prompt, or Add Simple PDU
    Saved config show startup-config matches show running-config

    Done means

    The completion percentage stops rising only on items you cannot do, every device shows the required config in show running-config, the required pings succeed, and every router and switch has been saved.

    PreviousNetworking flashcards for self-testNextPacket Tracer interface tour
    PT

    Packet Tracer interface tour

    jump:pt-interface

    Fast path

    1. Click a device to open its window. Routers and switches: CLI tab. PCs and servers: Desktop tab.
    2. Hover over a device to see its model, ports, IPs and link state.
    3. Pick cables from the Connections category by their tooltip name (which cable).
    4. Stay in Realtime mode for configuration. Switch to Simulation only when a task asks you to watch packets.
    5. Click Fast Forward Time (bottom bar, next to the clock) to speed up Spanning Tree and DHCP.

    #Logical and physical workspace

    Workspace What it shows When you need it
    Logical (default) Devices and cables as a topology diagram Almost all configuration and cabling
    Physical Intercity, City, Building, Wiring Closet, racks; wireless ranges; cable lengths Tasks that say "move the device to a closet or rack", or wireless range problems

    Switch with the Logical and Physical buttons near the top-left of the workspace. Most ITN 1-7 activities stay in Logical view.

    #Device and connection selection box

    The bottom-left panel has two parts: a box of device categories and a box with the models in the selected category.

    Category Contains
    Network Devices Routers, Switches, Hubs, Wireless Devices (for example WRT300N, HomeRouter-PT-AC, AccessPoint-PT), Security (ASA), WAN Emulation (Cloud, DSL and cable modems)
    End Devices PC, Laptop, Server, Printer, IP Phone, Tablet, Smartphone, TV, IoT items
    Components IoT sensors and actuators
    Connections All cable types
    Miscellaneous, Multiuser Prebuilt groups, multiuser connection

    To add a device, click the category, click the model, then click in the workspace (or drag it).

    #Cable types in the Connections box

    Hover over each cable icon to read its name. Pick by name; the icons are small and look alike.

    Tooltip name Use
    Automatically Choose Connection Type PT picks the cable and the first free port. Avoid it when the task names ports
    Console PC RS 232 port to a router or switch Console port (then PC > Desktop > Terminal)
    Copper Straight-Through Unlike devices: PC to switch, switch to router, PC to hub
    Copper Cross-Over Like devices: switch to switch, router to router, PC to PC, PC to router Ethernet
    Fiber Fiber port to fiber port only (FX, SFP or fiber Gigabit modules)
    Phone DSL modem to the cloud's modem port
    Coaxial Cable modem to the cloud's coaxial port
    Serial DCE Router serial to router serial; the end you click first is DCE (sets the clock rate)
    Serial DTE Router serial to router serial; the end you click first is DTE
    Octal Async module to many console ports
    IoT Custom Cable, USB IoT components, USB console

    To connect: click the cable type, click the first device, pick the port from the pop-up list, click the second device, pick the port. Pick the exact port the task names (for example FastEthernet0/1 or GigabitEthernet0/0).

    See port names on the diagram

    In Options > Preferences, tick Always Show Port Labels in Logical Workspace to show the port name at each cable end. Hovering over a device also lists its ports, IPs and link state.

    #Link lights and what the colors mean

    Light at the cable end Meaning Typical fix
    Green triangle Physical link up (blinking means traffic) Nothing
    Amber circle Switch port is up but Spanning Tree is still in listening/learning (about 30 seconds after connecting), or blocking a redundant link Wait, or click Fast Forward Time
    Red triangle Link down Interface shut down (routers default to shutdown), wrong cable, device off, wrong port type
    No light No connection Connect the cable

    Router interfaces are shut down by default, so a new link to a router stays red until you run no shutdown on the router interface (router interfaces).

    #Device window tabs

    Tab Found on What it does
    Physical All devices Picture of the chassis, power switch, module list for adding and removing modules
    Config All devices GUI forms for hostname, interfaces, IPs, routing, VLANs; Cisco devices show Equivalent IOS Commands at the bottom
    CLI Routers, switches The IOS command line (same as a console session), with Copy and Paste buttons
    Desktop PCs, laptops, servers, tablets IP Configuration, Command Prompt, Web Browser, Terminal, PC Wireless, Text Editor, Email, Firewall and more
    Services Servers HTTP, DHCP, DHCPv6, TFTP, DNS, SYSLOG, AAA, NTP, EMAIL, FTP, IoT, VM Management
    GUI Wireless routers (WRT300N, HomeRouter-PT-AC) Linksys-style web pages: Setup, Wireless, Security, Access Restrictions, Administration, Status
    Attributes Many devices Informational properties such as cost; rarely needed

    Display Name is not the hostname

    On a router or switch, the Config tab has both Display Name (the label under the icon) and Hostname (the IOS hostname). The grader checks the IOS hostname. Set it in the CLI with hostname <hostname>.

    Learn syntax from the Config tab

    When you change a setting in the Config tab of a router or switch, the matching IOS command appears in the Equivalent IOS Commands box. Some activities disable the Config tab, so know the CLI too.

    #Add or remove a module in the Physical tab

    Power off reloads from startup-config

    Turning a router or switch off and on reloads it from startup-config, so anything unsaved is lost. Run write memory first. PCs keep their IP settings.

    1. Open the device and click the Physical tab.
    2. Click the power switch on the chassis picture to turn the device off (the green light goes dark).
    3. If replacing a module, drag the old one out of its slot back onto the module list.
    4. Drag the new module from the list into the empty slot. Click a module name to see its description and picture.
    5. Turn the power on again.

    PT refuses to add or remove a module while the device is on.

    Catalyst 3650 starts without a power supply

    The 3650-24PS is placed with an empty power bay and stays off. In the Physical tab, drag the AC power supply module from the module list into the empty bay, and it boots.

    #Desktop tab apps on PCs, laptops and servers

    App Use
    IP Configuration Static or DHCP IPv4, subnet mask, gateway, DNS; IPv6 settings
    Command Prompt ipconfig, ping, tracert, arp -a, nslookup, ssh -l, telnet (full list)
    Terminal Console session to a router or switch over a Console cable (9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, no flow control)
    Web Browser Browse to a server, or to a wireless router's web pages (for example http://192.168.0.1)
    PC Wireless Join an SSID (only when a wireless card is installed)
    Text Editor Scratch pad for building configs to paste
    Email Mail client exercises
    Firewall, IPv6 Firewall Host firewall rules that can block pings and web traffic

    #Realtime and Simulation mode

    The bottom-right corner has Realtime and Simulation tabs.

    • Realtime: the network runs normally and pings complete in seconds. Do all configuration and graded work here.
    • Simulation: time stops and you step through every packet. Use it when a task asks you to observe PDUs or identify protocols, layers or headers.

    #Watch PDUs in Simulation mode

    1. Click Simulation. The Simulation Panel opens with the Event List and Play Controls.
    2. Click Edit Filters (or Show All/None) and select only the protocols you care about, for example ICMP and ARP, or HTTP, DNS and TCP.
    3. Create traffic: Add Simple PDU, ping from a PC Command Prompt, or open a web page in a PC's Web Browser.
    4. Click Capture/Forward to move one event at a time, or Play to run automatically. Back steps backwards. The slider sets play speed.
    5. Click an envelope on the topology, or the colored square in the Event List Info column, to open PDU Information.
    6. On the OSI Model tab, In Layers and Out Layers show what each layer did at this device. The Inbound and Outbound PDU Details tabs show header fields (Ethernet II MACs, IP addresses, TTL, TCP/UDP ports, ICMP type).
    7. Click Reset Simulation to clear events, then return to Realtime.

    Envelopes are color-coded by protocol (set in Edit Filters). A green check on an envelope means it arrived; a red X means it was dropped at that device.

    #OSI and TCP/IP layers for Simulation tasks

    OSI layer TCP/IP layer PDU name Examples seen in PT
    7 Application Application Data HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, DHCP, FTP, SMTP, POP3, Telnet, SSH
    6 Presentation Application Data Encoding, encryption, compression
    5 Session Application Data Session setup and teardown
    4 Transport Transport Segment (TCP), datagram (UDP) TCP, UDP, source and destination ports
    3 Network Internet Packet IPv4, IPv6, ICMP
    2 Data Link Network Access Frame Ethernet II, 802.11; ARP resolves IPv4 to MAC here
    1 Physical Network Access Bits Copper, fiber, wireless signal

    #Common protocol ports

    Protocol Transport Port
    FTP TCP 20 (data), 21 (control)
    SSH TCP 22
    Telnet TCP 23
    SMTP TCP 25
    DNS UDP (and TCP) 53
    DHCP UDP 67 server, 68 client
    HTTP TCP 80
    POP3 TCP 110
    IMAP TCP 143
    HTTPS TCP 443

    #Send a test with Add Simple PDU

    1. Click the closed-envelope Add Simple PDU button in the toolbar.
    2. Click the source device, then the destination device. PT sends one ICMP echo.
    3. Read the result in the PDU list (bottom-right): Last Status shows Successful or Failed, with source, destination, type and time.
    4. Double-click (delete) on a row to remove it. Double-click the Fire column to send it again.

    The first attempt often fails

    In Realtime, the first PDU or ping between two devices often fails or times out while ARP resolves the MAC address. Send it again before troubleshooting.

    #Other toolbar tools

    Hover over any toolbar button to see its name and keyboard shortcut.

    Tool How to use Use for
    Select (arrow) Click it, or press Esc Return to normal clicking
    Inspect (magnifying glass) Click it, then a device; pick a table View the ARP, MAC address or routing table without the CLI
    Delete (X) Click it, then a device or cable Remove a wrong cable. Do not delete devices the activity provided
    Place Note Click it, then the workspace Notes; not graded
    Draw, Resize Shapes and resizing Cosmetic
    Zoom in, out, reset Toolbar magnifier buttons Read small labels
    Fast Forward Time Bottom bar, next to the Realtime clock Skips ahead so STP ports turn green and DHCP clients get addresses sooner
    Power Cycle Devices Bottom bar, next to Fast Forward Time Reboots every device

    Power Cycle Devices reloads everything

    Every router and switch reboots from its startup-config, and anything unsaved is gone. Do not click it unless every device is saved.

    PreviousPacket Tracer challenge strategyNextIOS CLI basics and modes
    PT

    IOS CLI basics and modes

    jump:pt-ios-basics

    Fast path

    1. Open the device, click the CLI tab, click in the window and press Enter. If asked Would you like to enter the initial configuration dialog? [yes/no]:, type no.

    2. From the > prompt, enter privileged EXEC (type the enable password if one is set):

      enable

    3. Enter global configuration mode:

      configure terminal

    4. Stop mistyped commands from hanging on DNS lookups:

      no ip domain-lookup

    5. Configure what the task asks, then return to privileged EXEC and save:

      end
write memory

    #IOS command modes

    Mode Prompt How to enter What you can do
    User EXEC S1> Log in, or press Enter at the console Limited show, ping, enable
    Privileged EXEC S1# enable (then the enable secret if set) All show, copy, write, reload, debug, configure terminal
    Global configuration S1(config)# configure terminal Device-wide settings: hostname, passwords, banner, routes, SSH, users
    Interface configuration S1(config-if)# interface <interface> IP address, description, shutdown, switchport settings
    Interface range S1(config-if-range)# interface range <interface-range> Same as interface mode, many ports at once
    Line configuration S1(config-line)# line console 0 or line vty 0 15 Line passwords, login, exec-timeout, transport input
    VLAN interface (SVI) S1(config-if)# interface vlan 1 Switch management IP
    VLAN configuration S1(config-vlan)# vlan <vlan-id> VLAN name
    Router DHCP pool R1(dhcp-config)# ip dhcp pool <pool-name> DHCP pool settings

    #Move between modes

    Command or key From Goes to
    enable User EXEC (>) Privileged EXEC (#)
    disable Privileged EXEC User EXEC
    configure terminal (conf t) Privileged EXEC Global configuration
    interface g0/1, line vty 0 15 Global configuration or another sub-mode That sub-mode
    exit Any sub-mode One level up (sub-mode to global, global to privileged EXEC)
    end or Ctrl+Z Any configuration mode Straight to privileged EXEC
    exit or logout EXEC Ends the session

    Jump straight to another interface

    From (config-if)# you can type interface g0/1 to move to another interface without exit. The same works for line from (config-line)#.

    #Help, completion and abbreviations

    Technique Example Result
    ? alone ? at S1(config)# Lists every command available in this mode
    Partial word and ? (no space) sh? Lists commands starting with "sh"
    Command, space, ? show ip ? Lists the next keyword or argument options
    Tab conf then Tab Completes to configure
    Abbreviate conf t, sh run, sh ip int br, int g0/1, no shut, wr Any unique prefix works
    Short Full
    en enable
    conf t configure terminal
    sh run show running-config
    sh start show startup-config
    sh ip int br show ip interface brief
    int g0/1, int fa0/1, int s0/0/0 interface GigabitEthernet0/1, FastEthernet0/1, Serial0/0/0
    int ra fa0/1 - 24 interface range FastEthernet0/1 - 24
    no shut no shutdown
    wr write memory
    copy run start copy running-config startup-config

    Abbreviate commands, never values

    Shorten commands and keywords freely, but type hostnames, passwords, banner text, IP addresses and domain names in full.

    #IOS hotkeys

    Key Action
    Up arrow or Ctrl+P Previous command in history
    Down arrow or Ctrl+N Next command in history
    Tab Complete the current keyword
    Ctrl+A Cursor to start of line
    Ctrl+E Cursor to end of line
    Ctrl+Z Leave configuration mode, go to privileged EXEC
    Ctrl+C Abort the current command or leave configuration mode
    Ctrl+Shift+6 Break a running ping, traceroute or DNS lookup
    Space at --More-- Next page of output
    Enter at --More-- Next line of output
    Q or any other key at --More-- Stop the output

    #Stop the Translating delay on typos

    Press Ctrl+Shift+6 to break out of the lookup. Then, in global configuration mode, turn lookups off:

    no ip domain-lookup

    In EXEC mode, IOS treats an unknown word as a hostname and tries to resolve it with DNS. The delay looks like this:

    S1#shwo run
Translating "shwo"...domain server (255.255.255.255)
% Unknown command or computer name, or unable to find computer address

    no ip domain-lookup is standard in ITN labs and does not affect SSH. If the task configures a DNS server on the router or switch (ip name-server), check whether it also expects lookups to stay on.

    #Undo a command with no

    Put no in front of almost any configuration command to remove it. Run each in the mode where the original command was entered.

    Mode Command Removes
    (config)# no banner motd The MOTD banner
    (config)# no username <username> A local user account
    (config)# no enable password The plaintext enable password (keeps enable secret)
    (config-if)# no ip address The interface IP
    (config-if)# no shutdown The shutdown state (turns the interface on)
    (config-line)# no password The line password

    #Run EXEC commands from config mode with do

    In any configuration mode, put do in front of an EXEC command to run it without leaving configuration mode:

    do show ip interface brief

    do show running-config

    do write memory

    #IOS error messages and what they mean

    Message Meaning Fix
    % Invalid input detected at '^' marker. The command is wrong at the caret, you are in the wrong mode, or PT does not support it Check spelling at the ^; check the prompt ((config)# or #?); try do; try ?
    % Incomplete command. A required keyword or value is missing Press Up arrow, add a space and ?
    % Ambiguous command: "s" The abbreviation matches more than one command Type more letters
    % Unknown command or computer name... Typo in EXEC mode, treated as a hostname Retype; set no ip domain-lookup
    % Please define a hostname other than Switch. RSA key generation needs a non-default hostname hostname <hostname>
    % Please define a domain-name first. RSA key generation needs a domain name ip domain-name <domain-name>
    % Password too short - must be at least N characters. security passwords min-length is set Use a longer password, or recheck the instructions
    % Login invalid Wrong username or password with login local Check case; check the username line in show running-config
    % Bad passwords Three wrong enable or line passwords Retry; check case

    #Questions IOS may ask

    Prompt Answer
    Would you like to enter the initial configuration dialog? [yes/no]: no
    Would you like to terminate autoinstall? [yes]: Press Enter
    Press RETURN to get started! Click in the CLI window and press Enter
    Destination filename [startup-config]? Press Enter
    Proceed with reload? [confirm] Press Enter only if you mean it
    System configuration has been modified. Save? [yes/no]: yes to keep your changes, no if you are deliberately starting over
    PreviousPacket Tracer interface tourNextInitial switch configuration
    PT

    Initial switch configuration

    jump:pt-basic-switch

    Fast path

    1. From the Switch> prompt, enter global configuration mode:

      enable
configure terminal

    2. Set the hostname, stop DNS lookups and set the privileged EXEC password:

      hostname <hostname>
no ip domain-lookup
enable secret <enable-secret>

    3. Set the console and vty passwords:

      line console 0
password <console-password>
login
line vty 0 15
password <vty-password>
login
exit

    4. Encrypt plaintext passwords and add the banner:

      service password-encryption
banner motd #<banner-text>#

    5. Give the switch its management IP and default gateway:

      interface vlan 1
ip address <ip-address> <subnet-mask>
no shutdown
exit
ip default-gateway <default-gateway>

    6. Return to privileged EXEC and save:

      end
write memory

    This is the ITN Module 2 sequence. The same lines as one pasteable block are in the simple passwords template. For SSH, local users and other hardening, see securing device access.

    #Set the hostname

    In global configuration mode:

    hostname <hostname>

    The prompt changes immediately (for example S1(config)#). Hostnames start with a letter, contain no spaces, and are graded case-sensitively.

    #Choose enable secret or enable password

    Command Stored as Notes
    enable secret <enable-secret> Hashed (enable secret 5 $1$... in PT) Preferred. Wins if both are configured
    enable password <password> Plaintext, or type 7 after service password-encryption Legacy. Configure only if the task says "enable password"

    Use the one the task names

    "Encrypted privileged EXEC password" or "enable secret" means enable secret. "Enable password" means enable password. If both are asked, configure both with the given values. IOS warns when the two are identical, so check show running-config that both lines are there.

    To remove an insecure plaintext enable password while keeping the secret, in global configuration mode:

    no enable password

    #Set console and vty line passwords

    In global configuration mode:

    line console 0
password <console-password>
login
line vty 0 15
password <vty-password>
login
end
    • login makes the line ask for the password. A password without login is not enforced.
    • 2960 switches have vty lines 0 to 15, and line vty 0 15 configures all of them. Routers usually show line vty 0 4 (router differences).
    • If the task asks for usernames instead of line passwords, use login local with a username (local users).

    #Encrypt plaintext passwords

    In global configuration mode:

    service password-encryption

    This encrypts every current and future plaintext password in the config (console, vty, enable password, username ... password) with weak type 7. enable secret and username ... secret are already hashed and are unaffected.

    Verify

    show running-config shows password 7 0822455D0A16 style lines under line con 0 and line vty 0 4, and enable secret 5 $1$....

    #Set the MOTD banner and pick a delimiter

    In global configuration mode:

    banner motd #<banner-text>#
    • The first character after motd is the delimiter. Everything up to the next copy of that character is the banner.
    • The banner text cannot contain the delimiter. If the text has a #, use a character that is not in the text, such as $, % or ^:
    banner motd $<banner-text>$
    • For a multi-line banner, type the delimiter, press Enter, type the lines, then end with the delimiter on its own line. The session looks like this:
    S1(config)#banner motd #
Enter TEXT message.  End with the character '#'.
Authorized Access Only!
Violators will be prosecuted.
#
    • show running-config displays the banner as banner motd ^CAuthorized Access Only!^C. The ^C is how IOS stores the delimiter, whatever character you typed.
    • Remove a banner with no banner motd.

    Banner text must match exactly

    Do not put spaces between the delimiter and the text unless the instructions show them; # Text # stores the leading and trailing spaces. If the instructions put the banner in quotation marks, the quotes usually only mark the text, so leave them out unless the task clearly includes them.

    #Set the switch management IP on interface vlan 1

    In global configuration mode:

    interface vlan 1
ip address <ip-address> <subnet-mask>
no shutdown
exit
    • A Layer 2 switch has one management IP, on a switch virtual interface (SVI). Physical switch ports such as Fa0/1 do not get IP addresses.
    • interface vlan 1 is administratively down by default, so no shutdown is required.
    • The SVI becomes up/up only when at least one port in VLAN 1 is connected and up. On a switch with no cables it stays up/down, which is expected.
    • If the task names another management VLAN (for example VLAN 99), use interface vlan 99. That VLAN must exist and have an active port.

    #Set the default gateway on a switch

    In global configuration mode (not interface mode):

    ip default-gateway <default-gateway>

    The switch needs this to answer devices on other networks (remote SSH or Telnet, pings from another subnet). Use the router interface IP in the same subnet as the SVI. It does not affect traffic passing through the switch.

    On a Layer 3 switch (3650) with ip routing turned on, IOS ignores ip default-gateway; that switch needs a default route instead (static routes).

    #Add interface descriptions

    In global configuration mode, for each interface the task names:

    interface <interface>
description <description>
exit

    Descriptions are free text and are graded exactly as typed when the task asks for them.

    #Shut down unused ports

    In global configuration mode:

    interface range <interface-range>
shutdown

    Check which ports are in use first with show interfaces status (status connected). Never shut a port a cable uses. Range syntax and port security are in securing device access.

    #Save the configuration

    In privileged EXEC mode:

    write memory

    copy running-config startup-config does the same but asks for a filename first. Typed by hand, it looks like this (press Enter at the question):

    S1#copy running-config startup-config
Destination filename [startup-config]?
Building configuration...
[OK]

    From configuration mode, use do write memory.

    Config Where Survives reload?
    running-config RAM No
    startup-config NVRAM Yes

    Unsaved means lost

    A reload, power cycle, module change or Power Cycle Devices wipes anything not saved, and some graded items check startup-config. Save every device before you leave it.

    #Verify the switch

    In privileged EXEC mode:

    show ip interface brief

    show running-config

    show startup-config

    What correct looks like

    show ip interface brief shows a line like Vlan1 192.168.1.2 YES manual up up. show running-config shows hostname, enable secret 5 ..., banner motd ^C...^C, line con 0 with password 7 ... and login, ip default-gateway, and service password-encryption. A PC in the same subnet can ping the SVI address.

    #Reset a switch to start over

    Only do this if the task allows it and the config is beyond repair. Fixing individual lines with no commands is usually faster. Type these by hand in privileged EXEC mode, one at a time:

    erase startup-config

    reload

    Press Enter at each [confirm]. If asked System configuration has been modified. Save? [yes/no]:, answer no, or the bad config is saved again. VLANs are stored separately in flash:vlan.dat; to remove them too, run delete flash:vlan.dat before reload.

    PreviousIOS CLI basics and modesNextSecuring device access and SSH
    PT

    Securing device access and SSH

    jump:pt-security

    Create the username before login local

    login local on the console with no username configured locks you out of the console as soon as you log out. Create the user first.

    Fast path

    1. From privileged EXEC, enter global configuration mode and set the minimum password length before any other password:

      configure terminal
security passwords min-length <min-length>

    2. Set the enable secret and encrypt plaintext passwords:

      enable secret <enable-secret>
service password-encryption

    3. Create the local admin account:

      username <admin-username> secret <admin-password>

    4. Generate RSA keys and turn on SSH version 2 (hostname must already be set):

      ip domain-name <domain-name>
crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 1024
ip ssh version 2

    5. Allow only SSH on the vty lines with local login (use 0 4 on a router if 0 15 is rejected):

      line vty 0 15
transport input ssh
login local
exec-timeout <timeout-minutes> 0
exit

    6. Add the idle timeout on the console and block brute-force logins:

      line console 0
exec-timeout <timeout-minutes> 0
exit
login block-for <block-seconds> attempts <attempts> within <within-seconds>

    7. Save and check SSH:

      end
write memory
show ip ssh

    The same steps as pasteable blocks are in the secure switch template and the secure router template. For a list of everything CyberPatriot tends to score on Cisco devices, see the hardening checklist.

    #Set a minimum password length

    In global configuration mode:

    security passwords min-length <min-length>
    • Any new password shorter than the value is rejected with % Password too short. This applies to the enable secret, line passwords and usernames.
    • Passwords already configured are not checked, so set this first.
    • The accepted range is 0 to 16.

    #Block brute-force logins with login block-for

    In global configuration mode:

    login block-for <block-seconds> attempts <attempts> within <within-seconds>

    Example: login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60 means "if 3 logins fail within 60 seconds, block all Telnet and SSH logins for 120 seconds". Read the three numbers from the task carefully; the order is block time, attempts, window.

    If a 2960 in your PT version rejects the command with % Invalid input, that model does not support it. Skip it unless the task explicitly requires it on that switch.

    Verify

    show running-config | include login block shows the line. show login also shows the settings and whether the device is in quiet mode, on versions that support it.

    #Set exec-timeout and logging synchronous

    In global configuration mode:

    line console 0
exec-timeout <timeout-minutes> 0
logging synchronous
line vty 0 15
exec-timeout <timeout-minutes> 0
exit
    • exec-timeout <minutes> <seconds> logs out an idle session. 5 0 is 5 minutes. 0 0 disables the timeout and is insecure; never set it unless told to.
    • logging synchronous stops console log messages from breaking up what you are typing. It is not a security setting, but tasks often list it.

    #Use local usernames with login local

    In global configuration mode:

    username <admin-username> secret <admin-password>
line vty 0 15
login local
exit
    Line command Authenticates with
    login The line's own password
    login local A username and secret from the local database
    login with no password set vty refuses connections (Password required, but none set)
    no login Nothing at all (insecure; never configure unless told)
    • username <admin-username> secret <admin-password> stores a hash. username ... password ... stores plaintext (type 7 after service password-encryption). Use secret unless told otherwise.
    • username <admin-username> privilege 15 secret <admin-password> logs the user straight into privileged EXEC. Add privilege 15 only if the task asks.
    • Remove an unauthorized or default account with no username <username>.

    #Configure SSH step by step

    Every step is required. Missing any one makes SSH fail.

    Step Command Why
    1 hostname <hostname> RSA keys need a hostname other than the default Router or Switch
    2 ip domain-name <domain-name> The key name is built from hostname and domain
    3 crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 1024 Creates the keys and enables SSH
    4 ip ssh version 2 Allows only SSH version 2 (needs a key of at least 768 bits)
    5 username <admin-username> secret <admin-password> The account to log in with
    6 line vty 0 15, transport input ssh, login local Allow only SSH, authenticate with the local account

    In global configuration mode:

    hostname <hostname>
ip domain-name <domain-name>
crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 1024
ip ssh version 2
username <admin-username> secret <admin-password>
line vty 0 15
transport input ssh
login local
end
write memory

    Key generation prints something like this (example names R1 and ccna-lab.com):

    The name for the keys will be: R1.ccna-lab.com
% The key modulus size is 1024 bits
% Generating 1024 bit RSA keys, keys will be non-exportable...[OK]
%SSH-5-ENABLED: SSH 1.99 has been enabled
    • If you type only crypto key generate rsa, IOS asks How many bits in the modulus [512]:. Type 1024, or 2048 if the task says so. A 512-bit key does not allow SSH version 2.
    • Use line vty 0 4 on a router whose vty range ends at 4. Check the range with line vty 0 ?.
    • Some tasks also list ip ssh time-out 60 and ip ssh authentication-retries 2 (global configuration).
    • A switch needs a working management IP (SVI up, plus ip default-gateway for remote subnets) before SSH can reach it.

    #Choose the transport input setting

    Command Allows
